horseshoe-crab.context_blurb: The horseshoe crab is a round, armored, almost helmet-shaped marine arthropod that lives in shallow water along the Atlantic coasts of North America and the Gulf and coasts of parts of Asia. It is not a true crab; it is more closely related to spiders and scorpions, and its lineage goes back more than 450 million years. Horseshoe crabs come ashore in huge spawning groups every spring. Modern medicine depends on them in a way most people never hear about.

mantis-shrimp.context_blurb: The mantis shrimp is a long, colorful marine crustacean that lives in warm shallow seas, mostly in burrows it digs in the sand. Despite the name, it is not a shrimp but belongs to its own ancient group called stomatopods. Mantis shrimp are famous for two things: a pair of hunting arms that strike with astonishing speed, and some of the most unusual eyes in the whole animal kingdom. Scientists keep updating what they think the shrimp can actually do with those eyes.

mudskipper.context_blurb:
When the tide drains out of tropical mangrove swamps and mudflats in Africa, Asia and parts of Australia, it leaves wide stretches of glistening mud. Most fish would be stranded. The mudskipper is just getting started: a bulgy-eyed fish that walks, leaps, fights and courts in the open air.

The mudskipper is a true fish, finger-length, yet it spends most of its life out of water, hauling itself over the mud instead of swimming.

To walk, it plants its two muscular pectoral fins like a pair of crutches and drags its body forward across the mud. When it needs speed, it changes gait. A sudden flex and push of its tail flings it through the air in a leap of up to about 61 centimeters, roughly two feet, and that skip is where the mudskipper gets its name.

Life in the air brings two problems: breathing and staying wet. Gills work poorly out of water. So, like a frog, the mudskipper absorbs air through its damp skin and through the moist lining inside its mouth and throat. Before a long trek across the mud, it fills its enlarged gill chambers with a mouthful of water and air, puffing out its cheeks like a scuba diver's tank, because if its gills dry out it can no longer take in oxygen. A male defends his patch of mud with a wild show: he rears up in push-ups, flares the fin on his back, beats his tail and leaps high. The display does double duty, warning rival males away while also showing off to impress females.

A mudskipper father's real masterpiece is underground. In tropical Asia, a male hollows out a burrow whose arched roof holds a pocket of air, then makes trip after trip to the surface to gulp air and carry it down; the biologist Karen Martin found that he may need about 100 mouthfuls to build that first air bubble for his eggs. For days he keeps the chamber stocked while he watches the tide. When the moment is right, he swallows the trapped air out of the chamber and lets the rising sea pour in, so the eggs can hatch and the larvae swim off to sea. Martin called him "really a very good papa."

nautilus.context_blurb: The nautilus is a deep-sea cephalopod from the warm waters of the western Pacific. Unlike octopuses, squid, and cuttlefish, it has kept the external shell that its ancestors wore for hundreds of millions of years. The shell is a beautiful coiled spiral divided into gas-filled chambers, which lets the nautilus float and sink without burning energy. Nautilus bodies also keep features that other cephalopods have lost, which is why biologists keep returning to it as a window into cephalopod history.

ocean-sunfish-mola.context_blurb: The ocean sunfish, also called the mola, is a huge, round, nearly tailless fish of the open ocean. Adults can weigh over a ton, which makes them the heaviest bony fish in the world. They drift on their sides at the surface, dive deep after jellyfish, and are often covered in parasites they clean off in a strange social arrangement with other animals. Despite their size, molas start life as microscopic larvae that are nothing like the adults, and the transformation between the two stages is one of the biggest size jumps in all of vertebrate biology.

octopus.context_blurb: The octopus is a soft-bodied cephalopod found in every ocean on Earth, from tide pools to the deep sea. It has eight arms covered in sensitive, grippy suckers, three hearts, and a nervous system split between a central brain and the arms themselves. Octopuses solve problems, open jars, remember individual humans, and change their skin in ways that make them one of the clearest cases of intelligence outside of vertebrates. Scientists study them to understand how a mind so different from ours can work at all.

pistol-shrimp.context_blurb: The pistol shrimp is a small marine crustacean that lives in warm, shallow seas around the world. It has one normal pincer and one enormous one, and it uses the big one as a weapon in a way that would be hard to believe without high-speed video. Pistol shrimp also share burrows with gobies in one of the ocean's clearest examples of two unrelated species living together to each other's benefit.

portuguese-man-o-war.context_blurb: The Portuguese man o' war looks like a jellyfish but is actually something much stranger: an entire colony of specialized animals that live and work together as one unit. It drifts on the surface of warm ocean currents, especially the Atlantic and Pacific trade-wind zones, under a glassy, blue-tinted gas-filled float. Beneath the float trail long stinging tentacles that paralyze fish. The sting is painful to humans but almost never fatal; the man o' war's real trick is a kind of cooperation most animals cannot pull off.

sea-cucumber.context_blurb: The sea cucumber is a sausage-shaped marine invertebrate that lives on the sea floor in every ocean, from shallow reefs down into the deep abyss. Despite its soft, slow look, it is an echinoderm, a cousin of sea stars and sea urchins. The sea cucumber feeds by vacuuming up sand or filtering water, and when threatened it has a bizarre and genuinely weird defensive move that most people, on seeing it the first time, have trouble believing is real.

sea-star.context_blurb: The sea star, sometimes called the starfish, is a radially symmetric marine animal that lives in oceans worldwide, from shallow tide pools to the deep sea. It is not a fish at all; it is an echinoderm, a cousin of sea urchins, sand dollars, and sea cucumbers. Sea stars have no brain and no blood in the usual sense. They move, feed, and heal using a surprising hydraulic system under their skin and a few other tricks that biologists have been peeling apart for over a hundred years.

seahorse.context_blurb: The seahorse is a small, upright-swimming fish that lives in shallow, warm, seagrass-filled waters around much of the world. It has a horse-shaped head, a prehensile tail that grips weeds like a monkey's, and a cluster of body-plan features that make it one of the strangest fish on Earth. Everything about the seahorse is slow and precise, from how it feeds to how it reproduces. The male and female of a pair tend to stay together for a long time.

whale-shark.context_blurb: The whale shark is the biggest fish in the ocean, a slow, spotted shark that can grow more than 40 feet long. It lives in warm seas around the world and is a specialist on some of the smallest food in the sea. Whale sharks gather in a few predictable places each year, which is where researchers and tourists go to see them. The entire body of this huge animal is built around that one specialized meal, and biologists are still learning where they go when they leave the known gathering sites.

beaver.context_blurb:
The beaver, a hefty rodent with a paddle of a tail, lives along the streams and rivers of North America and Eurasia. Few animals reshape their world as it does: it fells trees, dams streams into ponds and turns ponds into wet meadows. Its waterproof fur, scaly tail and strange teeth all serve that life between land and water.

Its front teeth are bright orange, because the outer enamel is packed with iron instead of the magnesium found in most animal teeth, which makes them harder and more resistant to acid and decay. Those teeth keep growing for life: new tooth forms at the root as fast as the tip wears away, so even an old beaver has a working set and must gnaw constantly. Its home, a dome of mud and sticks called a lodge, has its entrance underwater, so a beaver family gets in by diving while a fox or wolf on the bank cannot follow. The dam floods a safe moat all around the home.

The iron-hard enamel coats only the front face of each incisor, while the softer dentin behind it wears away faster, so every bite grinds the tooth back into a sharp chisel edge and the teeth sharpen themselves. Underwater a beaver keeps its eyes open behind a see-through third eyelid that slides across each eye like built-in swim goggles. Its broad, flat, scaly tail is a rudder for steering, and when danger appears, the beaver slaps it hard on the water with a loud crack that warns the whole colony.

In autumn it stocks an underwater larder of branches for winter, and before diving with a branch in its teeth it seals itself shut: valve-like muscles close its nostrils and ears, and its lips seal behind the jutting front teeth, so it can carry wood underwater for up to about 15 minutes without swallowing water.

Beavers also build big: in Canada's Wood Buffalo National Park, generations of beaver families raised a dam about 800 meters long, as long as eight football fields, and in 2007 the researcher Jean Thie spotted it in satellite images. It is the largest beaver dam known, and today conservationists use beavers as ecosystem engineers to restore damaged land.

camel.context_blurb:
The camel is a long-legged desert mammal of North Africa, the Middle East and Central Asia. People have ridden and loaded camels for thousands of years, but the animal's own biology is the real marvel. Nearly every part of its body solves a single problem: staying alive where water is scarce and the heat is fierce.

The one-humped dromedary is the hot-desert specialist, while the Bactrian camel, with two humps and a thick coat, belongs to the cold Gobi of Central Asia, where a single year swings from roughly -20°F to 120°F. On loose sand, each broad, two-toed foot spreads and flattens under the camel's weight and then pulls in as it lifts, working like a snowshoe that keeps it from sinking where a horse's narrow hooves would bog down.

Contrary to popular belief, the hump holds no water: it is a concentrated store of fat that the camel burns when food runs short, which is why a hungry camel's hump shrinks and flops to one side. Packing the fat into one hump, rather than under all its skin, also helps the rest of the body shed heat. A camel can even chew up a spiny cactus, because cone-shaped bumps of keratin lining its mouth turn the needles so they slide down its throat point-first. A vet described those bumps as feeling almost like plastic.

A badly dehydrated camel can drink well over 100 liters in about ten minutes, up to 145 liters at one go by the San Diego Zoo's count, replacing about a third of its body weight almost at once. Instead of sweating away precious water, a camel lets its body temperature swing, cooling to about 34 to 35°C overnight and climbing to 41 or 42°C by day, storing the heat in its body rather than spending water to shed it.

cheetah.context_blurb:
On the dry grasslands of Africa, with a last small population in Iran, lives a slender spotted cat built for one thing: the sprint. The cheetah lacks the bulk other big cats use to wrestle prey or climb, and nearly every part of it, inside and out, serves the chase.

No land animal is faster than the cheetah: from a standstill it can top 110 kilometers an hour, about 70 miles an hour, barely three seconds later, out-accelerating many sports cars. Small black spots cover its golden coat, and the pattern they make, together with the rings on its tail, is unique to each cheetah, like a human fingerprint, so researchers can tell individuals apart from photographs.

A cheetah cannot roar. It purrs, growls, hisses and stutters. A mother calling her cubs out of the tall grass uses a high, birdlike chirp. Other cats keep sharp claws tucked away until they strike, but a cheetah's claws are blunt and only partly retractable, poking out like a dog's so they dig into the dirt with every stride, the way spikes grip on a sprinter's shoes. Ridged paw pads add grip like tire tread.

The black 'tear marks' running from the inside of each eye down to the mouth soak up the sun's glare off its cheeks, like an athlete's eye-black, so it can keep prey in sharp focus on the bright plains. Its unusually flexible spine coils and springs open with every bound, flinging its hind feet out ahead of its front ones. At full gallop it is airborne twice per stride, once stretched out and once bunched up. When a gazelle jinks sideways, the cheetah swings its long tail as a counterweight to shift its balance, with the flattened, ringed tip working as a rudder, so it can take hairpin turns that would send other animals tumbling.

All that speed has a price. A sprint devours oxygen, so the cheetah gulps air through enlarged nostrils that open into roomy, air-filled sinuses, its breathing leaping from about 60 breaths a minute to around 150, fed by an oversized heart and lungs. Even so, top speed lasts only seconds. Its muscles burn fuel faster than oxygen arrives, lactic acid floods them, and the cat runs out of energy, which is why it must catch its prey within about 30 seconds or give up.

When five wild Botswana cheetahs wore GPS-and-motion collars, they did hit 93 kilometers an hour, but most hunts were run at a moderate pace and won by footwork: a firm grip, sharp maneuvering, and the muscle power to brake hard and turn. During the ice age, North America was home to a lean, spotted sprinter called Miracinonyx, long counted as an 'American cheetah.' Genetic and skeletal studies showed it was really a close relative of the cougar that evolved the same fast-chasing body independently, a textbook case of convergent evolution. In 1985 Stephen O'Brien's team grafted skin between fourteen unrelated cheetahs. A graft between unrelated lions is rejected as foreign, yet all fourteen healed in, as if they had passed between identical twins. A severe population bottleneck in the species' recent past left cheetahs so nearly identical at the genes the immune system uses to tell self from stranger that one cat's skin reads to another as its own. Wild-born cheetahs are just as uniform, so zoo breeding is not the cause.

echidna.context_blurb:
The echidna is a spiny, short-legged mammal of Australia and New Guinea that shuffles through the bush digging for ants and termites. It looks a little like a hedgehog, but it belongs to one of the oldest and strangest branches of the mammal family, and its snout carries a sense that almost no other land animal has.

Nearly every mammal gives birth to live young, but five living species, the monotremes, lay eggs instead. The platypus is one of them, and the other four are echidnas, the only other egg-laying mammals on Earth.

Its spines look like a porcupine's quills, but each one is a stiff, overgrown hair made of keratin, the same protein as your hair and fingernails. They grow up to about 12.7 centimeters long. The common short-beaked echidna lives across Australia, while three larger long-beaked echidnas survive only on the island of New Guinea, to Australia's north. A mother echidna produces just one leathery, grape-sized egg and carries it in a pouch-like fold of skin on her underside. After roughly ten days a tiny, pink, jellybean-shaped baby hatches out, and a baby echidna is called a puggle.

The echidna has no teeth. It tears open an ant or termite nest with its strong front claws. Then it flicks out a long, sticky tongue, up to about 18 centimeters long and coated with gluey mucus, to snatch up the insects as they pour out. It is far too slow to run from a dingo. Caught on soft ground, it digs straight down where it stands until only a shield of sharp spines is left showing.

Its snout hides a sixth sense. Like a shark or a ray, an echidna can feel the faint electric signals given off by the muscles of living prey. About 400 electroreceptors in its snout let it home in on ants and termites hidden in their nests, out of sight and smell.

elephant.context_blurb:
Elephants are the largest animals on land. There are three living species, the African savanna, the African forest and the Asian elephant, and all of them live in close family groups led by an older female. Their trunks, ears, feet and even their genes hold surprises that scientists are still uncovering.

The African elephant is the biggest land animal alive, and the record is a bull shot in Angola in 1955 that stood about 13 feet at the shoulder and weighed an estimated 10 tonnes or more. Mounted and nicknamed Henry, it still stands in the Smithsonian. Keeping such a huge body cool under the sun is hard work. When fanning its ears is not enough, an elephant sprays water or wet sand over itself, or plasters sticky mud over its hide and behind its ears to cool down and block the sun.

The trunk is a muscular hydrostat, like your tongue or an octopus's arm: it holds no bone at all, only muscle, tens of thousands of muscle units, which is why the same limb can be brutally strong and delicately precise. The huge, thin ears are radiators. Large blood vessels run just under the skin, and as the elephant fans its ears, the blood flowing through them cools by 3 to 5 degrees Celsius before it returns to the body. In about 20 minutes an elephant can cool its whole blood supply this way. You can even tell the species apart by the tip of the trunk, because an African elephant's ends in two finger-like lips and an Asian elephant's in just one.

Tusks are not horns but overgrown incisor teeth that never stop growing, adding about 6 to 7 inches a year, and the longest pair on record measured more than 11 feet. The tip of the trunk is laced with hair-thin muscle bundles, so with no bone or joint anywhere, the same trunk that shoves over a tree can curl around one blade of grass and pick it up. Memory matters as much as strength. Each herd is led by its matriarch, the oldest female, whose memory of distant water can save the family in a drought. In Kenya's Amboseli during the severe drought of 2009, families with older matriarchs lost far fewer calves than those with younger leaders.

Elephants drink by pulling several liters of water up into the trunk and then pouring it into the mouth. One study clocked the water rushing up inside the trunk at up to 330 miles per hour. They also talk in voices we cannot hear. In 1984 Katy Payne was visiting the elephants at a zoo when she sensed a pulsing in the air but could hear nothing: the elephants were calling in infrasound, rumbles of about 14 to 35 hertz, too low for human ears, which carry for miles. Elephants respond strikingly to their dead. In Kenya, Namibia and Tanzania, scientists have seen herds gather quietly around the body of an elephant they knew, touch it with their trunks, and return to the bones for years. Researchers describe this as observed behavior, not proof of human-style grief.

Elephants can also listen through the ground: their rumbles travel through the earth as seismic waves, and Caitlin O'Connell-Rodwell's buried-speaker experiments at the Mushara waterhole showed that elephants pick up those vibrations with their feet. An alarm call played underground made a herd bunch together and freeze. Big bodies have trillions of cells and many chances for cancer, yet elephants rarely get it. Vincent Lynch found one reason: a broken, long-dead copy of a gene called LIF6, which the elephant line switched back on, so this reawakened "zombie" gene now makes a cell with damaged DNA destroy itself before it can become a tumor. An elephant appears to walk on five toes. CT scans made by John Hutchinson's team revealed a hidden extra support buried in the fat of the heel: a giant sesamoid bone that acts as a false sixth toe, propping up the foot like a stiletto heel. Museum preparers cut it off for centuries without realizing what it was.

giraffe.context_blurb:
The giraffe is a long-legged, long-necked plant-eater of the African savannas and woodlands, and the tallest living animal. Almost everything about its body, from its tongue to its heart to the skin on its legs, is shaped by the problem of being so tall.

Browsing at the crowns of acacia trees, where no other plant-eater can reach, the giraffe lifts its head as high as 5.5 meters, about 18 feet, and a big male is the tallest animal on Earth. A mother gives birth standing up, so her calf drops nearly 2 meters to the ground. The newborn is already about 1.8 meters tall, as tall as a grown man, and it can stand within about half an hour and run within an hour.

The giraffe's neck is about 2 meters long, yet it holds the same number of bones as yours, seven, and each of them is simply enormous, up to about 25 centimeters long. To pull down leaves, a giraffe snakes out its tongue, 45 to 50 centimeters long, and curls it around a twig like a hand to strip the leaves into its mouth.

The tongue is dark blue-black, and scientists think the dark pigment works as sunscreen, shielding it from sunburn as it hangs out in the blazing sun all day. Acacia branches bristle with thorns, but the giraffe's tongue is armored with tough bumps and coated in thick, sticky saliva, so it strips the leaves without getting hurt. Male giraffes settle rivalries by necking: they whip their necks around like sledgehammers and slam their heads into each other, with blows estimated at more than a ton of force.

Their duels are oddly honorable. Each giraffe swings as a lefty or a righty, and rivals respect each other's side. Researchers found that a giraffe will not strike a rival who has lost his balance. People assume such a tall animal needs a giant heart, but a 2016 study found the giraffe's heart is an ordinary 0.5 percent of its body mass. Its secret is the left chamber, walled with dense muscle 2 to 3.5 centimeters thick that generates the high pressure needed to push blood up the neck, and because that thick wall leaves only a small cavity, the heart makes up for it by beating fast.

Lowering its head to drink should send high-pressure blood surging into its brain. A sponge-like web of blood vessels where the neck meets the skull, the rete mirabile, soaks up the surge before it reaches the brain. When it swings its head back up, blood should pool in its legs, but tight, inelastic skin around the lower legs squeezes the veins like a compression stocking, so the giraffe does not faint.

Even the purpose of the famous neck is debated. Since Darwin's day it has been explained as a way to reach leaves no rival can. In 2022 a 17-million-year-old giraffe relative from China, Discokeryx, revived a rival idea: it had a helmet-like disc of bone on its head and the most reinforced head-and-neck joints known in any animal, built for ferocious head-butting duels. That fossil supports the idea that the neck was shaped as a weapon in battles over mates, though both pressures may have worked together.

gray-wolf.context_blurb:
The gray wolf is the largest wild member of the dog family, a hunter of forests, tundra and mountains across the northern half of the world. Wolves live and hunt as a team, run down prey bigger than themselves, and, as Yellowstone National Park has shown, can reshape a whole landscape.

A wolf pack is a family: a mother and father, the breeding pair, with the young they have raised over the last few years. A family spread over a huge territory needs a long-range voice. On the open Arctic tundra, with no trees to muffle it, one wolf's howl carries about 10 miles; in forest, about 6.

Wolves howl to gather the pack before and after a hunt, to find each other when a storm scatters them, and to warn neighboring packs off their territory. They hunt by endurance rather than speed; a fit deer wins a short dash. Trotting at about 5 miles an hour for hours, a wolf tracking prey can cover more than 50 miles in a day, and one was seen chasing a deer for 12 miles.

Seven or eight wolves facing a hundred elk cannot just charge in. Instead the pack works to cut one animal away from the group, testing many, since most hunts of big hoofed prey fail; an elk that stands its ground is often left alone, while one that runs or seems weak becomes the target. For decades people pictured an 'alpha wolf' that fought its way to the top. L. David Mech, the biologist whose 1970 book spread that idea, corrected himself in 1999: the alpha picture came from captive strangers thrown together, and in a wild pack the wolves the others follow are just the parents. The whole pack helps raise the pups: babysitters guard the den, and when the hunters return, the pups lick at their mouths and the adults regurgitate meat they swallowed at the kill for pups too small for raw meat.

When gray wolves returned to Yellowstone in 1995 after about 70 years away, elk stopped lingering in the exposed valleys along the streams, and the willow and aspen they had chewed down began to grow tall again. Taller willows brought beavers back to build dams, a chain scientists call a trophic cascade. Researchers caution that the effect, though real, is sometimes overstated, since drought, bears and human hunters also thinned the elk.

hippopotamus.context_blurb:
The hippopotamus is a barrel-shaped giant of three tons or more that wallows in African waters from the Nile to the Zambezi. Its name means 'river horse,' but it is no horse. It spends its days in the water and comes out at dusk to graze.

The hippopotamus eats nothing but grass, yet it kills an estimated 500 or more people in Africa each year, more than lions or sharks do. It does not hunt people; its danger lies in its temper and its sheer bulk.

A hippo is too dense to float, so it cannot really swim; to cross deep water it strides along the river floor, kicking off the bed in a slow-motion underwater gallop with its toes barely touching down.

Scientists once grouped the hippo with pigs because of its molars, but blood-protein and DNA evidence showed that its closest living relatives are the whales and dolphins. The two lines probably split from a shared, water-loving ancestor about 55 million years ago. When a hippo flings its mouth open almost flat, nearly 150 degrees from jaw to jaw, it is not yawning but warning a rival. The gape shows off its real weapons: tusk-shaped canine teeth that keep growing all its life, reaching about 50 centimeters, kept sharp by grinding against the lower incisors.

honey-badger.context_blurb:
The honey badger, Mellivora capensis, is a stocky, low-slung, thickly muscled carnivore of Africa, the Middle East and South Asia, more like an oversized weasel than a true badger. It weighs only about 9 to 16 kilograms, yet it has a reputation as one of the toughest animals alive.

Black with a pale back and no bigger than a small dog, the honey badger is listed by Guinness as the most fearless animal on Earth, because instead of fleeing lions or leopards it stands its ground and drives them off. It is also one of the best diggers among animals. With long, pick-like front claws, it can dig a fresh burrow into sun-baked ground in about 10 minutes. Its hide is part of its armor: the skin on its neck is about 6 millimeters thick, a quarter of an inch, and so tough and rubbery that bee stings, porcupine quills and even machete blows barely hurt it.

In the Kalahari, Colleen and Keith Begg, who spent years following wild honey badgers, saw a puff adder strike a hunting badger in the face. The badger went into convulsions and lay motionless for roughly two hours, then woke up, got up and went back to finish eating the snake that had bitten it. Part of its resistance is in its genes. Cobra venom works by grabbing a receptor on muscle cells. In the honey badger, a charged amino acid has been swapped into the receptor's binding site, so the venom cannot attach. Pigs and hedgehogs evolved almost the same change on their own.

kangaroo.context_blurb: The kangaroo is a group of large marsupials that live in Australia, where they are the dominant native grazer. The biggest, the red kangaroo, can top six feet standing up. Kangaroos travel using one of the most efficient movement systems any big animal has ever evolved, and they also do things related to reproduction and group life that no placental mammal matches. They are now so numerous in parts of the Australian outback that they are managed as both an icon and a problem.

koala.context_blurb: The koala is a small, grey, pouched tree-climbing marsupial that lives in the eucalyptus forests of eastern Australia. It is one of the pickiest eaters in the mammal world, surviving almost entirely on a single kind of plant that is tough, oily, and mildly poisonous. Koalas spend most of the day asleep because that diet gives so little energy. The animal is a specialist in every sense, from its gut to its paws to the slow rhythm of its day, and it is now listed as endangered in some Australian states after years of habitat loss and fire.

naked-mole-rat.context_blurb: The naked mole-rat is a small, pink, nearly hairless rodent that lives in long underground tunnels in the dry grasslands of East Africa. It looks almost like a wrinkled little sausage with teeth. The naked mole-rat is extraordinary among mammals for its social life, which is organized more like a bee colony than like a rodent nest. It is also extraordinary for how long it lives, how little it ages, and how it handles conditions that would kill almost any other mammal. Biomedical researchers study it closely for exactly these reasons.

pangolin.context_blurb: The pangolin is a scale-covered mammal that lives in Africa and across much of South and Southeast Asia. It is sometimes called a scaly anteater, but it is not closely related to anteaters at all; it belongs to its own order of mammals. Pangolins eat almost nothing except ants and termites, which they lap up with a tongue that is extraordinary even by the standards of ant-eaters. They are now the most trafficked mammal in the world because of demand for their scales, and every living species is at serious risk.

platypus.context_blurb: The platypus is a small, duck-billed, beaver-tailed mammal that lives in the freshwater streams and rivers of eastern Australia. When the first platypus specimen reached European naturalists in 1799, many assumed it was a fake. The platypus is a monotreme, one of only two mammal groups still laying eggs, and it has an unusually long list of features that no other living mammal shares. It swims with its eyes shut, finds prey with senses other mammals do not have, and the males carry a weapon unique among furred animals.

polar-bear.context_blurb:
The polar bear lives on the frozen sea of the Arctic, from Alaska and northern Canada through Greenland to the Russian coast. Its scientific name, Ursus maritimus, means 'sea bear,' and it earns it, hunting seals from the ice and swimming between floes. Almost everything about its body is built for cold.

The polar bear is the biggest bear alive and the heaviest meat-eater on land: a big male can weigh up to 800 kilograms, about 1,760 pounds, and rise nearly ten feet tall on his hind legs. Its signature hunting method takes patience, not speed. In still-hunting, the bear finds a seal's breathing hole in the ice and waits beside it without moving, sometimes for an hour or more, ready to strike the moment a seal comes up for air.

Its front paws measure up to 30 centimeters, a full foot, across, and like snowshoes they spread the bear's weight so it pads over soft snow without sinking; in the water they double as paddles. Under that famous coat is a surprise. A polar bear's skin is jet black, showing only on its nose and footpads, and the dark skin soaks up the sun's warmth like a solar panel. That black nose is a formidable tool. A polar bear can smell a seal's breathing hole about a mile away, and can sniff out a seal hidden under three feet of packed snow.

Even the white is an illusion. Each hair is clear, with a hollow, air-filled core, and the fur only looks white because the rough, hollow hairs scatter sunlight, just as snow does. With dense underfur and thick blubber beneath, that coat keeps the bear's body near 99°F at forty below. The fur, underfur and blubber hold its heat in so well that the bear's outer surface stays almost as cold as the snow, so on an infrared camera the huge animal nearly vanishes.

As the summer ice thins, a polar bear may have to cross long stretches of open water. In one tracking study, a female wearing a GPS collar in Alaska's Beaufort Sea swam about 426 miles without once hauling out, a nonstop swim of nine days, and lost 22 percent of her body weight before she reached solid ice.

sloth.context_blurb: The sloth is a group of slow-moving, long-clawed mammals that live upside down in the rainforest canopies of Central and South America. There are two living families, three-toed and two-toed, and both move more slowly than almost any other mammal. Sloths descend to the ground only every week or so and do almost everything, including eat, sleep, and give birth, hanging from branches. Their slowness is a strategy, not an accident, and it drives several surprising ecological relationships.

star-nosed-mole.context_blurb: The star-nosed mole is a small, nearly blind, insect-eating mammal that lives in the wet soils and shallow ponds of the northeastern United States and eastern Canada. The animal is best known for the strange, 22-fingered pink rosette on the tip of its snout. The star is not an olfactory organ; it is a touch organ, and it operates at a speed that puts the star-nosed mole into the record books among mammals. Scientists study it closely for what it says about how brains handle rapid sensory information.

vampire-bat.context_blurb: The vampire bat is a small bat that feeds entirely on the blood of other animals. There are three living species, all in Central and South America. The vampire bat is extraordinary in several ways: it can run on the ground almost like a four-legged animal, it shares food with roost-mates that are starving, and it has a specific set of body features for its very specialized meal. Scientists have also learned surprising things from vampire bats about how memory, friendship, and reciprocity work in a non-primate brain.

wolverine.context_blurb: The wolverine is a stocky, bear-like mammal that lives in the boreal forests and mountain tundras of the far north, across Scandinavia, Russia, Canada, and Alaska. It is one of the most powerful carnivores for its size on Earth and can drive even wolves and bears off a kill. Wolverines range over huge territories, cache food in the snow for lean times, and are built around life in deep cold. They are rare, hard to find, and remain one of the least-studied large carnivores in North America.

barreleye-macropinna-microstoma.context_blurb:
The barreleye, Macropinna microstoma, is a small deep-sea fish of the open Pacific that hovers some 600 to 800 meters below the surface, where the last sunlight dims to almost nothing. For decades scientists knew it only from damaged bodies hauled up in nets. Then robot submarines from California's Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute, or MBARI, filmed it alive and revealed one of the strangest heads in the sea.

Only about 15 centimeters long, the barreleye wears a transparent, fluid-filled dome over the top of its head, so you can look right through it. Inside the dome sit its real eyes, two glowing green tubes that rest pointing straight up through the clear skull, watching for prey silhouetted against the faint light drifting down from above.

The two dark spots on the front of its face, right where eyes ought to be, are not eyes at all but nostrils, its organs of smell, and they fooled the first people to see one. For decades scientists wondered how a fish that only looks up could guide food into its tiny mouth, until MBARI showed in 2008 that the tubular eyes can rotate forward inside the dome, swiveling like binoculars to follow prey down to the mouth.

The scientists Robison and Reisenbichler saw that the eyes swing forward as the fish tips its whole body from horizontal to vertical to feed, so the eye turn is tied to the body's roll rather than happening on its own. The barreleye barely swims, holding its place almost perfectly still with large, flat fins that make tiny, precise adjustments.

It is thought to steal from siphonophores, drifting colonies whose stinging tentacles stretch beyond 10 meters, plucking small animals already snared there, and its see-through dome probably protects its delicate eyes from the stinging cells. Captured barreleyes have had jelly fragments in their stomachs. The fish was named in 1939 by W. M. Chapman, but every specimen came up in a net with its fragile dome collapsed or torn away, so drawings left it out until MBARI filmed a living barreleye with its dome intact in 2004, 65 years later.

blobfish-psychrolutes-marcidus.context_blurb:
The blobfish, Psychrolutes marcidus, lives on the deep seabed about a kilometer down off Australia, Tasmania and New Zealand. It became famous online as the world's saddest fish, thanks to photos of a droopy pink blob on a boat deck. Those photos show what happens when the fish leaves home, not what it really looks like.

Down in the deep it looks like an ordinary fish, blunt-headed and pink, with big black eyes and feathery fins, its jelly-soft body held in shape by the weight of the water above.

At home the water presses on it 60 to 120 times harder than air presses on us, and its body is built to work against that squeeze, so when a trawl hauls it to the surface and the pressure disappears, the body sags and collapses like a washed-up jellyfish. Its body is mostly jelly, with almost no muscle and very little bone, because chasing prey would waste energy that is scarce in the hungry deep, so it hovers almost motionless and gulps small crustaceans, sea snails and drifting scraps that pass right in front of its mouth. As one expert put it, being lazy is a survival strategy.

The famous photo shows a museum specimen nicknamed Mr Blobby, netted in 2003 on the Norfolk Ridge northwest of New Zealand, and the alcohol used to preserve him tightened his skin and shrank his nose, making his droopy face look even sadder. In 2013 a British comedy group's poll crowned the blobfish the ugliest animal in the world.

deep-sea-anglerfish-ceratioidei.context_blurb:
Deep-sea anglerfish, the ceratioids, are several hundred kinds of fish that hang in the black water far below the sunlight. The females are toothy ambush hunters carrying a glowing lure; the males are tiny and live in a way found almost nowhere else among backboned animals. Their mating has been a showpiece of biology books for more than a century.

Ceratioid anglerfish live in the deep open sea, roughly 300 to 4,000 meters down, nowhere near reefs or shores, and even robot submarines have met them only a handful of times. A female's fishing rod is a spine grown from a fin, called the illicium, tipped with a glowing bulb, the esca. She waves it slowly, and small animals, curious about the only light for miles, swim right up to her jaws to inspect it. Each species has its own shape of lure.

Food is so scarce down there that weeks may pass without a meal, so she cannot let one escape. Her long needle teeth curve inward to trap whatever enters, and her trapdoor jaw stretches so wide that she can swallow prey bigger than she is. Her skin is ultra-black and soaks up almost every scrap of light, so prey sees only the glowing bulb and never the big fish waiting behind it.

She makes no light of her own: her lure glows because bioluminescent bacteria live packed inside it. In some species those bacteria depend on their host so completely that they can no longer glow anywhere else. The male, sometimes only fingernail-sized beside a female a foot long, finds her by smell. For the size of his head, he has the largest nostrils of any animal, and he follows the scent of a female of his own species through miles of dark water. When at last he finds her, he clamps his jaws onto her body and never lets go. Enzymes dissolve the skin where his mouth meets her body, and his flesh fuses into hers for good, a union biologists call sexual parasitism.

Joined to her bloodstream, the male takes all his food from her blood, and his eyes and inner organs waste away until he is little more than a lump of tissue that supplies sperm. The American biologist Ted Pietsch studied one such male, fused to the back of a 46-millimeter female of the species Photocorynus spiniceps. At only 6.2 millimeters, shorter than a rice grain, that male is the smallest sexually mature vertebrate, or backboned animal, ever recorded. Young females hatch with a dark, empty lure. Each one must pick up her own glowing bacteria from the surrounding seawater, because the bacteria are not handed down from the mother. The proof is in the bacteria themselves: their genes still carry tools for swimming free, their DNA turns up in ordinary seawater, and one kind lives in four separate anglerfish families.

Fusing with a stranger should set off the female's immune system, the way a human body attacks a transplanted organ. The fusing species survive because they have discarded major pieces of their adaptive immune system: the MHC genes, killer T cells and antibodies that guard humans from disease. Thomas Boehm, who led the study, pointed out that in a human such a loss would be fatal; the fish get by on a strengthened inborn defense that scientists are still trying to understand. This way of life is no single fluke, because fused males arose independently in five of the eleven ceratioid families, an experiment nature ran again and again. When Swann and colleagues compared species by how they mate, the losses formed a sliding scale. Species whose males cling on only for a while had lost one antibody-tuning gene, while species that fuse for life had also lost the RAG genes that build antibodies and T-cell receptors, along with other immune genes. The longer and more lasting the bond, the more of its immune defense a species has given up.

electric-catfish-malapteruridae.context_blurb:
Electric catfish are big, soft-skinned catfish of the slow, muddy rivers of tropical Africa, including the Nile. Malapterurus electricus grows up to about 1.2 meters long and 20 kilograms, with a blunt head, no fin on its back and six whiskery barbels around its mouth. It makes its own powerful electricity, and people knew it thousands of years before anyone understood what electricity was.

Its weapon is a powerful electric shock, measured at up to about 350 volts in a half-meter fish and more in big adults, enough to knock a grown person back.

It hides in the mud by day and hunts in the dark for about four to five hours after sunset, relying little on its tiny eyes. Bursts of shocks paralyze fish, frogs and other prey, and the catfish can gulp down a victim half as big as itself. In most electric fish, such as the electric eel, the shock organ is packed into the tail, but the catfish's organ is spread as a jelly-like layer under the skin over almost its whole body, so the shock radiates from all around it.

That organ evolved out of ordinary muscle: over millions of years, muscle tissue became millions of flat, stacked cells called electroplaques. To make one clean jolt, every one of them must fire in the same instant. A single giant nerve cell in the spinal cord commands them all, which is why scientists prize this fish for studying nerves.

The ancient Egyptians knew the electric catfish well and carved it on tomb walls at Saqqara more than 4,000 years ago. A catfish even named the first king of a united Egypt: around 3100 BC Narmer's name was written with two signs, a catfish and a chisel, so he was literally "Catfish-Chisel," and the catfish appears on his famous Narmer Palette.

elephantnose-fish-gnathonemus-petersii.context_blurb:
A small, dark fish of the slow, muddy rivers of West and Central Africa, the elephantnose hunts at night in water too murky for eyes to help, and it carries one of the biggest brains, for its size, of any fish. Nearly all of that brain serves one remarkable sense.

An organ near its tail gives off a weak electric field, and receptors all over its skin feel how nearby objects bend that field, letting the fish 'see' shape and distance in total darkness. Biologists call this active electrolocation.

The fish is named for the long, bendy flap that hangs from its face like an elephant's trunk, but the flap is no nose; its real nostrils are tiny and sit farther up. The 'trunk' is a movable extension of its chin, the schnauzenorgan, which the fish sweeps over the riverbed like a metal detector, feeling for buried insect larvae.

The electric sense can even tell the living from the dead. A larva and a pebble of the same size may lie side by side in the mud, and the fish knows which is which without seeing either. Living tissue stores electric charge like a tiny capacitor, while stone and mud only resist the current, and the fish feels that difference.

This sense is called electroreception, and it is costly: the brain that runs it burns about 60 percent of the fish's oxygen, roughly three times the share of any other backboned animal measured. It pays off in company. In a group, each fish can also read the pulses its neighbors give off, so the school works like a shared radar network and each member senses about three times farther than it could alone.

flashlight-fish-anomalopidae.context_blurb:
Flashlight fish are small, dark reef fish of warm oceans that hide in deep water or caves by day and come out at night. Each one carries its own headlights, and it uses them to hunt, to signal and to escape, switching them on and off at will.

Under each eye sits a pouch that glows with a bright bluish light, the brightest made by any bony fish, visible to divers more than 100 feet away. The fish does not make the light itself: billions of glowing bacteria live inside the pouch, and the fish houses and feeds them in return.

Light is also an escape tool. Morin's team described a trick called blink-and-run: chased by a predator, the fish flashes, then switches off and darts away at an angle in the dark, so the hunter lunges at the spot where the light was. The bacteria glow nonstop and cannot be dimmed, so to blink, a fish such as Anomalops rotates the whole light organ downward into a black-lined pocket, like turning a lamp face-down.

The pouch is built like a real flashlight. Behind the bacteria, its back wall is lined with mirror-like crystals of guanine that reflect the glow forward and make the beam far brighter. An active fish blinks about 90 times a minute at night. But when it spots a cloud of plankton, it stops blinking and holds the light steadily on, keeping the organ open nearly 90 percent of the time and using the beam as a headlight to find its food.

frogfish-antennariidae.context_blurb:
The frogfish is a small, lumpy, almost round fish of warm reefs around the world, and one of the sea's great masters of disguise. Matched in color and texture to the sponges, corals and seaweed around it, it can sit in plain view while divers swim past. It never chases a meal; it makes the meal come to it.

A frogfish hardly swims at all; it walks across the reef floor, setting down its stubby, limb-like fins one after another like feet. Its hunting gear grows from its head: the first spine of its back fin has become a thin fishing rod tipped with a fleshy bait shaped like a worm, shrimp or tiny fish, and the frogfish wiggles it until curious small fish swim close.

If a quick fish bites the bait clean off, the frogfish simply grows a new lure over about four to six months. When prey comes within reach, the strike takes about six milliseconds, some fifty times faster than the blink of an eye, which lasts around 300 milliseconds; no fish has been measured striking faster.

The strike is a vacuum, not a bite: the floor of the mouth drops and the cavity swells to as much as twelve times its resting volume, and the sudden space sucks the prey in with a rush of water. With no teeth to cut its food, the frogfish swallows everything whole, and its stomach stretches enough to take a fish as large as itself, or larger.

One species breaks even the frogfish rules: the psychedelic frogfish, found off Indonesia in 2008 and swirled with wild colors, pushes off with its fins and jets water from its gills, bouncing across the seabed like a rubber ball with its tail curled to one side.

gulper-eel-pelican-eel-eurypharynx-pelec.context_blurb:
The pelican eel, or gulper eel, Eurypharynx pelecanoides, is a slender deep-sea fish of the open ocean, drifting somewhere from half a kilometer to 3 kilometers down, where no sunlight reaches. It has a tiny head, a huge stretchy mouth and a long, whip-thin tail. Live ones are almost never seen; most are known from deep-sea nets.

With only tiny teeth, it has no hope of running down quick prey in the dark. Instead its mouth balloons open in an instant into a huge, pelican-like pouch, bigger than its own body, scooping up whatever drifts close.

That monstrous mouth looks built for swallowing big fish, but its jaw is thin and delicate. In fact the eel mostly eats small crustaceans, using the pouch as a net for whatever rare meal comes by. At the very tip of its tail sits a glowing organ that shines pink and gives off sudden red flashes, perhaps a lure to draw prey toward its mouth.

Most fish stay afloat with a gas-filled swim bladder. The pelican eel has none: pockets of jelly packed around its spine keep it afloat instead, a cheap, low-energy body plan for a place where food is scarce.

handfish-brachionichthyidae.context_blurb:
Handfish are tiny, brightly colored fish found only in a few patches of seafloor around Tasmania, off southern Australia. Several species are among the most endangered fish on Earth. Their family name comes from the Latin word for "arm," because instead of swimming they get around on fins that look like little hands.

A handfish is a hopeless swimmer, so it moves across the bottom by planting its splayed, hand-like fins on the sand and walking forward step by step.

A mother spotted handfish deposits a small cluster of eggs and stands guard over it. When a Northern Pacific seastar, an invasive starfish that reached Tasmania on foreign ships, creeps toward the eggs, she wedges herself between the predator and her clutch and sweeps it aside with her tail.

Their way of being born makes them fragile. Most reef fish release larvae that drift on the current and can resettle an emptied reef. Handfish eggs instead hatch straight into tiny, fully formed young that drop to the sand and start walking, so no larvae ever drift in from elsewhere. A reef that loses its handfish stays empty almost forever.

hatchetfish-sternoptychidae.context_blurb:
Hatchetfish are small, silvery deep-sea fish of the twilight zone, several hundred meters down in oceans around the world, where only a dim blue glow comes down from the surface and there is nothing to hide behind. Shaped like the blade of a hatchet, with huge eyes and glowing bellies, they are masters of vanishing in open water.

Seen from below, any fish is a dark shape against the dim light overhead. The hatchetfish erases that shadow with rows of light organs along its belly that glow pale blue and shine downward, matching the light from above, a trick called counter-illumination. Its body is a thin blade, so flattened from side to side that seen head-on it almost disappears, which is how it got its name.

Its eyes are tubes that point straight up, so it watches the faint glow above for the dark silhouettes of prey drifting overhead, the very weakness its own glowing belly hides.

Each night hatchetfish rise toward the surface to feed and sink back down by dawn. All the way, they turn their belly lights up or down like a dimmer switch to match the changing brightness of the water. Their skin holds countless tiny guanine crystals lined up in long parallel bundles. So when a hunter sweeps its glowing searchlight across a hatchetfish, the light scatters into a soft, diffuse blur instead of a bright glint.

leafy-sea-dragon-phycodurus-eques.context_blurb: The leafy sea dragon is a close relative of the seahorse that lives only off the southern coast of Australia. It is covered in long, leaf-shaped flaps of skin that blend in perfectly with the swaying kelp forests where it lives. The sea dragon is a slow, drifting predator on tiny crustaceans, and it does not swim with any of the usual power. Breeding sea dragons also share some of the strange reproductive habits of their seahorse cousins.

oarfish-regalecus-glesne.context_blurb: The oarfish is a long, silvery, ribbon-shaped fish that lives in the open ocean a few hundred meters below the surface. It can grow more than 20 feet long, which may make it the longest bony fish in the world. Oarfish are almost never seen alive; most known specimens are animals that washed up on beaches or came up sick. Their shape, size, and bright-red fins have fueled a very long history of sea-serpent stories around the world.

sarcastic-fringehead-neoclinus-blanchard.context_blurb: The sarcastic fringehead is a small, bad-tempered fish of the shallow coastal waters off California and Baja California. It is a territorial ambush hunter that lives inside empty shells, bottles, and crevices on the sea floor. The fringehead is best known among divers for an aggressive display it uses against rivals, which involves part of its own anatomy doing something no fish would be expected to do. Its face has gone viral in underwater photography more than once.

sheepshead-fish-archosargus-probatocepha.context_blurb: The sheepshead is a striped, panfish-sized fish of the shallow Atlantic coast of North America, from New York down into the Gulf of Mexico. It is a popular target for anglers in Florida and the Carolinas. The sheepshead lives mostly around rocks, pilings, and oyster beds, and it has an unusual set of teeth for a fish, teeth that look so much like a human mouth that photos of them regularly surprise people on the internet.

snakehead-fish-channidae.context_blurb: The snakehead fish is a family of long, air-breathing predatory fish native to Africa and Asia. They are famous among biologists both for their aggressive hunting behavior in their native rivers and for the environmental damage they can cause when released into waterways where they do not belong. Snakeheads have a trick in their respiratory system that lets them survive out of water for far longer than most fish could ever manage, and they can even cross small stretches of land between pools.

stargazer-uranoscopidae.context_blurb: The stargazer is a group of thickset, bottom-living fish that live buried in sand on continental shelves around the world. They are ambush predators, with eyes and mouths pointed straight up, so that they lie almost flat under the sand and strike at whatever swims directly over them. Stargazers combine several defensive and offensive tricks that very few other fish put together on the same body, including features that make them dangerous to step on.

stonefish-synanceia.context_blurb: The stonefish is a small, lumpy, ugly fish that lives on tropical reefs and rocky shallows across the Indo-Pacific. It is the most venomous fish in the world. Stonefish spend their days half-buried in sand or wedged among coral rubble, where they are nearly invisible. Everything about them, from the texture of their skin to their defensive spines, is a precise solution to the problem of being a slow, chunky fish on a reef full of fast ones.

viperfish-chauliodus.context_blurb:
Far below the surface, in the dark middle layers of warm and temperate oceans, hunts the viperfish: a slender, hand-sized fish with a huge head, a mouthful of needles and a body that can look almost see-through. Food is scarce down there, so the viperfish is built to catch anything it meets and never let it go.

Its fangs are too long to fit inside its mouth, so they curve back until their tips nearly touch its own eyes, and its jaws hang open in a permanent grin. When it lunges and the jaws slam shut, two long front fangs jutting up from the lower jaw close around the victim like the bars of a cage, leaving the prey no way out.

Light is its other weapon. A spine on its back arches forward over its head, tipped with a glowing photophore. The viperfish waves this lure like a fishing pole, flashing it on and off to draw small fish right onto its fangs. Light also hides it. Rows of tiny photophores along its belly glow to match the faint light filtering down from the surface, so a hunter looking up from below sees no dark silhouette, a trick called counter-illumination.

Meals can be days apart, so the viperfish takes whatever it catches, even prey 20 to more than 50 percent bigger than itself. To swallow such a meal, it unhinges its skull, opens its jaws as wide as 90 degrees, and stretches its stomach around the prey. Those inward-curving fangs carry a deadly risk. If a viperfish strikes blind and catches a fish too big to swallow, its teeth hold the meal so fast that it can neither swallow nor spit it out, and it starves.

blanket-octopus-tremoctopus.context_blurb:
The blanket octopus, Tremoctopus, drifts through warm tropical and subtropical seas around the world. The female spreads a shimmering purple web stretched from arm to arm, the "blanket" that gives the animal its name. The species also shows a startling size gap between the sexes, and a weapon no other octopus is known to use.

Unlike most octopuses, which hide in reef crevices and crawl the seafloor, the blanket octopus spends its whole life drifting in open water, from the surface down to about 250 meters, never touching rock or sand. With no shell or reef to hide behind, a female threatened by a tuna unfurls her webbing into a huge iridescent cape, suddenly looking big and frightening enough to warn off tuna, sailfish and even sharks.

It even steals weapons: a blanket octopus tears pieces from the venomous tentacles of a Portuguese man o' war, then holds them in its arms like whips, striking prey and fending off predators with the stolen stingers.

Females reach about 2 meters across, yet a male measures only about 2.4 centimeters, roughly the size of a walnut. To mate, the tiny male packs sperm into a special arm called the hectocotylus, then detaches the whole arm and gives it to the female, and he almost certainly dies soon after.

For centuries the male was known only from dead specimens in trawl nets and plankton samples, until in 2002 Mark Norman and colleagues found the first live adult male off Australia's Great Barrier Reef. In the 1820s naturalists kept finding a squirming thread inside females, and Georges Cuvier described it as a new parasitic worm, Hectocotylus octopodis, but in the 1840s Albert von Kölliker and Heinrich Müller, who found whole dwarf males whose big arm dropped off at a touch, proved the "worm" was the male's own detachable arm, left inside the female after mating.

Only tiny males and small young females have ever been seen carrying man o' war tentacles, never an octopus longer than about 7 centimeters, probably because the larger suckers of a bigger octopus cannot hold such thin stingers without injury. The borrowed weapon may give small males a refuge from predators, and researchers propose that this may itself have pushed females to grow huge while males stayed tiny.

blue-dragon-nudibranch-glaucus-atlanticu.context_blurb:
Glaucus atlanticus, the blue dragon, is a sea slug barely the size of a grape, striped electric blue and silver. It spends its whole life adrift on the warm open ocean, far from any shore or seabed, and this soft little drifter hunts one of the most feared stingers in the sea.

With no shell and almost no power to swim, the slug goes wherever wind and current take it. It rides the surface upside down, belly turned to the sky. It feeds on the Portuguese man o' war, which drifts like a jellyfish and trails tentacles loaded with venomous stinging cells. The slug swallows it, keeps the stingers and concentrates their venom, so the little thief can sting a person even worse than the man o' war it robbed, causing pain, nausea and vomiting.

Those stinging cells, called nematocysts, go down undigested. The slug then sorts them, moving the strongest out of its gut and into its own body, where they wait in its frilly blue arms as borrowed weapons. Scientists call this kleptocnidy, 'stolen stingers.' Its colors guard it against seabirds above and fish below. Because it floats upside down, its counter-shading is reversed: the side facing the sky, its belly, is brilliant blue to vanish against the sea, while the side facing the deep is silver-grey to melt into the bright surface.

For a slug that can barely swim, staying at the top is its own puzzle. The blue dragon swallows a bubble of air and holds it in its stomach, a gas-filled sac that works like a built-in life jacket, helped by the surface tension of the water.

The borrowed stingers outlive the slug: a blue dragon washed up dead on a beach still fires them on contact, so picking up the pretty blue shape can earn a sting. Inside the living slug the weapons are a hazard too, since a few always go off on the way down. It disarms them in two steps: its mucus quiets the stinging cells so fewer fire, and a tough chitin lining, studded with chitin discs called spindles, soaks up any that go off anyway, like sandbags around a blast.

Biologists long saw the blue dragon as a slug that lived on the man o' war and killed with borrowed stings. Then a 2025 aquarium study filmed it catching live small fish, and the stingers played no part. Its front cerata, the fingerlike arms nearest its head, are longer than the rest and muscled at the base. It used them like arms, seizing a fish, pinning it between them and biting near the gills.

blue-ringed-octopus-hapalochlaena.context_blurb:
The blue-ringed octopus, Hapalochlaena, is a golf-ball-sized octopus of tide pools and shallow reefs across the Indo-Pacific, from Australia to Japan. It is easy to miss and is one of the most venomous animals in the sea. Its little body is a kit of warning colors, borrowed chemistry and two kinds of venom, and medical researchers study it closely.

At rest it is a drab gray-brown that melts into the rocks, but when disturbed it flashes dozens of glowing blue rings, a "do not touch" signal that tells predators to keep their distance. It would rather warn than fight, and it bites a person only when it is grabbed or stepped on.

Although it measures only 12 to 20 centimeters including its arms, a single octopus carries enough venom to kill more than 20 adults within minutes. It hunts small crabs, hermit crabs and shrimp by ambush, piercing their shells with a hard, parrot-like beak and injecting paralyzing venom.

The venom is tetrodotoxin, which has no known antidote, the same poison found in the pufferfish, a fish Japanese chefs need a special license to prepare, and in some poison dart frogs and newts; the blue-ringed octopus was the first animal known to use it as a venom. A bite is tiny and painless, but the venom paralyzes the muscles of breathing within minutes, so a rescuer must keep the victim breathing with artificial respiration or a ventilator until the body clears the toxin, usually within about a day. Survive those first 24 hours on breathing support, and recovery is usually complete.

The octopus does not make the poison itself: symbiotic bacteria living in its rear salivary gland manufacture the tetrodotoxin, and the octopus hosts them and delivers their product. It also keeps two different venoms in separate glands, one to subdue prey and the other for defense against predators. Its warning flash is among the fastest color changes in the animal world, 50 to 60 rings in about a third of a second, because the blue comes from inert, mirror-like cells tucked inside skin pouches that muscles snap open, while the surrounding brown cells darken for contrast. In 2025 scientists filmed a close relative, the blue-lined octopus, using venom to mate: the much smaller male bites the female right over the aorta at the back of her head and injects tetrodotoxin, which stops her breathing and leaves her still for 40 to 75 minutes so she cannot eat him, and she recovers fully afterward. It was the first animal known to turn venom into a mating tool.

Why does the octopus not poison itself? Tetrodotoxin works by plugging the sodium channels in nerve and muscle cells, and in 2019 researchers found that the octopus's own channel carries three swapped amino acids that reshape the spot where the toxin docks, so the poison cannot get a grip. Pufferfish, newts and some snakes evolved the same kinds of changes on their own, a striking case of convergent evolution.

bobbit-worm-eunice-aphroditois.context_blurb:
The bobbit worm, Eunice aphroditois, is a long, shimmering sea worm of warm reefs around the world. It spends its life buried in the sand with only its head showing, a living trap that waits for prey to come close. On video its strike looks like a spring-loaded trap snapping shut.

Five thin antennae stick up around its head like fingers, and they work as tripwires: when a fish brushes against one, the hidden worm strikes. Most of its body stays out of sight, but the record specimen stretched 299 centimeters, nearly 10 feet, longer than a grown man lying down, though only about 2.5 centimeters wide.

The strike lasts mere milliseconds, and its scissor-like jaws, serrated and hooked, can sometimes cut a fish clean in half before dragging it under the sand. Once it has hold of prey, it pumps in a toxin that stuns or kills the victim, which lets it subdue and drag down animals far larger than itself.

Staff at Newquay's Blue Reef Aquarium in England saw coral shredded and fish vanishing night after night, and after weeks of empty traps they dismantled the display one rock at a time and found a bobbit worm 1.2 meters long, which they named Barry. When they cornered him, he bit clean through a 20-pound fishing line. Nobody had bought him: Barry arrived as a tiny youngster hidden in a piece of "live rock" the aquarium purchased, then grew unseen for years, ducking into his burrow whenever bright light hit him.

With no limbs to swing its jaws, the worm launches them by turning its muscular throat inside out, flinging the whole jaw apparatus forward like a spring-loaded trap and then pulling it back with the prey. A skeleton of pressurized fluid holds its long body in shape and helps power the launch. Despite its fearsome hunting, it also scavenges algae and dead matter, and it lives only about three to five years.

Soft worms rarely fossilize, but in Taiwanese rock about 20 million years old, Yu-Yen Pan and colleagues found 319 fossils of something the ancient worms left behind: the L-shaped burrows they hunted from, up to 2 meters long and only 2 to 3 centimeters wide. Near the top of each burrow, X-ray scans show a spike of iron left by the worm's mucus, a sign that it rebuilt its lair after every violent strike.

christmas-tree-worm-spirobranchus-gigant.context_blurb:
The Christmas tree worm, Spirobranchus giganteus, is a small marine worm of tropical reefs around the world. It spends its whole life inside a tube in a living coral head, and divers see only its colorful crowns, which handle several jobs at once. Its escape reflex is one of the quickest of any animal without a backbone.

What looks like a pair of tiny, brilliant spiral fir trees in red, blue, orange or yellow is really the two feathery crowns of one worm, which lives head-down in a tube bored into the coral.

Those crowns sit exposed on the reef, so at the slightest touch or even a passing shadow the worm whips them down into its tube in an instant, then creeps back out very slowly about a minute later to test the water. The hair-fringed branches of each crown, called radioles, do double duty: they net drifting plankton and pass it to the mouth, and they also take oxygen from the water like gills, so the worm eats and breathes with the same organ.

Once inside, the worm seals the tube with an operculum, a trapdoor lid reshaped from one of its own crown branches, which plugs the hole while it hides.

The early warning comes from the crown itself, because built into the feathery branches are compound eyes, each with an estimated 600 to 1,000 tiny lenses tuned to the blue light of the reef, which catch the shadow of anything approaching and fire the retreat before the worm is ever touched.

Whether the worm helps its coral is still argued: a 1986 Great Barrier Reef study by DeVantier and colleagues found living coral tissue clustered around the worms where crown-of-thorns starfish were feeding, hinting that the worms may shield their host from those coral-eating starfish, but a 2019 study off Curaçao found the worm's scraping lid often injured the coral instead. The relationship may swing between help and harm from one reef to the next.

coconut-crab-birgus-latro.context_blurb:
The coconut crab, Birgus latro, is a giant hermit crab of tropical islands across the Indian and western Pacific Oceans. It begins life in the sea, spends its adult life on land, climbs palm trees, and on some islands rules as the top predator.

It is the biggest arthropod living on land, spanning more than 3 feet from leg tip to leg tip and weighing up to about 4 kilograms, heavier than a house cat. The coconut crab is also the island animal that can open a coconut, a nut people usually need tools to crack: it climbs the palm, then husks and splits the fruit with its claws over hours of work.

Islanders call it the robber crab because it carries off pots, silverware and shiny objects, and its claws can lift about 29 kilograms. It is a hunter and scavenger too, eating carrion, and on Christmas Island it can tear apart a live red crab in seconds.

In 2016 on Okinawa, Shin-ichiro Oka's team measured the pinch of 29 wild crabs, and the strongest gripped with about 1,765 newtons, more than a lion's canine bite, while the biggest crabs may reach 3,300 newtons, beaten among land predators only by the alligator. Though it starts life in the ocean, an adult's gills have shrunk and it breathes air through a lung-like organ, so it will drown if held underwater. Young coconut crabs, like other hermit crabs, wear borrowed snail shells, but an adult grows too big for any shell and instead hardens the plates of its own abdomen into built-in armor.

Oka himself was pinched twice, and of those few minutes he said, "I felt eternal hell." Its breathing organ, a spongy branchiostegal lung, works only while damp, so the crab strokes water over it with its smallest, hindmost pair of legs and plugs its burrow to keep the air moist. Its larvae drift in the open ocean for three or four weeks, and once a survivor crawls ashore in a snail shell, it can no longer swim, ever. About once a year it molts, burrowing as deep as a meter and plugging the entrance for weeks, and when the old shell slips off, it eats the cast-off shell and reuses its calcium to harden the new armor.

Its sense of smell went its own way: its antennae and the brain region that reads scents came to resemble an insect's rather than a sea crab's, letting it find rotting meat and fruit from far off. On the Chagos Islands, Mark Laidre filmed a crab climbing up to a booby asleep in a tree and breaking its wing, and as rival crabs, drawn within about 20 minutes by the smell of blood, squabbled over the bird for hours, he admitted, "I had a lot of trouble sleeping that night." Laidre also compared three near-identical islands and found that only on the one without coconut crabs did seabirds dare to nest on the ground. In the 1830s Charles Darwin watched one tear a coconut's husk off fibre by fibre, always beginning where the three eye-holes sit, then hammer a claw on an eye-hole until it broke through to the meat. He called it as curious a case of instinct as he had ever heard of. Coconut crabs were the first arthropods tracked by GPS, and when Jakob Krieger's team moved tagged crabs away from home on Christmas Island, most made their way home, ending up a few hundred meters or less from where they were caught, and one retraced its exact outward route, S-bend and all. The team followed 55 crabs between 2008 and 2011, on treks that averaged 1.8 kilometers and reached 4.2, clear evidence of route memory in a crustacean.

comb-jelly-ctenophora.context_blurb:
Comb jellies are glassy, plum-sized animals that drift through every ocean, from sunlit bays to the black deep. They look like jellyfish, but they belong to a separate, very ancient line of animal life and carry no stinging cells at all. Scientists call them ctenophores, "comb bearers," and they may hold clues to how the first animals began.

Down each comb jelly's body run eight rows of "combs," and every comb is a plate of giant hairs, called cilia, fused together. The combs beat one after another and push the animal through the sea the way a crew rows a boat, with thousands of tiny oars. The flickering pink, green and blue bands along its sides are not its own light: the moving hairs scatter passing light like a prism, a structural color quite unlike the chemical glow called bioluminescence.

Most creatures that swim with beating hairs are microscopic, such as bacteria. Comb jellies use that same method at giant scale: some reach 1.5 meters, about 5 feet, which makes the comb jelly the biggest animal anywhere that rows itself along with cilia instead of muscle. With no stings to use, it trails long tentacles studded with colloblasts, mushroom-shaped glue cells. When a small shrimp touches one, the cells burst open and cement the prey to the tentacle, where a true jellyfish would fire venom-loaded stingers instead.

Comb jellies are fierce hunters, and some hunt their own kind. Beroe grows no tentacles whatever: nearly its whole body is one enormous mouth, lined with stiff, tooth-like bundles of hairs called macrocilia, and it swallows other comb jellies whole. In the dark twilight zone, Bathocyroe fosteri is clear as glass except for its bright red stomach, and red hides the blue-green glow of the luminous prey inside it, so a swallowed meal never shines out and draws a bigger hunter.

That taste for comb jellies once saved a sea. In the 1980s ships carried the sea walnut, Mnemiopsis leidyi, to the Black Sea inside their ballast tanks. With no enemies there, it multiplied wildly and gobbled up the zooplankton and young fish. Then, in the late 1990s, ships delivered Beroe ovata, a comb jelly that preys on other comb jellies, and it cut the sea walnut's numbers back down.

Comb jellies may even be our most distant animal cousins: textbooks usually put sponges on the oldest limb of the animal family tree, but some scientists who compare ancient gene patterns argue that the comb jelly split off first, before every other animal. The debate is still open. Comb jellies also seem to lack allorecognition, the check that lets most animals tell their own tissue from a stranger's and reject it. In 2024 Kei Jokura's team at the Woods Hole lab trimmed pieces off two sea walnuts and set the wounded animals side by side. In about nine cases out of ten the pair merged into a single animal: within roughly two hours their two nerve nets had wired together, their muscles pulsed in near-perfect time, and food swallowed by one mouth flowed through the shared gut.

dumbo-octopus-grimpoteuthis.context_blurb:
The dumbo octopus, Grimpoteuthis, is a small, pale octopus of the deep seafloor, living hundreds to thousands of meters down in every ocean. In that cold, dark world food is scarce and life moves slowly. It is gentler than its shallow-water cousins, and it takes its nickname from Disney's flying elephant.

Shallow-water octopuses get around by jetting, but the dumbo octopus flies. On top of its body sit two broad, ear-like fins, and it beats them slowly like wings, a way of swimming no shallow octopus uses.

It eats gently too: instead of tearing its food apart with a hard beak, it wraps a small worm or crab in the web between its arms to trap it, then swallows it whole.

The deep sea has no seasons, so the female does not breed by the calendar. Instead of laying one big clutch, she carries eggs at many stages of ripeness at the same time and lays one or two whenever conditions suit. She can even store a male's sperm until she chooses to use it.

Flapping fins need a firm anchor, and almost every octopus has lost all trace of a shell. Grimpoteuthis kept one: a tiny U- or V-shaped internal shell, shaped like a saddle and tucked inside its mantle, which gives the fin muscles something rigid to pull against.

flamboyant-cuttlefish-metasepia-pfefferi.context_blurb:
The flamboyant cuttlefish, Metasepia pfefferi, is a tiny cuttlefish of the sandy and muddy seabeds of the tropical Indo-Pacific, from Indonesia to northern Australia. It is famous for the hypnotic waves of purple, yellow and white that roll across its skin, and for a reputation that scientists are still arguing about.

It is one of the very few cuttlefish that walks instead of swimming, ambling across the seabed on a pair of its arms plus a pair of flaps on its lower fins, which work together like legs. A full-grown adult is only about 2.5 to 3 inches long, 6 to 8 centimeters, roughly half the size of a typical cuttlefish.

Its bright colors are not camouflage but a warning: Mark Norman of Museum Victoria reported that its muscle tissue was poisonous, reportedly as lethal as the venom of the blue-ringed octopus, which would make it the only toxic cuttlefish known. Its walking has a physical cause. Its cuttlebone, the internal shell other cuttlefish use as a buoyancy tank, is shrunken to two-thirds or three-quarters of its body length and lacks the outer cone the others rely on, so it gives too little lift to hover. The animal is effectively tied to the seafloor.

The poison claim is now in doubt. Norman had reported that the muscle held tetrodotoxin, the blue-ringed octopus's poison. But teams at Georgia Southern University and Utah State University tested directly for that toxin and found only trace amounts, far too little to harm a backboned animal. Whether the flamboyant cuttlefish is truly toxic, and what its real poison might be, is still disputed.
