giant-isopod-bathynomus-giganteus.context_blurb:
The giant isopod, Bathynomus giganteus, is a deep-sea crustacean that scavenges on the cold, dark floor of the Atlantic and Pacific, roughly 170 to 2,100 meters down. The biggest confirmed specimen was about 50 centimeters long, as big as a small dog. It can go years without eating, which has made it something of a celebrity.

It is a giant cousin of the little pillbug, or roly-poly, that you find under rocks in a garden, walking on seven pairs of legs beneath a fan of overlapping armor plates. Like its tiny relative, when a predator threatens its soft underside it curls into a tight ball, leaving only its tough back plates exposed.

Food is scarce in the deep. When a whale carcass or a large dead fish drifts down to the bottom, the giant isopod stuffs itself until it can hardly move, storing energy that may need to last months or years. Its seafloor gets barely a millionth as much sunlight as the surface. To catch the faintest glimmers, it has enormous compound eyes, each with close to 4,000 facets.

Its patience is famous. At the Toba Aquarium in Japan, an isopod known as No. 1 had its last meal on January 2, 2009, a 50-gram piece of horse mackerel. After that it refused all food for more than five years, 5 years and 43 days, until it died in 2014, still plump. A 2022 genome study of a close relative showed how this works. Its genes for breaking down fat are reduced, so it burns fat poorly and instead stores it in a stomach that swells to fill about two-thirds of its body cavity, a slow-release reserve that lasts through famine.

Why does the cold deep produce such giants? Scientists still argue. The leading idea, from a 1999 study by Chapelle and Peck, is that frigid water holds far more dissolved oxygen, so a bigger body can still take in enough to breathe. Other ideas, such as cold making cells larger or big bodies surviving starvation better, remain in the running.

giant-tube-worm-riftia-pachyptila.context_blurb:
The giant tube worm, Riftia pachyptila, is a red-plumed worm up to 2 meters long that lives in dense clusters on the deep floor of the Pacific. It has no mouth, no stomach and no way to eat, and its discovery in 1977 changed what biologists believed about where life can exist.

These worms crowd in red-plumed gardens around hydrothermal vents, cracks in the ocean floor about 2,500 meters down where hot, mineral-rich water gushes up in total darkness. An adult never eats: billions of bacteria living inside a special organ in its body make all its food.

The bright red plume at its tip, which takes in chemicals from the water like a gill, is red for the same reason our blood is: it is full of hemoglobin. When a new vent opens, young worms settle beside it and grow astonishingly fast, one of the quickest-growing animals in the ocean, reaching 1.5 meters in under two years. Its tube can lengthen by as much as 85 centimeters in a single year.

Plants make sugar with the energy of sunlight, but no sunlight reaches the vents. The worm's bacteria use chemosynthesis instead, drawing their energy from chemical bonds, no light needed. Their fuel is hydrogen sulfide, the rotten-egg gas that poisons most animals. The bacteria turn that poison into food for themselves and for their host. On February 17, 1977, the submarine Alvin dove nearly two miles to the Galápagos Rift and found these gardens. Yet no biologists were aboard: the crew were geologists, because nobody imagined anything could live down there.

The worm's hemoglobin is special, because it carries the sulfide and oxygen on separate binding sites at the same time, delivering both to the bacteria while keeping the poison away from the worm's own cells. A young worm hatches as a tiny larva with a working mouth and gut. But once its bacterial partners are inside, its entire digestive system closes up and disappears for good. Its food comes from those partners: in each lobe of its bacteria-packed organ, the trophosome, small bacteria near the center divide, swell and fatten as they are pushed outward, like goods on an assembly line, and at the outer edge the worm digests them. Tracer studies show carbon captured by the bacteria turning up in the worm's own tissue within about 15 minutes.

Zinc is the hidden hero of its blood, because zinc atoms built into its hemoglobin are where the sulfide clips on harmlessly. The bacteria are not swallowed at all. A 2006 study showed that free-living vent bacteria bore straight in through the young worm's skin, like an infection, and push deeper into its body while the worm kills off some of its own infected cells to clear space. The larvae hatch with no bacteria at all, and the trophosome is then built around the colonized cells that survive, a partnership that begins as an infection the worm tames.

sea-angel-clione.context_blurb: The sea angel is a tiny, transparent sea slug that lives in cold ocean waters, especially around the Arctic and Antarctic. It swims by flapping two wing-like fins that make it look like a floating cherub. Sea angels are predators, and they feed almost exclusively on one specific prey item that they hunt with a surprising piece of equipment. For something that drifts through dark polar seas and looks delicate enough to break, the sea angel is actually a very committed hunter.

vampire-squid-vampyroteuthis-infernalis.context_blurb: The vampire squid is a small, dark, deep-sea cephalopod of the oxygen-minimum layer in warm oceans around the world. Despite its name, it is not a true squid or an octopus; it is the only living member of its own order, with a mix of features from both groups. The vampire squid has webbing between its arms, light-producing patches scattered over its body, and a defensive behavior that makes dramatic use of the webbing. Its diet turned out to be nothing like what people assumed from its name.

venuss-flower-basket-euplectella-aspergi.context_blurb: Venus's flower basket is a deep-sea sponge that lives on the sea floor of the western Pacific. The animal is a hollow, cylindrical cage made of fused glass fibers, and in the dim light of the deep ocean it looks like a woven lantern. The sponge is famous for a specific relationship it has with a pair of shrimp that live trapped inside it for life. The structural engineering of the sponge's glass skeleton is also carefully studied for what it says about building strong materials from brittle parts.

yeti-crab-kiwa.context_blurb: The yeti crab is a group of pale, blind deep-sea crustaceans discovered in 2005 on the Pacific-Antarctic Ridge. The crabs live around hot hydrothermal vents a mile or more below the surface, and their most striking feature is a thick layer of hair-like bristles covering their claws and legs. Those bristles are not just decoration; the yeti crab grows a crop of chemosynthetic bacteria in them that it uses in a very specific way. The animal is one of the clearest living examples of ocean life running on the chemistry of the vents, not sunlight.

club-winged-manakin.context_blurb:
The club-winged manakin, Machaeropterus deliciosus, is a small bird of the wet, mossy cloud forests of western Colombia and Ecuador. The chestnut-brown male wears a bright red cap, and when he courts a female, his whole show is sound. Making that sound reshaped his body and, surprisingly, the female's as well.

He makes a clear, violin-like tone without opening his beak, because he is the only bird known to sing with his wings, rubbing two specially thickened wing feathers together behind his back.

One of those feathers has a shaft lined with a row of ridges like a tiny washboard, and a stiff neighboring feather scrapes across the bumps over a hundred times every second, each bump adding a click that blurs into a pure note. This rub-to-sing method is called stridulation, the same trick a cricket uses, and no other bird is known to do it.

To survive the constant knocking, the male's ulna, a wing bone, is solid and mineralized, nearly three times the volume of a normal bird's, and to the scientists' surprise the silent female carries the same dense, heavy wing bone, so the display reshaped the skeleton of the whole species and made every bird a slightly worse flier.

frogmouth.context_blurb:
Frogmouths are stocky night birds of Australia and Southeast Asia, as big as a small owl, with a huge, frog-like mouth. The tawny frogmouth of Australia's forests hides in plain sight by day and hunts insects and small animals after dark, and almost everyone who sees one mistakes it for an owl.

By day it perches lengthwise along a limb, stiffens its body, points its short beak at the sky and narrows its eyes to slits. With its gray, black and brown streaked feathers matching the bark, the frozen bird looks just like a broken-off branch stub.

Its owl-like look is a coincidence of lifestyle, not family. The tawny frogmouth belongs with the nightjars and their relatives, such as oilbirds and potoos. Unlike an owl, it has weak little feet that cannot grip prey, so it catches every meal with its bill, a wide, cavernous gape facing forward that it snaps shut on an insect or spider it pounces on from a perch.

If a hawk sees through the disguise and corners it, the frogmouth drops the act and does the opposite. It throws open its big yellow-green mouth, hisses loudly and puffs up its feathers to look as large and threatening as possible.

harpy-eagle.context_blurb:
The harpy eagle, Harpia harpyja, is a huge eagle of the rainforests of Central and South America and the top hunter of the Amazon canopy, powerful enough to pluck monkeys and sloths from the treetops. It hunts from perches rather than by soaring, and it is threatened across much of its range as the forests are cut.

Slate-gray and black above and bright white below, with a pair of feather crests it can lift on its head, the harpy eagle is the rainforest's top flying hunter, and no bird of prey on Earth is more powerful.

It carries the largest talons of any living eagle. A female's rear talon reaches about 12.3 centimeters, nearly 5 inches, about as long as the front claw of a grizzly bear.

Monkeys are on its menu, but in one Panama study sloths made up 79 percent of everything a harpy ate. It plucks prey off the branches, and a female can grab an animal nearly her own weight and fly off without landing. Though it hunts by day, it has a feature you would expect on a night-hunting owl: a disc of feathers around its face that it can raise to channel faint sounds to its ears, helping it hear hidden prey before it sees them.

Harpies breed very slowly. A pair raises just one chick every two to three years, one of the slowest rates of any eagle, so losing even one pair can set a forest's harpy population back for years.

hoatzin.context_blurb:
The hoatzin is a strange bird of the flooded forests along the Amazon and Orinoco rivers of South America, as big as a crow, with a spiky reddish crest, a naked blue face and red eyes. It eats almost nothing but leaves, which is nearly unheard of among birds, and its chicks carry a feature no other living bird keeps.

With its punk-rock crest, bare blue face and diet of leaves fermented in a huge crop like a little cow's, this Amazon swamp bird is the hoatzin. A hoatzin chick hatches with a pair of working claws on each wing, and it uses them to grip bark and clamber through the branches, the only living bird with wing claws that work. It loses them as it grows up.

Hoatzins nest on branches hanging over the water, which gives the chicks an escape route. When a snake creeps toward the nest, a chick that cannot yet fly flings itself off the branch into the river, swims away underwater and later climbs back up.

The hoatzin is the only bird known to digest leaves by fermentation, with bacteria in its crop breaking them down the way microbes do in a cow's stomach. The fermenting leaves give it a manure-like smell, so people in the Amazon call it the stinkbird.

hoopoe.context_blurb: The hoopoe is a slender, cinnamon-colored bird with a long curved bill and a dramatic black-and-white crest. It lives across Europe, Africa, and much of Asia and spends most of its time on the ground, probing for insects. The hoopoe has turned up in art, poetry, and religious writing from ancient Egypt to the Qur'an, and it is the national bird of Israel. Nesting hoopoes also combine several defensive tricks that have been giving ornithologists material to study for a long time.

kakapo.context_blurb: The kakapo is a huge, flightless, nocturnal parrot that lives only on a few predator-free islands off the coast of New Zealand. There are only about 250 individuals left, each one of them named by biologists. The kakapo is unlike any other parrot: it is heavier than any other, cannot fly, lives on the ground, and breeds only every few years, when a specific food source is abundant. The whole species is one of the most closely managed in the world.

kea.context_blurb: The kea is a large, olive-green parrot that lives only in the mountains of New Zealand's South Island. Keas live where snow sits for much of the year, and they get through that life with a combination of curiosity, playfulness, and problem-solving that puts them in the same mental league as crows and apes. They are also notorious for a specific habit at mountain parking lots that keeps them in the news.

marabou-stork.context_blurb: The marabou stork is a huge, bald-headed scavenging bird that lives across sub-Saharan Africa. It has one of the largest wingspans of any living bird and often weighs more than a human child. The marabou's bare head, huge beak, and dangling throat pouch are the kinds of features that get written into Victorian descriptions as hideous, but each of them is doing a specific job tied to how the bird feeds. Marabou storks are important parts of the African scavenger community.

oilbird.context_blurb: The oilbird is a nocturnal fruit-eating bird that lives in caves in the forested parts of northern South America and Trinidad. It is the only bird in the world that both lives in a cave in deep darkness and also eats only fruit. The oilbird uses a specialized sense to navigate through pitch-black cave passages, which is otherwise mostly associated with bats. Humans once hunted oilbirds for the thick layer of fat on their chicks, which gave the bird its name.

potoo.context_blurb: The potoo is a group of large, nocturnal birds that live in the forests of Central and South America. By day, a potoo sits on a broken-off branch stump with its beak pointed upward and its eyes mostly closed, blending into the stump so perfectly that it looks like part of the tree. At night, it hunts flying insects by diving from its perch and sailing back. The way the potoo spends its day is one of the most reliable camouflage tricks any bird has.

secretarybird.context_blurb: The secretarybird is a tall, long-legged bird of prey that walks across the savannas and grasslands of sub-Saharan Africa. It is unmistakable in silhouette, with the body of an eagle on the legs of a stork. The secretarybird can fly, but it does most of its hunting on foot. Its signature method of killing prey is unusual among raptors and gives it one of the strangest fight styles in the bird world. It is now listed as endangered as its grassland habitat shrinks.

superb-bird-of-paradise.context_blurb: The superb bird-of-paradise is a small, jet-black forest bird that lives in the rainforests of New Guinea. Males put on one of the most carefully choreographed courtship displays in the whole bird world, transforming themselves into a shape and face that look nothing like a normal bird. For a long time the superb bird-of-paradise was treated as one species. Modern DNA work has split it into at least two, each with slightly different dance moves.

sword-billed-hummingbird.context_blurb: The sword-billed hummingbird is a hummingbird that lives in the Andean cloud forests of northern South America. It is the only bird in the world with a bill of its particular shape and proportions. The sword bill is tied closely to a specific set of flowers it feeds from and to a problem of coevolution that keeps turning up in ecology textbooks. The way the bird grooms, perches, and sleeps all has to be adapted around that oversized bill.

toucan.context_blurb:
In the warm rainforests of Central and South America, flocks of toucans move through the canopy, each a black bird carrying a beak so big it looks like a cartoon. That bill is no clumsy ornament. Biologists have found that it is light, handy at mealtimes, and a tool for keeping the bird at the right temperature.

The toucan's brightly colored bill can be four times the size of its head and stretch almost the full length of the rest of the bird.

A toucan plucks fruit with the far end of its bill, well away from its mouth, so to eat it jerks its head back, flips the fruit into the air and catches it as it drops straight down its throat.

Such a beak should weigh the bird down, yet a toucan flies easily. The bill is built like a foam sandwich: a thin outer sheath of keratin, the stuff of fingernails, over an airy core of crisscrossing bony struts and closed, air-filled cells, so it weighs only a tiny fraction of the bird's body. It also works as a radiator the toucan can turn up or down. On hot days the bird sends more blood into its bill to shed heat, losing 30 to 60 percent of its body's heat there, and on cool nights it cuts the flow to hold its warmth in, a 'thermal window' that rivals an elephant's ears.

vulture.context_blurb: Vultures are a group of large scavenging birds that live on every continent except Antarctica and Australia. They clean up carcasses that would otherwise rot and spread disease, and the ecosystem job they do is far bigger than most people realize until it stops. Vultures are extremely well equipped for a diet of dead flesh, with chemistry and anatomy tuned to a job no other large bird will take. Several vulture populations around the world have collapsed in the last few decades, and the knock-on effects have been severe.

albatross.context_blurb:
No bird owns the open sea like the wandering albatross, a giant white glider of the stormy Southern Ocean that rings Antarctica. It comes ashore only to breed on remote, windswept islands and spends the rest of its long life on the wing, crossing whole oceans while barely moving a feather. Its secrets lie in its wings, its senses and its unhurried family life.

Tip to tip, its wings span 11 or 12 feet, roughly 3.5 meters, the widest of any bird alive; the record holder measured 3.7 meters. Holding such wings out would exhaust ordinary flight muscles. The albatross does not have to, because a tendon in its shoulder locks each wing straight out like a latch, so the bird can glide for hours with no muscle effort at all.

Its fuel is the wind itself: friction slows the air just above the waves while the air a few dozen meters up races faster, so the albatross climbs into the fast upper air, swoops down into the slow air by the sea and climbs again, harvesting energy from the difference every time. Biologists call this dynamic soaring. With it, a foraging wandering albatross can cover about 950 km in a single day, averaging some 40 km an hour, and keep that pace for days while burning almost no energy. Its meals of squid and small fish come with mouthfuls of seawater, so a salt gland above each eye pulls out the extra salt and concentrates it into brine that drips from the bird's tube-shaped nostrils and down its beak. Those nostrils give albatrosses and their relatives the family nickname "tubenoses." Few birds live so long: a wandering albatross that reaches adulthood can survive 50 to 60 years in the wild, sometimes longer.

Satellite tags show how far all that gliding adds up: a GPS-tracked wandering albatross flew a full loop around Antarctica, about 11,600 km, in just 46 days without landing. Finding food in that emptiness is a puzzle, because squid and krill gather in patches far apart that no eye can spot from the air. When krill graze on tiny drifting plants, the plants give off a gas called dimethyl sulfide, the smell of the ocean, and the albatross catches that scent on the wind and zig-zags upwind toward it, tacking like a sailboat. When Gabrielle Nevitt's team GPS-tagged 19 wandering albatrosses in 2008, those upwind zig-zags led to over a third of daytime catches and nearly half at night, the first hard proof that these birds smell their way to dinner.

Family life runs just as slowly. A pair lays a single egg and incubates it for about 78 days, the longest of any bird, and then the fluffy chick sits on its grassy nest for around 278 days, nearly nine months, before its first flight. Because raising a chick takes so long, a pair breeds only every other year. Partners mate for life, yet between seasons they roam the ocean apart for months. When they meet again at the old nest, the two renew their bond with an elaborate greeting dance of sky-pointing, wing-spreading and loud clucking calls. A smaller Pacific cousin, the Laysan albatross, holds the age record: a female nicknamed Wisdom, banded on Midway Atoll in 1956, is the oldest wild bird known anywhere, more than seventy years old and still raising chicks. She has hatched an estimated thirty or more of them.

Even the albatross's fossil past held a surprise. Giant fossil seabirds from Antarctica with 21-foot wingspans were long filed as the biggest albatrosses that ever flew, since their legs and feet were near copies of an albatross's. Their jaws told the truth: they belonged to a separate lineage, the pelagornithids or "bony-toothed" birds, whose beaks bristled with spikes of bone that looked like teeth. Convergent evolution had shaped their legs alike. Real fossil albatrosses were modest; a 3-million-year-old skull from New Zealand belonged to a bird a little smaller than any albatross alive today.

arctic-tern.context_blurb:
The Arctic tern is a small, slender seabird of cold northern coasts. Each year it breeds in the far north, then flies all the way to Antarctica for the southern summer and back again, chasing the sun from one end of the planet to the other. For decades nobody knew the real length of that commute, until tiny tracking tags revealed it.

It is easy to recognize: a black cap pulled low over the head, white cheeks, a deeply forked tail like a swallow's, and a bill and feet of blood-red. No animal on Earth migrates farther, as a 2010 tracking study by Egevang and colleagues showed: every year the tern flies from its Arctic nesting grounds to Antarctica and back.

Living in summer at both ends of the world, the tern enjoys two summers a year and very likely sees more daylight than any other creature. It does not head straight south but follows a giant S-shaped path down the Atlantic, so its true yearly round trip averages about 70,900 km, roughly 44,000 miles. The birds in the study flew anywhere from 59,500 to 81,600 km in a year. Since a tern can live past 30, a lifetime of these trips adds up to about 2.4 million km, the same as flying to the Moon and back about three times.

That S-shaped path follows each ocean's prevailing winds: the tern swings counterclockwise around the great South Atlantic gyre, and on its way north it circles clockwise around the North Atlantic gyre, instead of fighting a straight crossing. To track a bird weighing roughly 100 grams without burdening it, the researchers fitted 11 terns from Greenland and Iceland with geolocators weighing just 1.4 grams each, attached to their leg bands.

bowerbird.context_blurb:
Bowerbirds are forest birds of Australia and New Guinea, and the males build one of the most elaborate courtship displays in the animal kingdom. On the forest floor each male raises a structure of twigs, a bower, and decorates it with carefully chosen objects to impress visiting females. Their arrangements show real attention to color, pattern and even perspective.

The satin bowerbird's bower, a pair of tidy twig walls side by side, is not a nest at all: the male builds it purely as a stage on which to court females, and he comes back to the same spot year after year. The glossy blue-black male is obsessed with blue, decorating his stage with blue clothes pegs, drinking straws, bottle tops and parrot feathers, a color that matches his own plumage and violet-blue eyes, and he will steal blue objects from as far as 12 kilometers away. A female tours several rival bowers and judges each male's strutting display, and after mating she builds a plain, saucer-shaped nest of sticks as high as 30 to 35 meters up a tree and raises the chicks entirely alone.

He even paints, mashing berries and spit into a purple paint and smearing it on the inside of the walls with a wad of bark held in his beak as a brush. Young males stay drab olive-green like the females for seven years, practicing on scrappy trial bowers, before they finally molt into glossy blue-black adult plumage.

In northern Australia, the male great bowerbird arranges pebbles, shells and bones on the court beyond his avenue in order of size, smallest near the spot where the female stands and largest at the far end, a forced-perspective trick that makes the court look smaller and so makes him look bigger. The golden bowerbird of northeastern Australia builds the tallest bowers of all, twin towers of sticks that a young male inherits and rebuilds on the same spot, and the oldest known bowers are over forty years old and more than 2 meters tall.

cassowary.context_blurb:
The cassowary, a towering bird that cannot fly, lives in the rainforests of northern Australia and New Guinea. It can be dangerous when cornered, yet it is also one of the forest's great gardeners, because a long list of rainforest trees depend on it to spread their seeds.

Standing up to about 2 meters tall, the southern cassowary has glossy black feathers, bright blue skin on its head and neck, red at the back of the neck, and a tall grayish helmet called a casque. Zookeepers who handle ostriches, emus and rheas fear it above all of them, and it is widely called the most dangerous bird in the world; a 2019 death in Florida was the first human fatality blamed on a cassowary in 93 years.

Cornered, it leaps and kicks both feet forward, and each foot's inner toe ends in a dagger-like claw about 12 centimeters, or 5 inches, long that can slash open internal organs.

Chicks trot behind their father, and they hatch striped brown and cream down the back and thighs like little watermelons, camouflage they lose at about three to six months as they turn plain brown.

Deep in the foliage it gives booming calls near 32 hertz, among the lowest sounds known from any bird and right at the bottom of human hearing, probably because such a deep note carries far through thick rainforest where higher calls fade. Its casque may help to send or pick up these calls, though what the helmet is really for is still debated.

emperor-penguin.context_blurb:
The emperor penguin is the giant of the penguin world, a flightless seabird that lives on the sea ice of Antarctica and raises its chick through the darkest, coldest winter on Earth. Its survival depends on fathers who fast for months, on huddles of thousands of birds, and on a body built for long, deep dives.

Standing about 1.15 meters, roughly 4 feet, and weighing up to about 45 kilograms, around 100 pounds, the emperor penguin is the biggest penguin alive. Its stiff wings are flippers for swimming, and it lives only in Antarctica, where it breeds in the coldest, darkest months of winter, when no other bird raises young.

In the black of winter the mother lays a single egg, passes it to the father, and walks for weeks back to the sea to feed. An egg that touches the ice can freeze in seconds. So the father balances it on the tops of his feet and covers it with a warm fold of belly skin called the brood pouch. For the 65 to 75 days until it hatches, he eats nothing at all, living on his stored fat.

Across the whole breeding cycle a father can go about 120 days without food and lose about 20 kilograms, dropping from around 38 to about 18. To survive temperatures near minus 40 degrees Celsius in howling wind, more than 4,000 fathers press together in a huddle. Birds on the edge would freeze, so the huddle keeps shuffling forward in slow waves every 30 to 60 seconds, which rotates each bird in turn through the warm center. Deep inside, the temperature can climb to about 37.5 degrees, close to human body heat. If the chick hatches before the mother returns, the starving father can still nourish it briefly with "crop milk," a protein-rich, curd-like food made in his throat. He can produce it for only about 3 to 7 days.

No other bird dives as deep as an emperor, and the deepest reliably measured dive reached 564 meters. Of more than 137,000 dives recorded, the only 12 that went past 500 meters were all made by one single penguin. On long dives the bird rations its oxygen by throttling its heart. A resting emperor's heart beats about 73 times a minute, but in one 18-minute dive it fell to just 3 beats a minute, one beat every 15 seconds.

Long before emperors, giant penguins ruled the same coasts. In rocks about 34 million years old on Seymour Island, off Antarctica, Carolina Acosta Hospitaleche studied the bones of Palaeeudyptes klekowskii, the "mega penguin," and in 2014 estimated that it stood up to 2 meters tall and weighed as much as 115 kilograms, nearly twice an emperor's weight.

hummingbird.context_blurb: The hummingbird is a group of tiny, nectar-feeding birds that live only in the Americas. The smallest, the bee hummingbird of Cuba, weighs less than a penny. Hummingbirds have the fastest wingbeats of any bird, hover in place at flowers, and have the highest metabolism of any vertebrate for their size. All of these features drive a specific set of biology problems that hummingbird research keeps unpacking.

kiwi.context_blurb: The kiwi is a group of flightless, chicken-sized birds that live only in New Zealand. They are the national symbol of the country. Kiwis are nocturnal and have soft hair-like feathers, very poor eyesight, and a long flexible bill with nostrils at the tip. The nostrils-at-the-tip trick is almost unique among birds, and they are built around a very different kind of foraging than most of their flying cousins ever use.

lyrebird.context_blurb: The lyrebird is a large, ground-dwelling bird that lives in the forests of eastern Australia. The male has a long tail that fans up like a lyre in display. The lyrebird is one of the greatest vocal mimics in the natural world and can copy almost any sound it hears, including other birds, human machinery, and even camera shutters. The amount and precision of its mimicry is well-documented, and it has made the lyrebird a repeating star of nature documentaries.

new-caledonian-crow.context_blurb: The New Caledonian crow is a medium-sized black crow that lives only on a few islands in the southwest Pacific. It looks like any other crow at first glance, but it is one of the most skilled tool-using animals in the world. Researchers in Oxford and elsewhere have run careful experiments on these crows for decades. The results keep pushing bird cognition into territory most people associate with chimpanzees.

ostrich.context_blurb: The ostrich is the largest living bird on Earth, a flightless runner that lives on the savannas of Africa. An adult male can stand over nine feet tall. Ostriches cannot fly, but they can run faster than any other bird and defend themselves with a powerful kick. Their eggs, their eyes, and their lungs are all record-setters in their own ways. Ostriches are also still farmed in a number of countries for meat, leather, and feathers.

owl.context_blurb: The owl is a group of mostly nocturnal birds of prey found in every habitat on every continent except Antarctica. Owls combine almost silent flight, forward-facing eyes, and an extraordinary sense of hearing to hunt in near-total darkness. Each of those abilities depends on a specific anatomical feature not shared by most daytime raptors. Species of owl range from palm-sized elf owls to the Blakiston's fish owl, which has a wingspan close to six feet.

peregrine-falcon.context_blurb: The peregrine falcon is a widespread bird of prey found on every continent except Antarctica. It is best known for its hunting dive, which uses gravity to reach some of the fastest speeds ever measured in a living animal. Peregrines nearly went extinct across much of North America in the mid-twentieth century because of DDT contamination; they are now one of the most famous success stories of modern conservation. City skyscrapers in New York, Chicago, and London are now important peregrine nest sites.

shoebill.context_blurb: The shoebill is a huge, slate-grey wading bird that lives in the papyrus swamps of central and eastern Africa. It is one of the tallest wading birds in the world and has a gigantic shoe-shaped bill, from which it gets its name. Shoebills hunt by standing almost perfectly still for hours and then striking in a single motion that biologists have measured carefully. They are also famous for a specific sound they make instead of a call, and for a disturbing look at anyone who gets too close to their nest.

woodpecker.context_blurb: Woodpeckers are a group of birds found in forests on every continent except Antarctica and Australia. They are specialized tree-poundingclimbers with chisel-like beaks, stiff tails, and feet built for gripping bark. Woodpeckers hammer into wood at speeds and forces that would knock out any other bird's brain, and the way they manage to not get hurt is one of the most carefully studied puzzles in avian biomechanics.

17-year-cicada.context_blurb:
In the eastern United States, the forest floor can lie quiet for seventeen years and then, in one summer, boil with insects. Periodical cicadas spend nearly their whole lives in the dark soil and surface by the billions at once, staking their survival on timing and sheer numbers.

The periodical cicada is unforgettable once seen: a glossy black body as long as your thumb, two bulging eyes as red as coals, and clear wings veined in bright orange. For about 99.5 percent of its life it is a pale nymph underground, feeding on the sap of tree roots for 13 or 17 years. Then a whole brood climbs out together in the same few days. Biologists call this survival trick, safety in overwhelming numbers, predator satiation.

The nymphs seem to count the years by sensing seasonal changes in the sap of the roots, then wait for one last cue: the soil about eight inches down warming to roughly 64°F. Out they come, and the males begin to sing. Each male snaps a stiff, ribbed membrane on either side of his body, the tymbal, so fast that the clicks blur together. His abdomen is hollow, and that empty chamber resonates like the body of a guitar, swelling the clicks into a roar of about 100 decibels, among the loudest calls of any insect. After all those years in the dark, an adult lives just four to six weeks above ground, long enough to sing, mate and lay eggs.

A cicada cannot sting, hide or outrun anything, so its defense is arithmetic. A single acre can hold more than 1.5 million of them. Birds and foxes gorge until they can eat no more, and still most of the brood survives to mate. Even the length of the wait may be a weapon, because 13 and 17 are prime numbers, divisible only by themselves and one. As the entomologists Monte Lloyd and Henry Dybas proposed in 1966, a predator whose numbers peak every two, three or four years will almost never peak in the same summer a prime-numbered brood appears, while a 12-year brood would meet all of those hunters at full strength. Stephen Jay Gould later made the idea famous, though it remains a leading hypothesis, not a proven fact.

army-ants.context_blurb:
Army ants live in the tropical forests of the Americas, Africa and Asia, and they never settle down. Instead of building a permanent nest, a whole colony marches through the forest in long columns, overwhelming prey far too big for any single ant. In Central and South American rainforests, Eciton burchellii sends out raids of hundreds of thousands of workers at once.

When the march halts for the night, the workers hook their feet together and become the nest themselves, a living shelter called a bivouac that walls in the queen and the young.

Remarkably, the workers that steer a raid are blind or nearly so, and they hold the swarm together by touch and by chemical scent trails, called pheromones, that they lay down with their own bodies. When a column meets a gap, such as a split between two leaves, ants hook together with the claws on their feet and span it with their bodies, a living bridge the raid pours straight across without slowing.

When Scott Powell and Nigel Franks set out planks full of holes of different sizes on a raiding trail, each worker picked a hole that matched its own body size and flattened into it, so ants carrying prey could run home at full speed over a road paved with their nestmates. Even a nest made only of ants has climate control: the colony opens and closes air passages through the cluster, holding its core near 28.5°C while the air outside heats and cools.

bombardier-beetle.context_blurb:
Barely half an inch long, the bombardier beetle is a ground beetle of fields and forests on every continent except Antarctica. It carries one of the most dramatic chemical weapons in the animal kingdom, blasted out of its hind end and aimed in almost any direction, and scientists still study the chemistry behind the blast.

Grab one and it fires back with a loud pop: a jet of scalding chemical spray, shot from its rear, that makes the attacker drop it at once. The jet comes out near 100°C, or 212°F, as hot as boiling water, enough to scald an attacker's mouth or feet.

The beetle stays safe from its own weapon by storing the two ingredients, hydrogen peroxide and hydroquinone, in separate reservoirs and letting them meet only at the instant it fires. In a lab experiment, faint pops sounded from inside toads that had swallowed bombardier beetles, and 43 percent of the toads threw the beetle back up, after it had spent anywhere from 12 to 107 minutes inside; the slimy beetles scuttled away, and nearly all survived, one for at least 562 more days.

The ingredients meet in a reinforced chamber lined with the enzymes catalase and peroxidase, which make the reaction so fast and hot that it boils and blasts outward. High-speed photography showed that the spray is not a steady stream but a pulse jet of about 70 tiny explosions fired at roughly 500 a second, and the pulsing protects the beetle, since each blast escapes before the next builds up, so the chamber never overloads.

dragonfly.context_blurb:
Dragonflies are long-bodied, four-winged hunters that patrol ponds and streams on every continent except Antarctica. Nearly their whole lives are spent hunting, first underwater and then in the air, and every part of their bodies is built for catching other insects. They have ruled the air over fresh water for hundreds of millions of years.

The dragonfly is the acrobat of the pond: it can stop dead in midair and hover, then dart sideways, backward or straight up, tricks most insects cannot manage. Its head is almost all eye. The two glossy domes wrap so far around that a dragonfly sees nearly a full circle at once, everything except the patch straight behind its head.

It is also one of the deadliest hunters alive: high-speed films show that a dragonfly catches its prey on about 90 to 95 percent of its tries, close to 19 of every 20 attempts, a better record than any lion or shark. It cruises at around 30 miles per hour, yet it beats its wings only about 30 times a second, where a honeybee manages roughly 200. The secret is in the wiring, because in most insects the wings beat in unison, but each of a dragonfly's four wings is worked by its own set of muscles and moves independently, which lets it hover, fly straight backward and turn on a dime.

A dragonfly does not chase its prey the way a hawk or a dog does. It aims at the empty sky ahead, because it has already worked out where the prey will be and flies to meet it at that point. A winged adult lives just a few weeks, but by then the insect can be years old, because it spent nearly all that time underwater as a fierce hunting nymph. The nymph is a stocky brown creature that creeps along the pond floor and breathes through gills. It hunts with a hinged lower jaw called the mask: when a tadpole, mosquito larva or small fish comes near, the mask shoots out almost too fast to see, grabs the prey, and folds back under the head. When the nymph is ready to change, it climbs out of the water onto a reed, its skin splits down the back, and the winged adult pulls itself free, leaving an empty husk called an exuvia clinging to the reed.

About 300 million years ago, in the Carboniferous period, a giant cousin named Meganeura soared on wings roughly 75 centimeters wide, as broad as a hawk's. Textbooks explain its size by the air of the time, which held about 30 to 35 percent oxygen, roughly a third, against about a fifth today, so an insect breathing through tubes could power a giant body. Some living dragonflies are champions of distance. The small globe skimmer rides the monsoon winds over the Indian Ocean from India to East Africa and back, with no land below, and its round trip of about 11,000 miles, flown in relay by parents, children and grandchildren, is the longest migration of any insect. And its hunting brain is astonishingly simple. Just sixteen nerve cells, eight pairs running from the brain to the wing muscles, carry the direction of the prey, tracking a target all the way around the dragonfly with an error of only about one degree.

That tidy oxygen story has a problem. Edouard Harlé first proposed it in 1911, but the biggest insect ever known, Meganeuropsis, had wings nearly 71 centimeters across. Meganeuropsis lived later, in the Permian period, after oxygen levels had already fallen. Some scientists now suspect other reasons for the giants, such as a sky with no birds or pterosaurs yet to hunt them.

dung-beetle.context_blurb:
Dung beetles are stout, glossy beetles that live on droppings. They are found on every continent except Antarctica, and by burying dung they recycle nutrients across grasslands and farms. Many kinds roll their prize away as a ball, and scientists keep discovering how a beetle pushing a ball backward knows where it is going.

On the African savanna a fresh heap of droppings soon draws a dung beetle, which shapes some of the dung into a tidy sphere and rolls it off to bury in the ground, a store of food for itself and its young. In many species the mother shapes a special brood ball like a pear, lays one egg in the slim end and buries the ball deep. Then, unlike most insects, she stays down in the burrow, tending and guarding the ball while her young grow up, a kind of parental care that is rare among insects.

The ancient Egyptians watched this daily labor along the Nile and saw something cosmic in it. To them it was the sacred scarab, and they pictured the god Khepri rolling the sun across the sky each day, just as the beetle rolls its ball, so the scarab became a symbol of the rising sun and of rebirth.

A roller must flee in a straight line before rivals steal its prize. Before setting off, the beetle climbs on top of its ball and turns a full circle in a little dance, storing a snapshot of the sky in its brain to fix a straight bearing. By day it steers by the sun and by night by the moon. On moonless nights it still rolls straight, guided by the faint glowing band of the Milky Way, and Marie Dacke's team proved it in a planetarium, making the dung beetle the first animal known to navigate by the galaxy.

Some dung beetles are astonishingly strong. A male Onthophagus taurus can pull 1,141 times its own weight, making it the strongest insect for its size, comparable to a person hauling six double-decker buses. That strength did not evolve for moving dung but for fighting: horned males brace and shove head-to-head against rivals in the breeding tunnel, and the strongest wins the female.

firefly.context_blurb:
Fireflies, also called lightning bugs, light up warm summer nights on every continent except Antarctica. Their glow is a language, a chemical marvel and, for some fireflies, a deadly trap. Each species blinks its own code, and biologists study firefly light both for its evolutionary story and for its uses in medicine.

Despite both nicknames, a firefly is neither a fly nor a true bug: it is a beetle, one of about 2,000 species in the family Lampyridae.

A firefly's light is "cold light." An old light bulb wastes about 90 percent of its energy as heat, but nearly all of a firefly's energy leaves as light and only a tiny amount as heat. Each species has its own flash code of single, double or multiple pulses. A male patrols in the dark flashing his code, a female of his kind flashes back, and the two keep up this conversation of flash patterns until they find each other, sometimes for more than an hour.

The light is made in the firefly's lower belly, where a molecule called luciferin combines with oxygen and the energy molecule ATP, a reaction sped along by an enzyme called luciferase. On certain June nights, crowds gather in the Great Smoky Mountains to watch Photinus carolinus, the one North American firefly whose males blink together in perfect unison: bursts of 5 to 8 flashes, then about eight seconds of shared darkness. Whole hillsides seem to switch on and off at once.

Some fireflies use light as bait. A predatory Photuris female, nicknamed the femme fatale, copies the answering flash of a Photinus female. When the fooled Photinus male lands beside her, she seizes him and devours him. She gains more than a meal: Photinus males carry defensive steroids called lucibufagins that Photuris cannot make, and eating them gives her toxic chemicals that protect her from birds and spiders.

hercules-beetle.context_blurb:
The Hercules beetle is a giant rhinoceros beetle of the tropical forests from Central America to South America, reaching almost seven inches and ranking among the biggest beetles in the world. Much of that length is horn, and only the males carry it.

A male has two horns that close like a giant pincer. The smaller one juts up from his head, and the much bigger one grows from his back, arching forward above the wing covers. Two males wrestle on a branch over a female. Each tries to catch the other between his horns, then uses the long horn as a lever to pry his rival loose and hurl him off the branch.

The hard wing covers change color with the weather: olive-green or yellow when the air is dry, darkening toward black as the humidity rises.

The adult is only the short last chapter of its life. Before that, it lives for as long as two years as a plump white grub curled in a C, chewing through rotting logs. The grub can reach about 11 centimeters and more than 100 grams, heavier than the horned adult it becomes. The adult then lives only three to six months, sipping sap and fruit.

honeybee.context_blurb:
Honeybees live in colonies of tens of thousands, with a single queen, a few hundred males and a vast crowd of female workers, in a hollow tree or a hive box. Kept by people for thousands of years and vital for pollinating crops, they are among the most studied insects on Earth, above all for the dance they use to share directions.

Nearly all the bees in a hive are workers, females unable to produce eggs, and they do almost every job: gathering nectar and pollen, building wax comb, feeding the larvae and guarding the entrance.

A forager who finds rich flowers flies home. There she dances on the comb in the dark, tracing a figure eight again and again, a straight run with her body shaking and then a turn back to where she began, while the others press close to follow her: this is the waggle dance. Meanwhile the queen does one job at a staggering pace, laying about 2,000 eggs a day, more than her own body weight, each egg only half as big as a rice grain.

Karl von Frisch, an Austrian biologist, worked out the code in the 1940s. The angle of the straight run tells the other bees which way to fly, judged by the sun's position: a run pointing straight up means fly toward the sun, and a run 45 degrees to the left means fly 45 degrees left of it. The length of the waggle tells them how far away the flowers are, a short waggle for nearby food and a long one for a longer flight. Every larva starts out the same, yet one becomes a queen, because the workers feed the chosen larva royal jelly all through her growth, while worker larvae are cut off after three days. Workers make the wax for the comb themselves. It oozes as pale flakes from eight wax glands beneath her abdomen, and she chews it soft and shapes it, but only when the hive is warm, around 95 degrees Fahrenheit, 35 Celsius. Defending the hive costs a worker her life. Her stinger is barbed like a fishhook, so it lodges in the victim, and when she pulls away it tears free, ripping out part of her abdomen. A wasp's smooth stinger slides out, so a wasp can sting again.

She dances in total darkness on a vertical comb, so she uses gravity in place of the sun, treating straight up as the sun's direction. When von Frisch argued in 1927 that the dance was a real coded language, many scientists laughed. He settled it by reading a dance and watching the recruits: bees that had only watched it flew straight to a feeding spot none of them had ever visited. He later shared the 1973 Nobel Prize. Wax is costly, about 8 pounds of honey eaten for every pound of wax made, so the colony builds its cells as hexagons, the shape that holds the most honey with the least wax and stays strong. A meadow also looks different to a bee, because its eyes see ultraviolet light, invisible to us, which reveals glowing bull's-eyes and stripes on many flowers that guide it to the nectar.

Honeybees have an odd family system too. A female hatches from a fertilized egg, with 32 chromosomes from both parents, but a drone grows from an egg that was never fertilized and carries only his mother's 16, so a drone has no father at all. The dance itself was once fiercely disputed: in 1967 Adrian Wenner argued that bees find food by smell and that the dance means nothing. In 1989 Axel Michelsen's team built a robot bee of brass and beeswax with a razor-blade wing buzzing about 280 times a second, programmed it to dance, and it sent real bees to a spot that only it had named, proving that the dance itself carries the location.

leafcutter-ants.context_blurb: Leafcutter ants are a group of ants that live in the tropical forests of Central and South America. They are famous for marching columns of workers each carrying a cut piece of leaf back to the nest. The ants do not actually eat the leaves. Instead, they use them to grow a crop in underground chambers, and the colony arrangement around that crop is one of the most striking cases of farming anywhere outside the human world.

monarch-butterfly.context_blurb: The monarch butterfly is a large orange-and-black butterfly that lives across North America, with populations in Mexico, the United States, and Canada. It is best known for one of the most famous animal migrations on Earth, a multi-generation journey between winter roost sites in central Mexico and summer breeding grounds far to the north. Monarchs are also chemically defended as caterpillars, and both of those features are at the heart of modern conservation efforts to save a species that has been declining fast.

peacock-spider.context_blurb: The peacock spider is a group of tiny jumping spiders that live mostly in Australia. The males fit on a fingernail, but they put on an elaborate visual courtship display that has made them an internet sensation. The dance is complicated enough that researchers have mapped out individual moves. For a species this small, the show is extraordinary.

praying-mantis.context_blurb: The praying mantis is a group of long, slender predatory insects found across most of the world, especially the tropics. They are named for the way they hold their folded forelegs together as they wait in ambush for other insects. Mantises have forward-facing eyes, extremely fast strike reflexes, and a famous courtship pattern that often makes it into high-school biology classrooms. They are the only insects that can turn their heads to look over their shoulders.

tardigrade.context_blurb: The tardigrade, also called a water bear or moss piglet, is a microscopic eight-legged animal that lives in mosses, lichens, and water puddles almost everywhere on Earth. Tardigrades are famous for surviving conditions that would kill almost any other animal, including the vacuum of space, deep radiation, and complete dehydration. The way they manage all this is still being worked out, and researchers have launched tardigrades on space missions on purpose to test the limits.

axolotl.context_blurb:
The axolotl is a soft, pale-pink salamander with black eyes and a frilly crown, found in the wild only in the old lake canals of Mexico City. Millions live in laboratories and home aquariums around the world, because the axolotl does two things almost no other animal can: it keeps a baby-like body all its life, and it rebuilds lost body parts.

Its frilly crown is made of six feathery branches fanning out behind its head, and they are external gills: oxygen passes straight from the water into the blood flowing through them. Its famous grin says nothing about its mood; the smile is simply the fixed, upturned shape of its mouth.

The axolotl never grows up in the usual way: it keeps its feathery gills, soft body and tail fin for life, yet it becomes fully mature and breeds while still in that larval form, a condition biologists call neoteny. It is also a champion of regrowth: if a tankmate bites off a leg, a complete new leg grows back within weeks, with bone, muscle, nerves, blood vessels and even the pigment pattern, and no scar. Yet in the wild it is critically endangered: pollution and sewage cut the population by 99 percent between 1998 and 2014, and perhaps 50 to 1,000 survive, all in the canals of Xochimilco, the last scrap of the great lakes that once surrounded Mexico City.

Legs are only the start, because the axolotl can also regrow its tail, its jaw, sections of its spinal cord, portions of its brain and even parts of its heart. The secret lies in how a wound heals: a human cut closes with a patch of collagen that toughens into scar tissue, but an axolotl stump clears away the debris and then switches its cells back into embryo-style growth, rebuilding the part perfectly. Its immune system is unusually tolerant, too: scientists have grafted eyes and even pieces of brain from one axolotl onto another, and the foreign organs settled in and worked normally, with no rejection. Its baby form can even be undone: given thyroid hormone, an axolotl loses its gills, its tail fin shrinks, and it crawls onto land as a gill-less salamander that looks almost exactly like its cousin the tiger salamander.

In a 1968 experiment reported in the journal Science, researchers grafted a second head onto an axolotl, and the extra head not only survived but grew and behaved like a normal head, snapping at and eating prey on its own. Regrowth depends on the immune system: in 2013 Godwin, Pinto and Rosenthal wiped out an axolotl's macrophages, a type of immune cell, before amputating a limb, and the stump healed like a mammal's wound, sealed for good under thick collagen scar tissue, so no leg ever grew back, even after the macrophages returned.

When scientists read its genome in 2018, it was the largest ever assembled, about 32 billion letters, more than ten times the human genome, and it held a shock: Pax3, a gene every other backboned animal was thought to need, is missing, and its close cousin gene Pax7 has taken over the job.

chameleon.context_blurb:
Chameleons are slow, mostly tree-dwelling lizards of Africa, Madagascar, southern Europe and parts of Asia. They are famous for turret eyes that move on their own, a tongue fired like a projectile, and skin that changes color. Modern research has shown that each of these tricks works differently from the old textbook story.

Perched motionless, a chameleon catches an insect with its tongue, which rockets out about 2.5 times the length of its body and hits the bug in roughly 20 milliseconds, a fraction of a blink.

Its two eyes sit in cone-shaped turrets and swivel independently, so it can watch a hawk overhead with one eye and a beetle behind it with the other, scanning almost a full circle without turning its head while its brain handles two separate pictures. The moment it spots prey, both eyes swing forward and lock onto the same target, sizing up the distance to within a few millimeters, because once the tongue fires there is no correcting its aim. Its famous color change is mostly not camouflage: a chameleon changes color mainly to signal its mood and intentions and to warm up or cool down, so a calm chameleon and an angry one are literally different colors.

About half of the roughly 200 chameleon species live only on Madagascar, the big island off Africa's east coast. There lives the nano-chameleon, Brookesia nana, whose male has a body just 13.5 millimeters long, about 22 with the tail, small enough to perch on a fingertip and possibly the smallest reptile on Earth. Male Jackson's chameleons of the East African mountains carry three forward-pointing horns like a tiny Triceratops, and rival males lock horns and try to push each other off the branch.

In 2015 Swiss researchers studying panther chameleons found that the skin holds a grid of tiny guanine crystals, and tightening or loosening that grid changes which colors of light bounce back, blue when packed tight and yellow or red when spread apart, a structural color rather than pigment. The club-shaped tongue tip is coated in mucus about 400 times more viscous than human saliva, and the quicker the tongue whips home, the stronger that grip becomes, letting a chameleon haul in surprisingly heavy prey. Per kilogram of muscle its tongue launch delivers about 14,000 watts, more than any reptile, bird or mammal, and among all backboned animals only salamanders beat it.

The launch works even when its body has cooled to 3.5°C, because the tongue is a spring: a slow accelerator muscle first stretches a sleeve of coiled collagen sheaths around a stiff bone in the tongue, and the loaded sheaths then slide off its tip and recoil all at once like a drawn bow. In tests, cold cut the power of the launch only slightly, while the muscle-powered pull back weakened sharply. A chameleon can also judge range with only one eye, the only vertebrate known to do so, by focusing that eye on the prey and treating the focus setting as a measure of distance, helped by a lens and cornea that enlarge the image so tiny focus changes show up clearly.

glass-frog.context_blurb:
Glass frogs are small, lime-green tree frogs of the cloud forests and rainforests of Central and South America, about 160 species in all. They spend their nights on leaves above rushing streams, and their bodies are partly see-through, a disguise scientists have only recently begun to understand.

Flip a glass frog onto its back and you can see straight through the skin of its belly to the organs inside. Most of them sit still, but one never stops moving: through that clear skin you can watch its heart beat as it pumps blood, along with the liver and looping intestines.

Glass frogs lay their eggs on the underside of leaves that hang over streams, so the hatching tadpoles drop straight into the water. It is the male that guards the eggs, standing watch for days and driving off egg-eating wasps, sometimes over several clutches at once.

By day a sleeping glass frog is two to three times more transparent than an active one. In 2022 scientists filming resting frogs discovered how: the frog hides nearly 90 percent of its red blood cells, which would give away its red tint, crammed inside its liver, whose mirror-like lining conceals them. At night it releases them again, and somehow the packed blood never forms a deadly clot.

goliath-frog.context_blurb:
The goliath frog, Conraua goliath, is the biggest frog on Earth. It lives only along fast, rocky rainforest streams in Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea, where the adults perch on boulders amid the white water. Hunting and habitat loss have put it in serious trouble.

It can grow to about 34 centimeters long and 3.3 kilograms, roughly the size and weight of a house cat.

Most male frogs call by puffing up a vocal sac on the throat, but the goliath frog has none and cannot croak. To attract a female, the male simply opens his mouth and gives a whistle. In 2019 scientists found these frogs doing something never seen before in any frog or toad of Africa. They build nests, clearing little ponds along the riverbank and dragging rocks around the edges to wall them off, then guarding the eggs inside.

Those rocks can weigh more than half the frog's own weight, up to about 2 kilograms. The scientists who study it think that all this heavy hauling of nest stones may be what drove the goliath frog to grow so far beyond every other frog.

king-cobra.context_blurb: The king cobra is the longest venomous snake in the world, a long, slender hooded snake that lives in the forests of South and Southeast Asia. Despite the name, it is not a true cobra; it belongs to its own genus. King cobras are specialists at eating other snakes, including other venomous ones. The female is also unusual among snakes for the way she treats her eggs, and the whole species has a far more carefully controlled lifestyle than its reputation suggests.

komodo-dragon.context_blurb: The Komodo dragon is the largest living lizard, found only on a few small islands in Indonesia. Adults can exceed 10 feet in length and 150 pounds in weight. Komodos are ambush predators that take down deer, pigs, and even water buffalo, and they combine several nasty features in their bite that scientists are still sorting out. Their reproductive biology also has a quirk unusual for a vertebrate this size.

poison-dart-frog.context_blurb: Poison dart frogs are a group of small, brilliantly colored tree frogs that live in the rainforests of Central and South America. The colors are warnings: many species are among the most toxic animals on Earth, a few drops of their skin chemistry enough to kill much larger animals. Indigenous peoples of the Choco region of Colombia have used the toxins to tip blowgun darts for centuries. The chemistry turns out to come from the frog's diet, not from the frog itself.

saltwater-crocodile.context_blurb:
From the river mouths of northern Australia and India east through Southeast Asia to the islands of the western Pacific, one reptile rules the brackish water and even the open sea. The saltwater crocodile is an ancient design with record-breaking power, and it crosses wide stretches of water between islands.

The saltwater crocodile is the largest reptile alive: a big male reaches about 20 feet from snout to tail and can weigh around a ton. Nearly every other crocodile lives in fresh water. The saltie, as it is nicknamed, thrives at sea and in the salty water where rivers meet the ocean, and it turns up far out at sea, hundreds of miles from the nearest river.

It hunts by ambush, floating like a log with only its eyes showing until a buffalo or other big animal wades too close, then bursting upward to seize it. The crocodile drags a victim too heavy to wrestle on the bank into deep water and holds it under until it drowns. Its teeth are made to grip, not chew, so a carcass larger than one gulp is a problem. It solves this by clamping onto a limb and spinning its whole body over and over until the piece twists free, a move called the death roll.

That grip comes with record force. Gregory Erickson measured it in Australia's wild salties with a cushioned bite gauge between their jaws. The biggest clamped down with some 3,700 pounds of force on every square inch, the strongest bite measured in any living animal, enough to crush bone or a turtle's shell in one bite. When Erickson's team tested all 23 kinds of crocodilian, from little caimans to the largest crocodiles, the saltwater crocodile topped the list, beating even the mighty American alligator, which managed about 2,980 pounds. It does not even need to see its prey. Thousands of tiny black domes freckle its jaws and skin, pressure sensors so delicate they can feel the ripple a single drop of water makes, so the crocodile can strike at a fish or bird moving in pitch-black water.

Out at sea, salt is the danger, and there is no fresh water to drink. Special glands on its tongue pump the extra salt back out, and they work nearly three times as hard when the crocodile is in the sea as in a river. Satellite tags revealed how it travels so far. Tracked crocodiles moved with the current on 96 percent of their long journeys and almost never fought against it, riding the tides like surfers; one male traveled 590 kilometers in 25 days after leaving the Kennedy River. Steve Irwin, famous worldwide as the Crocodile Hunter, helped tag the animals for that research, and the discovery appeared in print only after he died suddenly in 2006.

Crocodiles are often called living fossils, because their basic body plan is more than 200 million years old. But the shape and the species keep different clocks. Jamie Oaks used DNA to map how the true crocodiles are related, and found that the whole genus Crocodylus, the saltie's own group, arose and spread only about 13.6 to 8.3 million years ago, from an ancestor in the tropical Indo-Pacific. The saltwater crocodile is a young species wearing an ancient design.

sea-turtle.context_blurb: The sea turtle is a group of large, long-lived marine turtles found in oceans around the world. All seven living species are classified as threatened or endangered. Sea turtles come ashore only to lay eggs, and most of their adult lives are spent swimming across huge ocean distances. Their navigation, their diet, and their long migratory routes are each the subject of major modern conservation projects.

tuatara.context_blurb: The tuatara is a lizard-shaped reptile that lives only on a few islands off the coast of New Zealand. It looks like a lizard, but it is not one; the tuatara is the only living member of an order of reptiles that otherwise died out around the same time as the dinosaurs. It has features of its skeleton, teeth, and even eye that have not changed in a very long time. Everything about the tuatara's slow life, from how long it takes to grow up to how long it lives, is on a scale almost unmatched among reptiles.

wood-frog.context_blurb: The wood frog is a small, dark-masked frog that lives in forests across much of Canada and the northern United States, farther north than any other North American amphibian. It survives winters that would kill every other North American frog by doing something to its own body that biologists find hard to believe the first time they read about it. The wood frog is one of the clearest living examples of how an animal can survive conditions that would otherwise be lethal.

dire-wolf.context_blurb:
The dire wolf was a big, heavily built hunter of ice-age America, ranging across North America and into South America until it died out about 10,000 years ago. Thousands of its skeletons have come out of the La Brea tar pits of Los Angeles, and ancient DNA has shown that it was no ordinary wolf.

The largest dire wolves averaged about 68 kilograms, around 150 pounds, while a big male gray wolf weighs about 43. Its powerful jaws were made for crushing, and it specialized in giant ice-age plant-eaters such as camels, ground sloths, western horses and ancient bison. When those big animals died out at the end of the ice age, the dire wolf vanished with them, while smaller, more adaptable gray wolves survived.

For over a century scientists treated it as simply a larger cousin of the gray wolf. Then in 2021 a team led by the biologist Angela Perri recovered ancient DNA from dire wolf bones and found it was no close relative of wolves at all, so distinct that it was moved into a genus of its own, Aenocyon dirus. At La Brea, sticky asphalt seeped up and held fast any animal that stepped in. When a big plant-eater got stuck, its cries drew predators and scavengers, and the dire wolves that came for an easy meal got stuck as well, again and again over thousands of years.

The DNA showed that the dire wolf line had branched off on its own about 5.7 million years ago. After so long apart it could not interbreed with gray wolves, and its genes show no mixing. Its closest living relatives turned out to be African jackals; its wolf-like look evolved separately, a case of convergent evolution. Between 5 and 17 percent of La Brea dire wolf specimens have cracked or broken teeth, while among modern wolves and lions the figure is 0.5 to 2.7 in every hundred. That damage points to bone crunching during hard, competitive feeding on big carcasses.

There were really two kinds of dire wolf, split by the Rocky Mountains, and Björn Kurtén named them in 1984. The eastern form, about 68 kilograms, had long legs like a modern wolf's, built for the chase. The western form, the one dug up by the thousand at La Brea, averaged about 60 kilograms and stood on shorter, stockier legs, its hind limbs about 8 percent shorter than a Yukon wolf's, which made it the weaker runner of the two. A 2019 study has since questioned whether the two are truly separate subspecies.

giant-ground-sloth.context_blurb:
Giant ground sloths were huge relatives of today's tree sloths that walked the Americas during the ice age. The biggest, Megatherium of South America, was the size of an elephant and survived until about 12,000 years ago. Unlike its small modern cousins it lived on the ground, and its bones and footprints are still revealing surprises.

Megatherium stretched about 6 meters long and weighed around 4,000 kilograms, the size of a bull elephant, yet its closest living relatives are the cat-sized tree sloths that hang in South American rainforests. Those tree sloths move so little that green algae grows in their grooved hair, tinting them green and hiding them among the leaves.

To reach high leaves, Megatherium rose up onto its hind legs and tail, braced like a tripod against a tree trunk, standing about 3.5 meters tall and pulling branches down with its forelimbs. Its front claws were about 30 centimeters long, too long for it to plant its feet flat. Like a modern anteater, it walked on the outer edges of its feet with the claws curled inward.

Those claws were also weapons: a single swipe could kill an attacker, so even sabre-toothed cats and dire wolves rarely challenged a full-grown adult. Under its shaggy fur, the skin was studded with thousands of tiny bones, from lentil-sized to about 2 centimeters, forming a chain-mail mesh that armored it against a predator's bite. At White Sands in New Mexico, fossil footprints at least 11,700 years old show a person stepping inside a giant sloth's own tracks, stalking it across an ancient mudflat.

For a century, scientists sorting sloths by their skeletons thought today's two-toed and three-toed sloths were close cousins. In 2019, ancient DNA and fossil proteins showed otherwise: the three-toed sloth sits among the relatives of Megatherium, while the two-toed sloth groups with another ground sloth, Mylodon. So each of the two took up its slow life hanging in the trees independently, descended from a different giant ground sloth. Richard Fariña and Ernesto Blanco noticed that Megatherium's elbow lever, the spot where the triceps muscle anchors, is short, built for speed rather than force, as in meat-eaters. They proposed that it may have been a part-time predator or scavenger that drove its claws in like daggers, though chemical evidence from its bones points to a plant diet, and the idea remains debated.

glyptodon.context_blurb:
Glyptodon was a giant armored relative of the armadillo that grazed the grasslands of South America during the last ice age. Picture an armadillo blown up as big as a small car, its whole back hidden under one huge bony dome. Glyptodons died out along with most of the other big American animals, and DNA has since revealed where they belong.

The glyptodon grew to about 3 meters long, and the biggest species reached around 2 tonnes, as big as a Volkswagen Beetle. For all its armor and the helmet of fused bone on its head, it was a plant-eater, with a broad muzzle for grazing low grasses and plants along forest edges.

A modern armadillo can roll into a ball because its shell is made of flexible bands. Glyptodon could not: its dome was about 1,800 bony plates fused solid into a single rigid shell and locked onto its hip bones. At the Pay Paso 1 site in Uruguay, human spear points lie beside glyptodon fossils. Researchers think early South Americans may have sheltered under the huge empty shells in bad weather, like ready-made domed tents.

Doedicurus, a close cousin, carried a spiked club of bone at the end of its tail that could deliver about 60 kilonewtons of force, far more than the roughly 4 needed to snap a human thigh bone. Some glyptodont shells carry dents that match the size and shape of such a club, evidence that these living tanks clubbed each other, probably in fights over mates or territory. Micro-CT scans show why a single plate, about 2.5 centimeters thick, could take a blow: each is built like a sandwich, with dense outer layers of bone wrapped around a porous inner lattice that absorbs the impact and stops cracks from spreading. Armor engineers now copy the design.

In 2016 Delsuc, Poinar and their colleagues read the mitochondrial DNA of Doedicurus and found that glyptodonts sit deep inside the armadillo family tree. Their common ancestor with modern armadillos weighed only about 6 kilograms, so the glyptodon line multiplied its body mass more than 300 times over, reaching about 2,000 kilograms.

irish-elk-giant-deer.context_blurb: The Irish elk, more properly called the giant deer, was a huge deer that lived across Eurasia from the British Isles to central Russia during the ice age. The name is misleading: it was not an elk and was not confined to Ireland. The males of the species carried the largest antlers of any deer that ever lived, which is why so many well-preserved specimens have come out of Irish peat bogs. The giant deer went extinct between roughly 10,000 and 7,000 years ago.

mastodon.context_blurb: The mastodon was a huge elephant-like mammal that lived in the forests of North and Central America during the ice age and died out around 10,000 years ago. Despite looking like a mammoth, the mastodon belonged to a different family of elephant relatives. Its tusks, its teeth, and the way its molars were shaped are the clearest clues that it was a browser, not a grazer, and the differences from mammoths show up on almost every skeleton pulled out of a bog or quarry.

short-faced-bear.context_blurb:
In ice-age North America lived the giant short-faced bear, Arctodus simus, a long-legged, blunt-muzzled bear that vanished with most of the continent's great beasts at the end of the last ice age. No bear yet found stood taller, and much of what people once believed about it has been overturned.

On its hind legs Arctodus reached about 11 or 12 feet, high enough to peer down over a basketball hoop's rim, which hangs at 10 feet.

People once imagined it as a racing super-predator that chased saber-tooths off their kills, and older chemical studies read it as a pure meat-eater. In 2010 Borja Figueirido's team studied its teeth and argued instead that it was a giant opportunistic omnivore: the teeth show wear from eating plants and lack the meat-slicing shape of a true super-predator. What Arctodus ate is still debated. It was not even the heaviest bear. That record belongs to Arctotherium angustidens, a South American cousin of the short-faced bears, known from a skeleton about a million years old found during hospital construction in La Plata, Argentina, and estimated at about 1,588 kilograms, roughly double a large Arctodus.

Even its name may be a mistake. Arctodus looks stubby-faced because of a deep snout and short nasal bones. But when Figueirido measured the skull, the face proved no shorter than other bears' at all, just taller and wider, so it only looked short.
