the-five-vertebrate-classes-the-recognit.context_blurb: The vertebrates, animals with a backbone, are usually sorted into five big living classes: fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals. The interesting questions are how biologists tell the five apart, what the key features of each one are, and the places where the lines get blurrier than textbooks suggest. The idea that each class has a tidy definition is useful for a 10th-grade reader but hides some real surprises in modern taxonomy.

the-rule-breakers-monotremes-and-marsupi.context_blurb: Most mammals carry their young inside the body and give birth to live, fully-formed babies. Monotremes and marsupials are the exceptions. Monotremes, which include the platypus and echidnas, still lay eggs; marsupials, including kangaroos, koalas, and opossums, give birth to tiny, barely-formed young that finish developing outside the body. These two rule-breaking groups are important for understanding what being a mammal really means.

what-makes-a-bird.context_blurb: Birds are the only living animals with feathers, and feathers are the single most useful feature for picking a bird out of a lineup. But birds also share a specific body plan: a toothless beak, hollow bones, a large keeled breastbone, and air-sac lungs. Look closely at the main features that make a bird a bird, which of them show up elsewhere in the animal kingdom, and how birds inherited their key traits from a specific group of dinosaurs.

what-makes-a-mammal.context_blurb: Mammals are a diverse group of animals that includes everything from mice to blue whales. All of them share a specific set of features: hair, milk-producing mammary glands, three middle-ear bones, and a four-chambered heart. Look closely at the key features that define a mammal, how biologists use them to tell mammals apart from the other vertebrate groups, and the handful of mammal species that break the usual rules in surprising ways.

what-makes-a-reptile-an-amphibian-dry-sc.context_blurb: Reptiles and amphibians are easy to confuse at first glance, but they are two very different animal groups. Reptiles, including snakes, lizards, turtles, and crocodilians, have dry scaly skin and lay shelled eggs on land. Amphibians, including frogs, salamanders, and caecilians, have soft moist skin and mostly lay unshelled eggs in water. Look closely at the key features that separate the two groups and why the differences are more than just skin-deep.

antifreeze-blood-and-freezing-solid.context_blurb:
Below freezing, ice is a killer, because sharp crystals that form inside a living cell burst it like a water balloon. Animals of the polar seas, the northern forests and the Arctic tundra have found two ways around the danger. Some keep their bodies liquid with natural antifreeze; others let themselves freeze solid and come back to life when spring arrives.

In the forests of Canada the wood frog spends the winter under the leaf litter frozen solid, with up to about two-thirds of its body water turned to ice, no heartbeat and no breath, then thaws in spring and simply hops away. In the waters around Antarctica the crocodile icefish is stranger still: no other vertebrate lacks red blood cells and hemoglobin entirely, and without that red pigment its blood runs clear and white.

Those seas sit near minus 1.9°C, cold enough to turn an ordinary fish's blood to slush, but the notothenioid fish carry antifreeze proteins that latch onto any tiny ice crystal that gets inside and hold it so it cannot grow. The wood frog guards its cells another way: before it freezes, the frog's liver floods its cells with glucose, blood sugar, which keeps the inside of each cell from freezing while ice forms only in the safe gaps between them.

When the April soil warms, the frozen frog's heart and brain restart on their own after months of silence, and within about 10 hours it is hopping and behaving normally again. Inside a knobby gall on a goldenrod plant, the larva of the goldenrod gall fly freezes on purpose: in autumn it fills itself with glycerol, and as the cold deepens it adds a second protectant, sorbitol, which lets it survive frozen at temperatures as low as minus 40°C, thawing and refreezing all winter. The Arctic ground squirrel of Alaska hibernates at a body temperature of minus 2.9°C, the lowest ever measured in a mammal, and its blood stays liquid because it supercools: the squirrel clears out the tiny specks that ice needs to start forming around.

Antifreeze has a cost. The notothenioid's proteins grip ice so tightly that trapped crystals refuse to melt even when summer water warms above their normal melting point, so the fish may carry ice inside its body all its life. The gene for that antifreeze was not invented from scratch: in 1997 biologists showed it had been rebuilt from the gene for trypsinogen, a gut enzyme from the pancreas that digests food, by keeping the old gene's ends and copying a tiny snippet over and over to grow the long backbone. The switch happened about 5 to 14 million years ago, around the time the Antarctic Ocean first froze. The icefish copes with thin, clear blood by pumping a great deal of it: its heart is oversized, moving four to five times more blood for its weight than a normal fish's, through extra-wide vessels. Why it lost its red cells at all is still argued, and a leading 2006 review by Sidell and O'Brien finds no measured benefit: the mutation probably survived only because cold, predator-poor Antarctic water relaxed the pressure of natural selection long enough for the giant heart and other fixes to evolve. Icefish live right beside red-blooded cousins, and their blood carries only about a tenth as much oxygen, so other biologists still debate whether the loss was ever useful.

coming-back-from-dry-death-cryptobiosis.context_blurb:
A few tiny animals can dry out until they seem dead, wait for years, and then wake up when water returns. Biologists call this power cryptobiosis, meaning "hidden life." The most famous champion is the tardigrade, a microscopic animal of damp moss, but brine shrimp, midge larvae and rotifers share the trick, and scientists are still working out how it is done.

Squeeze a clump of wet moss and the drop that falls may hold a tardigrade, a plump animal about half a millimeter long that clambers on eight stubby, clawed legs. Its rounded body and slow, lumbering walk have earned it the nickname water bear, and sometimes moss piglet. When the moss dries in the sun, the tardigrade tucks in its head and legs, loses over 95 percent of the water in its body, and shrivels into a little barrel called a tun. Hours after one drop of water lands on it, the tun swells, and the water bear walks away. Brine shrimp play the same game with their eggs, which can sit bone-dry for years. That is why old comic-book ads sold brine shrimp to American kids as "Sea-Monkeys": a packet of dried eggs poured into water becomes a bowl of swimmers a few days later.

The famous toughness has a catch. An active, water-filled tardigrade is soft and fragile; a hungry mite can eat it, and a careless finger can crush it. Only the dried, dormant tun can shrug off boiling heat, deep cold and crushing pressure. In September 2007 European scientists ran a test named Tardigrades in Space, fixing dried water bears to the outside of the Foton-M3 satellite. For about ten days the animals sat in the bare vacuum of space, beyond the air, and many revived back on Earth, making the tardigrade the first animal shown to survive it. The same shutdown guards against more than thirst: cryptobiosis is the umbrella word for going dormant to survive drought, freezing or a lack of oxygen.

How does a dried animal keep its cells from falling apart? As a tardigrade dries, special proteins called CAHS proteins team up with a little trehalose, a sugar, and set the fluid inside its cells into a solid glass. The glass locks each cell's parts in place until water returns. In that state the animal's metabolism falls below 0.01 percent of normal, so faint it is almost undetectable, and a tun can last for years with nothing to eat or drink, by some reports up to about thirty. The water bear has rivals. In seasonal pools of central Africa lives the larva of a midge, a small mosquito-like fly. When its pool dries up, the larva loses about 97 percent of its water and turns glassy too, and one dried larva has revived after about 17 years.

The deepest secrets lie in the tardigrade's own genes. In 2016 Japanese scientists reading the DNA of a tardigrade species, Ramazzottius varieornatus, found a protein never seen elsewhere in nature and named it Dsup, for "damage suppressor." Dsup binds to DNA and wraps it like a shield against radiation damage, and it still protects DNA when its gene is placed in human cells grown in a lab dish.

Cold survivors may last far longer. In 2021 Russian scientists thawed a bdelloid rotifer, a microscopic freshwater animal, out of Siberian permafrost. Radiocarbon dating of the frozen mud around it showed the rotifer had been dormant for about 24,000 years, and once warmed, it woke and began to reproduce.

Scientists long assumed every dry survivor leaned on trehalose, because brine shrimp pack their dried eggs with the sugar. Tardigrades break that rule. In 2008 Ralph Hengherr's team found that the common lab tardigrade Milnesium tardigradum dries and revives perfectly with no detectable trehalose at all, because its own CAHS proteins do the main work of turning the cell to glass. That glass also marks the water bear's true limit. Headlines say a tun survives 150 degrees Celsius, and it can take a quick scald, but when Hengherr heated nine dried species in 2009, revival stayed high up to roughly 80 degrees, then fell steeply. The drop matched the temperature at which each species' inner glass softens back toward a liquid, and once the glass melts, the protection is gone.

heat-exchange-plumbing-countercurrent.context_blurb:
Many animals save heat with a simple piece of plumbing: they run warm blood flowing one way right beside cold blood flowing the other. Heat crosses from the warm stream to the cold one before it can escape. This countercurrent exchange keeps penguins' feet from freezing, keeps fast fish warm, and can even be run in reverse.

A penguin can stand on bare Antarctic ice for hours. Warm feet would melt the ice beneath them, which would then refreeze into a trap, and they would waste precious heat. So the penguin keeps its feet just above freezing: cold, cheap to run, and losing almost no heat.

Inside each leg, the vessels taking warm blood down to the feet are wrapped around the vessels bringing chilled blood back up. As they pass in opposite directions, the warm blood hands its heat across to the returning blood, so the heat is recycled into the body instead of being lost at the feet. Herons and ducks standing in icy water use the same leg bundles. Fish use the trick too. Most fish are cold-blooded and turn sluggish in cold water, but a great white shark keeps its swimming muscles 6 to 10 degrees Celsius warmer than the sea, so it can hunt hard where its prey slows down.

In tuna and great whites, the net of blood vessels that does this is called the rete mirabile, Latin for "wonderful net": warm blood leaving the muscle passes cold blood coming in and hands its heat back before it can escape through the gills. The swordfish warms a different organ. Its heater organ, made from an altered eye muscle, keeps its eyes and brain 10 to 15 degrees above the icy sea, and a warm retina responds faster, so it can spot fast-darting squid and fish that a cold-eyed fish would miss. A reindeer breathes Arctic air at minus 40 degrees, yet scroll-like bones in its nose, wrapped in blood vessels, warm each breath to body temperature. When it breathes out, the same bones recapture warmth and water from the air leaving its body, so almost nothing is wasted. Tuna and sharks warm only certain patches, while their hearts pump cold blood. In 2015 scientists found that the opah, a round, silver deep-sea fish, is warm throughout its whole body, even its heart. It makes heat by constantly flapping its wing-like fins and holds it in with fat-wrapped vessel nets inside its gills.

Tuna and the great white's shark family are only distant relatives, yet each evolved this warm-muscle plumbing separately, and penguins and reindeer reached the same trick on their own too, a textbook case of convergent evolution. The plumbing can also run in reverse. A whale working hard builds up heat in its huge muscles, and its flippers and tail flukes are its only thin, bare-skinned parts. To cool down, it skips the heat-saving vein bundles and floods the flukes with warm blood, so the heat pours out into the sea. Fish gills use the same countercurrent idea for oxygen. Water streams across the gill filaments in one direction while blood runs the opposite way, so the blood keeps meeting fresher water and pulls out about 90 percent of the oxygen in it. The swim bladder of a deep-sea fish goes further, because its vessel net works as a multiplier. Oxygen leaving in the outgoing vein leaks across to the incoming artery, so each pass adds to the one before and the oxygen keeps building, until the fish can force gas into the bladder against pressures of hundreds of atmospheres.

living-without-water.context_blurb: Some animals almost never drink water. Desert rodents like kangaroo rats, camels, and a handful of insects extract nearly all the water they need from their food and metabolism. Look closely at the specific body chemistry, kidney function, and behavior that let an animal keep its tissues wet in an environment where free water is almost always out of reach.

size-ears-and-heat-radiators-and-bergman.context_blurb: Animals in cold climates tend to be larger and more compact, while animals in hot climates tend to be smaller and have longer limbs and ears. The pattern is called Bergmann's and Allen's rules, and it is tied to a simple physics problem about surface area and volume. The interesting questions are how the rules play out in real animals, where they break, and how body parts like elephant ears or fennec fox ears work as built-in radiators.

sleeping-through-winter-hibernation-and-.context_blurb: A number of mammals and a few other animals get through winter by lowering their body temperature and metabolism and sleeping it off. The deepest version is hibernation, used by ground squirrels and marmots among others; a shallower version, torpor, is used daily by hummingbirds and some bats. The interesting questions are what the body does during these shutdowns, how it protects itself from damage, and why only some animals have this strategy available.

the-two-engines-warm-blooded-vs-cold-blo.context_blurb: Vertebrates split roughly into two groups by the way they manage body temperature. Mammals and birds burn food fast to generate their own body heat, which lets them stay active in the cold but costs a lot of food. Fish, reptiles, and amphibians rely on the sun and the surrounding environment, which is cheaper but much more dependent on weather. Look closely at the trade-offs each strategy brings and the animals that blur the line between the two.

compound-eyes-and-the-insect-mosaic.context_blurb:
Insects and many of their relatives see through compound eyes: big domed eyes built from thousands of tiny units packed side by side, each pointing a slightly different way and catching its own scrap of the view. Such an eye is poor at fine detail, but it is superb at catching movement, exactly what fast hunters and fast escapers need.

A dragonfly's eyes wrap around most of its head, and each one holds up to 30,000 of those units, called ommatidia. Every ommatidium is a lens over a light catcher that registers a single dot of light, and the brain stitches the dots into a mosaic picture.

Motion is where this design shines. A housefly takes in about 250 flashes of light per second, where a human manages about 60, so a fly sees roughly four times faster than you do. To the fly, a swatting hand drifts down in slow motion, leaving plenty of time to escape.

The dragonfly turns its eyes into a weapon, snatching mosquitoes and midges out of the air about 95 percent of the time. High-speed films of its head, wings and eyes show why. Its brain does not simply chase the spot where the prey is now: sixteen special nerve cells track the target, and the brain forecasts where the prey is heading, then steers the wings to meet it there.

The mantis shrimp, a bright reef hunter of the Indo-Pacific, owns the oddest compound eyes on the planet. Each eye rides on its own movable stalk, worked by eight tiny muscles, so the two eyes can swivel independently and look in completely different directions at the same moment.

eyeshine-and-seeing-in-the-dark.context_blurb:
Many night-active animals, from cats and deer to raccoons and crocodiles, have eyes that blaze back at you in a beam of light. That glow is a side effect of a trick for seeing in near darkness. Other night hunters solve the same problem in completely different ways.

A deer's eyes flash greenish gold in headlights because of the tapetum lucidum, Latin for "bright tapestry," a mirror-like sheet behind the retina: light that slips past the light-sensing cells hits the mirror and bounces back through them, giving the eye a second chance to catch it.

Humans and most other primates have no tapetum, so our eyes never shine. In a flash photo, the light reaches the back of the eye and lights up the blood-rich retina, and the camera records that red as red-eye. A cat gives up color for night sight: its retina is packed with rod cells, six to eight times as many as ours, and holds very few cones. Rods catch dim light and movement superbly but not color, so a cat can spot a mouse in near blackness yet cannot tell red from green as we do. Eyeshine comes in different colors, green in cats, yellow in raccoons, blue in many dogs, because the mirror itself is built from different materials, such as crystals of zinc, riboflavin or collagen, and each reflects its own band of light.

The tarsier, a mouse-sized primate of Southeast Asian forests that hunts insects by moonlight, has no mirror at all, so instead each of its eyeballs grew enormous, about 16 millimeters across and as big as its whole brain, the largest eyes for body size of any mammal. Its daytime ancestors lost the tapetum, and its kind never regained it.

Arctic reindeer live through months of dim twilight. In 2013 Stokkan and colleagues found that the reindeer's mirror changes color with the seasons, from gold in summer to deep blue in winter, the first seasonal change of its kind seen in a mammal. Blue reflects less light straight back out and scatters more of it through the retina, making the eye more sensitive in the long Arctic dusk. In the near-black middle depths of the ocean, the barreleye fish hangs still and gazes upward through a see-through forehead. Its eyes are shaped like tubes, since a tube collects much more light than a round eye of equal width.

The colossal squid has the largest eye in the history of the animal kingdom, as wide as a dinner plate, about 27 centimeters, with a lens as big as an orange. According to the vision scientists Nilsson and Warrant, the giant eye is built to spot the faint glow a hunting sperm whale, the squid's chief predator, stirs up in the plankton as it dives, an early warning in the black deep.

focusing-light-underwater.context_blurb:
Seeing clearly underwater is a different problem from seeing in air, because light behaves differently once it enters water. Fish, octopuses and some deep-sea oddities have each solved it, with eyes that work very differently from ours.

On land, most of your focusing happens at the transparent bulge on the front of your eye, the cornea, because light bends sharply as it passes from thin air into the denser eye. Underwater there is no such jump: water bends light almost as much as the cornea does, so the cornea has little left to do, and the lens must do nearly all the work. To do that heavy bending, a fish's lens is a hard, nearly perfect sphere, clear as glass and bulging out through the pupil, nothing like the soft, flattened lens of a land animal.

A human focuses by squeezing a soft lens fatter or thinner. A fish cannot reshape its rigid ball, so it slides the whole lens back and forth inside the eye, the way you would slide a projector's lens to sharpen the picture.

The puller is a small muscle called the retractor lentis, anchored to the iris. At rest the fish eye is set for close-up viewing, so to focus on something far away, the muscle hauls the lens backward, toward the retina at the back of the eye. An octopus, a mollusk more closely related to snails and clams than to fish, has almost the same eye, with a round lens that it focuses by sliding. It did not inherit that eye from a shared ancestor: octopuses and fish split more than 500 million years ago, when their ancestors had only patches of light-sensing skin, and each line invented the same camera eye entirely on its own.

A plain glass ball focuses badly, because edge rays and center rays come to a focus in different places. A fish lens beats this blur because it is graded, watery at the surface and much denser at the core, and that change from rim to center bends every ray to a single point. The German scientist Ludwig Matthiessen compared the eyes of goldfish, tuna and sharks in the 1880s and found the same number in every one. The distance from the center of the lens to the retina is about 2.5 times the lens's radius, so measuring a fish's lens tells a biologist how far behind it the retina must sit.

In the barreleye Rhynchohyalus, a pouch bulges from the side of each tube-shaped eye and throws a clear picture of the deep water beneath it onto an extra retina. Partridge and colleagues showed that a curved mirror of stacked guanine crystals does the focusing there, reflecting the image instead of bending it, which makes this fish one of only two backboned animals known to see with a mirror.

predator-eyes-vs-prey-eyes.context_blurb: Most predators have forward-facing eyes that give them good depth perception for pouncing, while most prey animals have eyes on the sides of the head that give them wide fields of view. The pattern shows up in cats versus rabbits, hawks versus doves, and across most of the vertebrate world. Look closely at the specific trade-offs between depth and breadth, and at the animals that mix the two in interesting ways.

seeing-colors-we-cant-ultraviolet.context_blurb: Many animals, including birds, bees, and a surprising number of fish and reptiles, see in parts of the spectrum that human eyes cannot pick up. The most common extension is into the ultraviolet. The interesting questions are which animals have UV vision, what they use it for, and why some human-visible flowers and bird feathers look very different when photographed in UV light.

the-mantis-shrimp-color-myth.context_blurb: The mantis shrimp has 12 to 16 types of color-receiving cells in its eyes, far more than our 3. For years, popular science articles reported that this means the shrimp sees many more colors than humans can imagine. More recent experiments have shown that the real story is subtler than that. The interesting questions are what mantis shrimp vision actually does and does not do, and why their eyes are still some of the most unusual in the whole animal kingdom.

the-strangest-eyes-in-the-animal-kingdom.context_blurb: Across the animal kingdom, eyes have been invented and reinvented many different times. Some animals see through pinholes, some through mirrors, some through compound arrays, some through transparent heads. Look closely at the strangest eye designs biologists know of, from scallops' hundreds of little blue eyes around their shells to the enormous eye of a colossal squid, and at what each design is actually doing for the animal that carries it.

anomalocaris.context_blurb:
Anomalocaris hunted the Cambrian seas more than 500 million years ago, ages before fish ruled the oceans. Its flattened fossils come from the Burgess Shale, a bed of dark stone in the Canadian Rockies of British Columbia. It was the top hunter of its world, and scientists needed nearly a century to piece its body together.

Reaching about a meter in length, Anomalocaris was the largest predator in the Burgess Shale, a giant in a world where most animals measured a few centimeters.

Its name means "odd shrimp," because in 1892 the paleontologist Joseph Whiteaves found a single detached grasping arm and took it for the curled tail of a shrimp, so the whole animal was named after a misread body part. Those two arms, jointed into about fourteen segments, reached forward from its head, and their inner edges carried rows of trident-like spikes that seized prey and swept it toward the mouth. The mouth itself was a ring of hard, overlapping plates edged with tooth-like points; seen head-on it looks like a pineapple slice, and it closed like a clamp on its victims. Anomalocaris swam by rippling sixteen flexible flaps down each side of its body in overlapping waves, steering sharp turns with a three-part tail fan.

It hunted by sight. A whole fossil eye found in 2011 in the shale of South Australia holds some 16,000 tiny lenses, giving Anomalocaris stalked compound eyes that rivaled those of a modern dragonfly. For decades nobody knew what the whole animal looked like. Before 1985 its body parts were catalogued as separate creatures: the arm as a shrimp, the body as a sponge or sea cucumber, and the round mouth, which Charles Walcott named Peytoia, as a jellyfish. Not until 1985 did Harry Whittington and Derek Briggs find the pieces joined and see a single animal. Anomalocaris shared some arthropod hallmarks, such as stalked compound eyes and segmented grasping arms, but it never grew jointed trunk limbs, the jointed legs every living crab and beetle walks or swims on, so it sits just outside the arthropods as an early side branch. Its body carried only soft swimming flaps.

For a century it was pictured prying open trilobites, and real clues pointed that way: trilobites with healed bite wounds, and fossil droppings full of crushed shell. But a 2023 computer test of the stress its arm could bear showed the slender gripping spines bending and breaking against hard shell, so scientists concluded the arms were built to catch soft-bodied prey. Whether some of its relatives tackled harder prey is still debated.

arthropleura.context_blurb:
Arthropleura was a giant millipede relative that crawled through the coal-swamp forests of what are now Europe and North America in the Carboniferous period, more than 300 million years ago and long before the first dinosaurs. It is the largest land invertebrate known to have lived, and its size has puzzled scientists ever since.

The biggest reached about 2.6 to 2.7 meters, more than 8 feet, roughly the length of a small car, and weighed around 50 kilograms. A big adult had about 28 to 32 armored segments, and each carried two pairs of legs, the signature of the millipedes, while centipedes have only one pair per segment.

Most Arthropleura fossils are not bodies but cast-off skins, like the 75-centimeter piece that fell from a cliff and landed on Howick Bay's beach in Northumberland in 2018: a section of armor the animal had shed as it grew, later filled with sand and turned to stone. The geologist Neil Davies called it a complete fluke of a discovery. Despite its size it was no hunter: with no venom fangs or grasping claws, it is now thought to have eaten like a modern millipede, munching rotting wood, fallen leaves, nuts and seeds.

Textbooks long credited the oxygen-rich Carboniferous air for giants like Arthropleura and the huge dragonfly Meganeura, but Davies argued that oxygen alone cannot explain them and pointed instead to the rich, nutrient-packed food of those ancient forests.

hallucigenia.context_blurb:
Hallucigenia was a fingernail-sized ocean animal shaped like a worm, that lived over 500 million years ago, in the Cambrian, when strange new body plans burst onto the scene. It is known from flattened fossils in Canada's Burgess Shale, and it is famous for how badly scientists first pieced it together.

For decades it was drawn upside down, with its row of stiff spines mistaken for legs. Around 1991, researchers drilled away the rock covering better fossils and uncovered a second set of soft legs tipped with claws, so the spines really stood up along its back as armor.

It was back to front as well. Scientists had taken a dark smudge at one end for its head, but a 2015 study showed the blob was fluid from decay that had oozed out of the body as it fossilized. The real head, at the other end, had a pair of eyes and a mouth ringed with tiny needle-like teeth.

Its claws revealed its relatives. Each claw is made of three cones fitted inside each other like a stack of paper cups, a structure found today only in velvet worms, soft caterpillar-like animals.

meganeura.context_blurb: Meganeura was a huge dragonfly-like insect that lived in the forests of what is now Europe during the Carboniferous period, around 300 million years ago. Its wingspan reached about two and a half feet, making it one of the largest flying insects that has ever lived. Oxygen levels in the Carboniferous atmosphere were higher than today, which may be part of why insects could grow so large. The interesting question is how an insect this size could even stay airborne.

opabinia.context_blurb: Opabinia was a strange little swimming animal from the Cambrian seas of what is now British Columbia, more than 500 million years ago. It had five eyes on top of its head and a long flexible nozzle on the front of its face. When the first careful reconstruction of Opabinia was shown at a scientific meeting in 1972, the audience reportedly laughed, assuming it was a joke. It is now one of the most famous animals of the Cambrian explosion.

trilobites.context_blurb: Trilobites were a huge group of marine arthropods that lived in the oceans for more than 270 million years, from the Cambrian explosion to the great end-Permian extinction. There were tens of thousands of species, in a huge range of sizes and shapes. Trilobites are among the most common animal fossils in the world and are a favorite of amateur paleontologists. Their eyes, their hard shells, and the way they molted have all left extraordinary records in rock.

growing-it-back-regeneration.context_blurb:
Many animals can regrow lost body parts, but how much varies enormously. Lizards regrow tails, deer regrow antlers every year, axolotls rebuild whole legs, and some flatworms and starfish can rebuild an entire body from a scrap. People can regrow only a few tissues, which is why scientists study these champions closely.

The axolotl, a Mexican salamander prized in biology labs, can lose a whole leg and grow it back in 40 to 50 days, including its bones, muscles, nerves and blood vessels, and the new leg is perfect, with no scar at all. Many lizards drop their tails to escape a predator, a trick called autotomy, and grow new ones within weeks. But X-rays show the replacement is a copy: the original tail had a chain of small bony vertebrae, while the new one is built around one unjointed tube of cartilage, with no bone. Male deer regrow a full set of antlers every year, and antler is the fastest-growing bone of any mammal. At peak summer growth, a wapiti or elk antler can lengthen by roughly an inch, about 27 millimeters, in a single day.

A sea cucumber, a soft, sausage-shaped relative of starfish, defends itself by blasting part of its own guts out of its back end to tangle or scare an attacker, and it grows the missing organs back within a few weeks. A lizard's new tail has a cost: one solid tube of cartilage cannot bend at joints the way a backbone does, so the spare is much less flexible all along its length. A deer's growing antlers are covered in velvet, a furry skin laced with nerves and blood vessels that feeds the fast-growing bone. Each late fall or winter, falling testosterone levels make the hardened antlers drop off, and the cycle starts again. Most starfish can rebuild a body only if some of the central disc remains, but a single arm of a Linckia starfish can rebuild a whole new animal. While it does, the new disc and tiny arms look like the bright head of a comet, with the old arm trailing behind like its tail, so these are called comet stars. The planarian, a freshwater flatworm no bigger than a rice grain, is the true champion: cut it into pieces, even more than a hundred, and each piece regrows into a complete worm, with a new head and brain.

The axolotl's powers go beyond limbs: it can also regrow its jaws, sections of its spinal cord, pieces of its brain and even parts of its heart, which is why labs study it in hope of repairing human spinal injuries. Scientists tie that gift to its strange life, because unlike other salamanders, which change into land animals, the axolotl never fully grows up, keeping its feathery gills and larval body for life. After it loses a leg, a bud of new cells called a blastema starts forming at the stump within the first week and goes on to rebuild the missing tissues. A planarian's secret is its neoblasts, adult stem cells that can become any body part and make up a fifth or more of its cells. Destroy them with radiation and the worm cannot regenerate and dies, yet transplanting a single neoblast back into it restores the power. A fragment as small as one 279th of a planarian can rebuild a complete worm, which is why nineteenth-century scientists described it as immortal under the knife's edge. Its regrowth is steered by a chemical signal called the Wnt pathway, which tells each cut end whether to become a head or a tail, and when scientists block that signal, a second head grows where the tail should be, making a two-headed worm. Starfish regrowth once backfired on people: in the 1960s, when crown-of-thorns starfish were killing vast stretches of Australia's Great Barrier Reef, fishermen chopped them into pieces and threw them back, which may have multiplied them rather than wiping them out.

Velvet antler grows so fast that its pattern of active genes looks more like bone cancer than normal bone, yet deer get cancer about five times less often than other mammals. Three defenses keep it in check: strengthened tumor-suppressor genes, mass cell suicide, in which up to about 64 percent of the cells in the antler's inner layer are programmed to die, and the yearly casting of the whole antler, which throws away any rogue cells.

living-fast-dying-young-the-mayflys-sing.context_blurb: Mayflies are a group of flying insects that live for years as aquatic larvae and emerge as adults for a very short period, sometimes only a single day. During that short adult life, mayflies have no working mouthparts and do nothing but mate and lay eggs. Look closely at the strange schedule of a mayfly's life and at the specific trade-offs that come with putting almost all of life into one window of time.

not-dying-of-old-age-the-immortal-jellyf.context_blurb: A tiny jellyfish called Turritopsis dohrnii, native to the Mediterranean and found around the world as a stowaway on ships, can rewind its life back to an earlier stage when it is injured or stressed. In theory, it never has to die of old age. In practice, almost all of them do get eaten or killed by disease, so the trick is more interesting biologically than it is practically. The interesting question is how the rewinding actually works at the cellular level.

the-great-migrations.context_blurb: A number of animals cover huge distances every year as part of their life cycle. Some seabirds fly nearly pole to pole, monarch butterflies migrate across generations between Mexico and Canada, wildebeest circle the Serengeti, and salmon return to the specific streams where they were born. Look closely at the different ways animals navigate and the specific pressures that make this kind of long-distance commute worth the energy.

the-oldest-animals-alive.context_blurb: Some animals are extraordinarily long-lived. Certain cold-water sharks are thought to live more than 400 years. Bowhead whales reach well over 200. Ocean quahog clams can live more than 500 years, and glass sponges may live for several thousand. Look closely at the oldest-known individuals among living animals, how researchers age them, and what they share about how biological aging can be slowed.

learning-a-voice-vocal-mimicry-and-learn.context_blurb: A small group of animals, including parrots, songbirds, mockingbirds, lyrebirds, dolphins, and even a few elephants, learn their vocal signals rather than being born knowing them. Vocal learning is actually quite rare in the animal kingdom, and it shares some surprising brain-wiring features with human speech. Look closely at the animals that have cracked the vocal-learning problem and the ways researchers test what they are actually doing with it.

making-light-bioluminescence.context_blurb: Many animals produce their own light. Fireflies flash to find mates, deep-sea anglerfish dangle glowing lures, dinoflagellates light up ocean waves, and jellyfish sparkle when disturbed. Biologists call this bioluminescence, and the chemistry behind it is surprisingly similar across very distant lineages. Look closely at the different ways animals use light and the common chemical tricks that keep showing up in nature.

recognizing-yourself-the-mirror-test.context_blurb: In a classic experiment, a researcher puts a mark on an animal and shows it a mirror. If the animal uses the mirror to notice and investigate the mark on its own body, biologists say it has passed the mirror test, which is one standard way of asking whether an animal has some sense of itself. Great apes, elephants, dolphins, orcas, magpies, and more recently a particular cleaner fish have all passed in some form. The interesting question is what the test does and does not prove.

the-waggle-dance-how-a-bee-maps-the-flow.context_blurb: When a honeybee finds a good food source, she returns to the hive and performs a specific sequence of movements on the comb that tells her nestmates where to go. Other bees are able to read those movements accurately enough to fly to the right flower patch. The behavior was decoded in the mid-twentieth century by the Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch, who later won a Nobel Prize for the work, and it remains one of the clearest examples of a non-human communication system that encodes real information.

tool-users.context_blurb: A number of animals, from chimpanzees and sea otters to crows and octopuses, use tools in the wild. Some use sticks, some use stones, some use shells, and a few even make tools from scratch rather than just picking them up. Look closely at the main tool-using species biologists study, what each one actually does, and how the definition of tool use has become more careful over the last several decades of fieldwork.

air-breathers-in-water-lungs-where-youd-.context_blurb:
Gills pull oxygen out of water, so a creature that lives in water should need nothing more. Yet whales, lungfish, bettas, beetles and even a spider all breathe air, and many of them drown if they cannot reach it. In warm, stagnant ponds, gills alone cannot gather enough oxygen, and the mammals that went back to the sea never had gills at all.

Whales descend from land mammals that walked on four legs, and they still breathe with lungs. Over millions of years a whale's nostrils drifted to the top of its head and became the blowhole, so it can breathe while the rest of its body stays underwater. The spout even tells the two great families apart: a baleen whale such as the blue whale has two blowholes side by side, while a toothed whale such as a dolphin has just a single opening. Fish found the same answer. The African lungfish, an eel-shaped fish of muddy swamps, owns a true lung and gulps air at the surface, so a lungfish kept away from the air actually drowns. The betta, or Siamese fighting fish, thrives in warm rice-paddy puddles thanks to a labyrinth organ in its head, a maze of folded, blood-rich tissue that does the job of a lung.

Breathing air brings its own puzzles. A whale breathes only by choice, opening its blowhole on purpose each time, so it can never fall fully asleep; instead it rests half its brain at a time while the other half stays awake and remembers to surface. The Amazon's electric eel has gills so feeble that it takes about 80 percent of its oxygen from air gulped into its mouth, and it must rise for a breath about every ten minutes. The great diving beetle carries its own scuba tank: as it dives it traps a bubble of air beneath its hard wing covers, held there by water-repellent hairs, and the bubble glints like liquid silver. The Galapagos marine iguana, the only lizard that grazes in the sea, dives about 15 meters to eat algae, but the cold water drains its heat, so afterward it hauls out and bakes in the sun on the black volcanic rocks until it can move well again. The diving-bell spider of Europe's ponds spins a silk dome among the water plants and fills it with air it ferries down from the surface, a shimmering bell where it spends its whole life.

Some air-breathers push the trick to extremes. When drought bakes its pool into a crust, the African lungfish digs into the mud, curls up and seals itself in a cocoon of hardened slime. In that sleep, called aestivation, it slows almost to a stop, and some lungfish have survived buried and dried out for up to four years, then swum away when the rains returned. The diving beetle's bubble is also a physical gill: as the beetle burns its oxygen, fresh oxygen diffuses into the bubble from the surrounding water, so the pond keeps topping up the tank. It cannot last forever, because nitrogen builds up in the bubble while oxygen is spent faster than the water replaces it, so the beetle must let the old bubble go and rise for a fresh supply. Cuvier's beaked whale holds the mammal diving records: it has stayed under for 3 hours and 42 minutes on a single breath, and on another dive it reached 2,992 meters, nearly 3 kilometers down.

The deepest divers store their breath somewhere surprising, because a sperm whale's lungs fill only about 3 percent of its body cavity and squeeze nearly empty under pressure. Instead the whale banks its oxygen inside its muscle, which holds about ten times as much myoglobin as human muscle; myoglobin is the oxygen-binding protein that makes red meat red, and it stains the whale's flesh almost black. In deep divers each myoglobin molecule carries a strong positive charge, so the crowded copies push apart like matching magnet poles instead of clumping. Air-breathing fish also hold a secret about our own past. For a century scientists argued whether the coelacanth, the "living fossil" rediscovered in 1938, or the lungfish was the closest living fish kin of the backboned animals on land, until whole-genome studies settled it for the lungfish. Our deepest fishy cousin is the air-gulper that sleeps out droughts in the mud.

breathing-water-how-gills-pull-oxygen-fr.context_blurb:
Fish and many other water animals breathe with gills, and water makes breathing hard. It holds far less oxygen than air, so a gill has to be a remarkable piece of plumbing: a huge, thin, blood-filled surface across which oxygen slips from water into blood. The details of that design explain how a fish lives, from a resting goldfish to a tuna that can never stop.

Beneath the stiff gill cover, or operculum, on either side of a fish's head lie neat rows of soft, red, feather-like filaments: the gills, the organs a fish uses to breathe underwater. They are vivid red because each filament is crammed with tiny blood vessels, so what you see is blood lying just beneath a wafer-thin surface, where it picks up oxygen. Even a resting fish keeps water moving: a goldfish that has stopped swimming still opens its mouth and flares its gill covers in a steady flutter, driving new water over the gills without a single stroke.

Water travels in at the mouth and out under the gill covers, and unlike lungs, where fresh and used air share the same pipe, this one-way flow means the gills never bathe in water they have already stripped of oxygen. That matters because air holds roughly thirty times more oxygen than the same volume of water, so a fish must pass an enormous amount of water over its gills just to get by. Bony fish have four pairs of gill arches lined with comb-like filaments, and the more active the fish, the richer those combs, so a tuna that swims nonstop packs far denser filaments than a bottom-dweller resting on the seafloor, because its hard-working muscles need far more surface to feed them.

Freshwater is especially poor, holding about 8 cubic centimeters of oxygen per liter against about 210 in air, so above all gills need enormous surface area, vast thin sheets where plenty of oxygen can cross into the blood at once. Inside each thin plate, or lamella, the blood runs against the flow of water outside, a design called countercurrent exchange, so at every point the blood faces water that holds a little more oxygen than it does and keeps loading along the whole plate.

If blood and water ran the same way, they would soon level out at about half the oxygen, but running them against each other lets a fish harvest about 80 to 90 percent of the oxygen in the water. A tuna swims too fast to pump with its gill covers, so it rams water through by swimming with its mouth open, and that ram ventilation binds it for life: if it stops swimming, the flow stops and it suffocates. Great white, mako and whale sharks live by the same rule. The nurse shark rests on the seafloor for hours by pumping water over its gills with its cheek muscles, and when its mouth is buried in sand, it draws water in through spiracles, small openings behind its eyes. Most amphibians trade gills for lungs as they grow, the way a tadpole becomes a frog, but Mexico's axolotl and North America's mudpuppy keep feathery external gills on their heads for life and never leave the water. Gills have a second job too: wedged among the breathing tissue are cells called ionocytes that hold the blood at the right saltiness, pumping salt out in seawater, which is saltier than a fish's blood, and pulling scarce salts in for a freshwater fish. The same gills also dump the fish's nitrogen waste as ammonia.

The African lungfish faces the opposite danger from the tuna, because its shrunken gills can no longer pull enough oxygen from water and nearly all its oxygen comes through a true lung, so if it is held below the surface, even in clean, oxygen-rich water, it suffocates. A tuna that halts will drown, and so will a lungfish that cannot reach the top.

extraordinary-hearts-and-blood.context_blurb:
Hearts and blood come in surprising forms. The octopus has three hearts and blue blood, the giraffe must push blood up a neck 2 meters long, the horseshoe crab's blue blood is prized by medicine, and the Antarctic icefish has blood as clear as water. Each odd design solves a physical problem its owner faces.

An octopus has three hearts: a pair of branchial hearts pump blood through the gills to pick up oxygen, and a third, the systemic heart, drives that fresh blood around the rest of the body. Its blood is blue, not red, because it carries oxygen with a protein built around copper instead of iron. On the African savanna the giraffe, the tallest animal alive, has the hardest pumping job of all: its heart must drive blood up a neck about 2 meters long to the brain high overhead. On Atlantic beaches a helmet-shaped living fossil with a spiked tail, a design that predates the dinosaurs, crawls ashore each spring to breed. That creature is the horseshoe crab, and medical labs collect its pale blue blood because it turns solid at once on contact with bacteria, keeping vaccines free of contamination.

Why does an octopus need separate hearts just for its gills? Loading oxygen at the gills takes a high pressure of its own, while the systemic heart supplies a different push to the body, so the gill job gets its own pumps. The metal explains the color: our hemoglobin carries oxygen on iron, which turns blood red, but the octopus's hemocyanin carries it on copper, which turns blue when it holds oxygen. Copper blood carries oxygen more weakly than ours, and the octopus pays for it in speed. When it jets through open water, its systemic heart actually stops beating, which exhausts it, so an octopus usually crawls instead.

A giraffe's blood pressure reaches about 280 over 180, roughly double a human's, enough to force blood all the way up the neck. Lowering that head to drink should send blood rushing into its skull. But valves in the veins of its neck let blood flow only one way and block the backflow, so the giraffe does not black out. The horseshoe crab's blood is worth roughly 60,000 dollars a gallon. When bacteria taint a vaccine or medicine under test, the blood clots into a gel around them and traps the contamination.

No other backboned animal lacks red blood cells and hemoglobin, the iron-based pigment that carries oxygen in our blood, the way the Antarctic icefish does. With colorless blood, it has to move enormous volumes using an outsized heart, about five times the output of a normal fish, helped by the cold, oxygen-rich water. The earthworm has no single heart at all: five pairs of muscular tubes called aortic arches encircle the forward part of its gut and squeeze in turn to push its blood along. Inside horseshoe crab blood, cells called amebocytes are packed with granules of a protein named coagulogen, and when they meet bacterial toxins, a chain reaction turns the coagulogen into the clot.

Biologists once assumed the icefish had simply switched off its hemoglobin in the cold. Reading its genome showed something more final: in 15 of the 16 species the beta-globin gene is gone entirely and the alpha-globin gene is partly deleted, so the DNA itself is missing, not merely silenced. Even with its huge heart and wide blood vessels, the icefish's blood carries less than a fifth of the oxygen that its red-blooded relatives' blood holds.

why-insects-cant-be-giant-the-tracheae-p.context_blurb: Insects breathe through a network of tiny tubes called tracheae that run from pores in the body wall directly to the tissues. The system is efficient at small sizes, but it does not scale up: the tubes have to get wider as an insect gets bigger, and at some point they take up so much room that there is nothing left for muscle. Look closely at the physics and anatomy of why no modern insect gets as big as the giant Carboniferous ones ever did.

archaeopteryx-dinosaur-becomes-bird.context_blurb:
Birds are living dinosaurs, and Archaeopteryx shows the road between the two better than almost any other fossil. This raven-sized animal lived about 150 million years ago where southern Germany now lies, and the fine Solnhofen limestone kept its bones and feathers in startling detail.

It had a wishbone and true feathers like a bird, but also a dinosaur's teeth, finger claws and a long tail of bone, a blend that marks it as a fossil caught partway through the change from one group into another over deep time. When one specimen was dug up with feathers that had left only faint traces in the stone, the first scientists to study it missed them and filed it as Compsognathus, a little two-legged dinosaur.

Because it kept its old teeth, claws and tail after gaining feathers and a wishbone, Archaeopteryx shows that the change came piece by piece, with evolution swapping one body system at a time rather than remaking the whole animal in a single leap. One superb specimen was feathered from head to foot, its legs wrapped in feathery "trousers," and since the animal flew poorly at best, the researchers concluded that feathers first evolved for warmth or showing off rather than for flight. They summed up the order of events as "first show off, then take-off."

Modern birds need a deep keel on the breastbone to hold their flight muscles, but Archaeopteryx had a flat breastbone with no keel, so the paleontologist Mark Norell judged that it probably did not fly like a bird at all and, if it really tried, might have managed about as well as a turkey. Feathers are older than flight: along the forearm of Velociraptor, a ground hunter that never flew, six bumps sit in an even row, quill knobs like the anchor points where living birds fix the shafts of their long wing feathers. Its growth was still a dinosaur's: thin slices of its bone show dense tissue with few blood vessels, the slow-growing kind seen in cold-blooded reptiles, and it took years, roughly 970 days by one estimate, to reach adult size.

In 2018 Dennis Voeten imaged the inside of its wing bones with a synchrotron X-ray beam and found thin walls threaded with blood-vessel channels like those of birds that actively flap, and the closest match was the pheasant, which flies in short powered bursts to hop over obstacles or escape danger. Yet its shoulder could not raise the wing high above its back for the modern flight stroke, so Archaeopteryx flew, but not the way any bird flies today.

our-hominin-cousins-neanderthal-and-deni.context_blurb: Modern humans are not the only humans who have lived on Earth. Neanderthals lived across much of Eurasia for hundreds of thousands of years before dying out around 40,000 years ago. Denisovans, known mostly from DNA extracted from one remote Siberian cave, lived across much of Asia at roughly the same time. Look closely at what paleontologists and geneticists have learned about these groups and the ways their DNA still shows up in people today.

tiktaalik.context_blurb: Tiktaalik was a shallow-water fish that lived in what is now Arctic Canada about 375 million years ago. It had fish features, like scales and gills, but also features of a four-limbed land animal, including a mobile neck and limb-like bones in its front fins. Tiktaalik was discovered in 2004 by Neil Shubin's team after a very careful prediction of where fossils of this kind of transitional animal should turn up. It is one of the clearest fossils of the fish-to-tetrapod transition.

whale-evolution-pakicetus-to-modern.context_blurb: Whales descend from four-legged land mammals that walked into shallow water around 50 million years ago. The fossil record now includes a long sequence of transitional forms, from Pakicetus, which still had legs and lived on land, through Ambulocetus and other walking whales, to animals that could no longer walk out of the water at all. Look closely at the stepping stones in that transition and what each fossil adds to the picture of how a land animal became a whale.

champion-jumpers.context_blurb:
Some animals are built around the jump. Tiny sap-sucking bugs, grasshoppers, ants and kangaroos all push off with forces enormous for their size. The secret, again and again, is a spring: tendons and bows of rubbery shell that store energy and give it back, because muscle on its own cannot do the job, and physics sets hard limits on how a leg can launch a body.

The flea is famous as a high-jumper, but the true insect champion is the froghopper, or spittlebug, a 6-millimeter garden bug that springs 70 centimeters into the air, over double a flea's best. Its young hide in blobs of froth on plant stems, which explains the second name. Measured in body lengths, that leap tops 100 of them, like a six-foot person clearing a stack of tall buildings.

Its jumping legs are only about half its body length and 2 percent of its mass, nowhere near enough muscle to throw it so high, so muscle first slowly bends springs inside its body, and the springs then release the energy all at once. To fire, it locks its cocked hind legs with microscopic grippy teeth, then trips the latch, and the leap goes off with an audible click. A kangaroo uses springs differently, treating its huge hind-leg tendons as pogo-stick springs that store and return energy on every bound, so its hopping gets more efficient as it speeds up: at 6 meters per second the tendons can save a red kangaroo up to about 70 percent of its energy. Dawson and Taylor found in 1973 that its oxygen use barely rises with speed. Moving slowly, a kangaroo plants its thick tail like a fifth leg, and in 2014 O'Connor and colleagues measured that the tail supplies as much forward push as the front and hind legs together.

The froghopper's spring is a curved bow of hard cuticle lined with resilin, a rubbery protein that glows bright blue under ultraviolet light, tracing exactly where the spring sits. Its launch lasts less than a thousandth of a second and accelerates it at about 5,400 meters per second squared, a jolt of roughly 400 to 550 times the pull of gravity, while a fighter pilot starts to black out near 9. In a grasshopper, two crescent-shaped struts at the knee, made of cuticle and resilin, flex and store about half the jump energy, with the big thigh muscle supplying the rest. Tiny jumpers need springs because muscle cannot contract fast enough to deliver its power in an instant, so small animals load a spring slowly and trip a latch to release it at once, a system biologists call latch-mediated spring actuation. Trap-jaw ants latch their jaws open under spring tension and can slam them against the ground to fling themselves away, and when Larabee and Suarez glued some ants' jaws shut and set them against antlions, only about a quarter of those ants escaped, 26 percent, against 60 to 79 percent for ants that could jump.

moving-without-legs.context_blurb: Many animals get around on land without any legs at all. Snakes, worms, slugs, and even certain lizards move by shaping their bodies against the ground in specific ways. Look closely at the different limbless locomotion styles biologists recognize, from the sidewinding of desert snakes to the muscular waves of earthworms, and at the surprising situations in which no legs can be better than many.

sticking-to-walls.context_blurb: Several animals can climb vertical surfaces and even walk on ceilings. Geckos, tree frogs, flies, and some spiders all stick in different ways. Geckos use microscopic ridges on their toes that take advantage of weak molecular forces; frogs use tiny wet pads; flies use sticky secretions. Look closely at the different sticking mechanisms and the problems each one has to solve, from falling off to coming unstuck again when the animal wants to move.

the-fastest-runners.context_blurb: Across the animal kingdom, some animals are built for pure speed on land. Cheetahs, pronghorns, horses, greyhounds, and ostriches all specialize in sprinting or long-distance running. Look closely at the specific body features that make an animal fast, from leg length and muscle fiber type to spine flexibility, and at the handful of species that come out at the top of each category.

deep-diving-bodies.context_blurb:
A human diver without gear is in trouble a few dozen meters down. Sperm whales, elephant seals, Weddell seals and beaked whales go hundreds or even thousands of meters deeper on one breath. To manage it, a deep diver's body has to beat crushing pressure, ration its oxygen for a very long time, and store that oxygen somewhere other than its lungs.

The sperm whale, biggest of all toothed hunters, plunges over a mile into total darkness to hunt the giant squid. The squid fights back, and whales come up with round wounds the size of saucers ringed across their skin, the marks of the giant squid's suckers. The southern elephant seal, the largest seal on Earth, hunts squid off Antarctica, can reach depths of 2,000 meters, and may stay under for as long as two hours on a single breath.

Instead of gulping a huge breath, a sperm whale empties roughly nine-tenths of the air from its lungs just before it dives, because the less gas it carries, the less there is for the pressure to squeeze or force dangerously into its body. A mile down, the water pushes down with some 200 times the surface pressure. Its flexible rib cage simply folds inward, the ribs hinging back toward the tail, and its lungs collapse flat on purpose instead of breaking.

So where does a diver keep its oxygen? Not in its lungs, as a human holding a breath does, but in its blood and in its muscles. Its muscle is packed so densely with myoglobin, a protein that grabs and stores oxygen, that the meat looks almost black instead of red. The Weddell seal of Antarctica shows how that store is rationed. It takes a last breath at a hole in the sea ice and may stay down for over an hour. As soon as it dives, its heart drops from a normal mammal's pace to just 16 beats per minute at its slowest, a slowdown called bradycardia. It also starves its skin, flippers and gut of blood, letting them go cold, and sends the oxygen-rich blood to its brain, heart and lungs, the organs that cannot do without it. When its oxygen runs low partway through the dive, the seal squeezes its spleen like a sponge, pouring a fresh supply of stored red blood cells into its bloodstream.

The deepest diver of all is Cuvier's beaked whale: in 2014 researchers off southern California followed a tagged one down to nearly 3,000 meters, about 2,992, the deepest dive ever measured for any mammal. Scuba divers who breathe compressed air can suffer the bends, when nitrogen dissolved in the blood under pressure fizzes out as bubbles. A whale's collapsed lungs stop that nitrogen from being forced into its blood in the first place. Diving muscle hides a chemical secret too. In a land mammal, myoglobin packed too tightly clumps into a toxic solid. In 2013 Mirceta and colleagues found that divers' myoglobin carries an unusually strong positive electric charge on its surface, and because like charges repel, the molecules push one another apart instead of sticking. Yet the protection is not perfect. In 2003 Jepson and colleagues examined beaked whales that had stranded in groups during naval sonar exercises and found gas bubbles spread through the soft tissues of their whole bodies, damage that experts had thought impossible in a whale. A leading idea is that the loud sonar panics the whales into surfacing too fast, and scientists still debate it.

jet-propulsion.context_blurb: Several marine animals swim by shooting water out of their bodies in short bursts. Squid, octopuses, jellyfish, scallops, and nautiluses all use jet propulsion to one degree or another. Look closely at the specific body plumbing each group uses, the trade-offs between fast jetting and slow efficient cruising, and at why jet propulsion keeps turning up in soft-bodied animals that need a sudden burst of speed.

staying-up-or-sinking.context_blurb:
Left to itself, an animal's body is usually a little denser than seawater, so it sinks. Every creature of open water must solve that problem, and the sea is full of different answers: gas, oil, chalk chambers and even chemistry.

A perch can hang motionless in mid-lake because most bony fish have a swim bladder, a gas pocket inside the body that the fish inflates to rise or shrinks to sink, so that, set just right, it neither rises nor falls. Sharks lack this organ entirely, so their dense bodies ought to drop to the seabed. A shark's lift comes from an enormous liver packed with oil lighter than seawater.

Most of that oil is squalene, a light molecule the body makes on the way to building cholesterol, and in some deep-sea sharks it fills 80 percent or more of the liver. Even so, most sharks remain slightly heavier than water and get extra lift from water flowing over their fins, the way an airplane's wings work only while it moves. A shortfin mako would slowly sink if it ever stopped swimming. The cuttlefish chose a stiff solution. Its buoyancy tank, the flat white cuttlebone that washes up on beaches, is almost all chalk, about 95 to 97 percent aragonite, divided into hundreds of tiny chambers that the animal floods with fluid to sink or fills with gas to rise. Even fish eggs need help. About 70 percent of ocean fish release floating eggs, and many of those eggs carry a droplet of oil that keeps them riding near the sunlit surface, where the young will find food.

Gas has a weakness: it swells and shrinks with pressure. When an angler reels a rockfish up too fast from 300 or 400 feet down, the falling pressure lets its swim bladder balloon from the size of a thumb to the size of a party balloon, pushing the fish's stomach into its mouth. Herring, carp and eels have a safety valve, a duct running from the bladder to the gut. These fish can burp gas out through it and climb quickly without bursting the bladder, while a perch or bass, its bladder sealed, would rupture if it rose too fast. Thousands of meters down, gas fails entirely, so deep-sea fish such as the orange roughy and the coelacanth fill their bladders with oil or wax. Oil is almost impossible to compress, so it keeps the same volume under crushing pressure and gives steady lift where a gas bladder would be squeezed flat. The sperm whale's blocky head holds up to 1,900 liters of waxy spermaceti, and one leading idea says chilling the wax would make the whale sink and warming it would help it rise. Many researchers doubt this, noting that the temperature change would barely shift its buoyancy, and they see the head mainly as an echolocation organ, a kind of sonar. The debate is not settled. In the dim middle depths, the see-through glass squid fills one huge body chamber with a watery solution of ammonium chloride, lighter than seawater, which can make up half or more of its body mass and holds it up with no gas and no swimming.

The nautilus carries the oldest design of all: a coiled shell divided by inner walls into sealed chambers of gas, the same rig the extinct ammonites used for hundreds of millions of years. To rise, it does not add gas; it slowly pumps liquid out of a chamber through the siphuncle, a living tube that threads through every chamber, and gas expands into the space left behind.

the-tuna-body-plan-thunniform-swimming.context_blurb: A specific streamlined body shape, with a crescent-shaped tail, has evolved in several different fast-swimming marine predators, including tunas, mackerels, swordfish, mako sharks, and even some extinct marine reptiles. Biologists call it the thunniform body plan. Look closely at the hydrodynamics behind sustained high-speed swimming in the open ocean, and at why so many unrelated animals have ended up looking so similar to one another below the waist.

ears-at-the-extremes.context_blurb:
Animal ears can do things no human ear can. Some pick up sounds far too high for us to hear, some find a mouse in total darkness, and some are so tiny they seem impossible. For owls, moths, bats and one small fly, a single faint sound can mean dinner or death.

In a pitch-black barn a barn owl can drop from the rafters and pin a mouse on the first try without ever seeing it, because it hunts by hearing alone, homing in on the faint rustle of the mouse.

Its flat, saucer-shaped face is a working instrument. The ring of stiff feathers around it, the facial ruff, works like a satellite dish, collecting faint sounds and reflecting them toward the owl's ear openings.

In 1971 Roger Payne tested a trained barn owl in a totally dark room. It struck not only live mice but a mouse-sized wad of paper dragged across dry leaves. The paper gave off no body heat and could not be seen, so its rustle was the only clue, which ruled out sight and heat sensing and left sound alone. The owl's strikes landed within one degree of the target, the most precise sound-finding ever measured in a land animal. In the northern forests lives the great gray owl, which has the largest face disc of all owls, and in winter it listens for voles tunneling beneath the snow, then punches down through as much as 18 inches of snow to seize prey it never sees.

Hunters are listened for, too. Many night-flying moths have the simplest ears in nature: a thin patch of skin connected to as few as one to four nerve cells. Those ears are tuned to one sound, the ultrasonic sonar calls of a hunting bat, and when the calls arrive, the moth swerves or tumbles out of the sky. The tiger moth Bertholdia trigona goes further and fights back, firing about 4,500 ultrasonic clicks a second. The clicks drown the bat's returning echoes in static, the first proven case of sonar jamming in nature, and attacking bats often break off.

Snow refracts sound as a lens bends light, so to a great gray owl a vole can seem up to 5 degrees away from where it really is, an acoustic mirage. Just before it dives, the owl hovers in place on beating wings, probably to fix the vole's true position from the angle where the error is smallest. Some moths beat sonar with their coats. Their microscopic wing scales act as a natural sound-absorbing material, soaking up as much as 72 percent of the ultrasound that strikes them, so almost no echo returns and the bat sweeps past. The highest bat calls reach about 212 kilohertz, yet in one study the ear of the greater wax moth still responded at about 300 kilohertz, far beyond any bat.

The parasitic fly Ormia ochracea finds crickets by their chirps so it can lay its eggs on them, but its two eardrums sit only about half a millimeter apart, so the chirp arrives at the nearer one only about one or two microseconds sooner. In 1995 Miles, Robert and Hoy found the fix: a stiff bridge joins the two eardrums and pivots in the middle like a see-saw, magnifying that tiny difference into a movement the nerves can read. The fly can point to a chirp about as accurately as a human can.

echolocation-built-twice.context_blurb:
Echolocation means hunting and finding your way by sound: an animal calls out and reads the echoes that bounce back. Bats, toothed whales such as dolphins and sperm whales, and a few cave birds all do it. Bats and whales sit on distant branches of the mammal tree, yet each invented this sonar separately, one of nature's best examples of convergent evolution.

A bat hunting on a moonless night cannot see the moth in front of it. Instead it gives out high-pitched cries, mostly too high for human ears, and builds a picture of the moth from the shape of the echoes that return. The oilbird of northern South America does something similar in the black caves where it lives, clicking with its tongue. Its clicks are around 2,000 cycles per second, low enough for people to hear, and that lower pitch gives a blurrier picture than a bat's ultrasound, missing fine detail.

Dolphins echolocate in murky water where their eyes are nearly useless. They send out rapid clicks, and the melon, a lens of fatty tissue in the forehead, focuses them forward in a narrow beam, the way a flashlight aims its light. The echoes come back by another route: fat inside the lower jaw carries them through a thin plate of bone, the pan bone, to the inner ear.

A searching bat clicks slowly and steadily. In the last split second before it grabs a moth, the clicks speed up into a feeding buzz of up to 200 a second, giving rapid updates that fix the prey's exact position for the catch. When biologists compared the gene for prestin, a protein that powers the sound-sensing hair cells of the inner ear, they found it had changed in the same direction in echolocating bats and in toothed whales: the same molecular answer, reached twice, independently.

The match goes all the way down: at a single spot in that protein, both echolocating bats and toothed whales carry the identical swap of one building block for another, asparagine replaced by threonine, which is tied to sharper hearing of high notes. The sperm whale takes echolocation to extremes. Hunting squid a kilometer down, it makes clicks of nearly 230 decibels, the loudest sound of any animal. Those clicks are produced by the spermaceti organ, a huge structure that fills the whale's blocky head. In 1998 Simmons, Ferragamo and Moss found that a big brown bat can tell apart two echoes arriving only about 2 microseconds apart, so it can sense two surfaces just 0.3 millimeters apart as separate, a gap shorter than a single wavelength of its call.

Inside the sperm whale's head, the sound begins at two lip-shaped flaps near the front of the skull, nicknamed monkey lips, as air is pushed past them. That first pulse then bounces back and forth between two air sacs inside the head, and with each pass a slice of its energy escapes forward as a click. The horseshoe bat, named for the horseshoe-shaped flap of skin around its nose, works differently. It holds its call on one steady tone, and its ears are tuned to exactly that note. As it flies toward a target, its own speed raises the pitch of the echo. So the bat lowers the pitch of the call it sends out, keeping the echo on the note its ears expect. That steady tone lets it find a moth hidden in a bush, because the moth's beating wings put a quick, rhythmic flicker, or glint, on the returning echo, a sign of living prey. Some moths fight back. A desert tiger moth, Bertholdia trigona, answers with up to 4,500 clicks a second of its own, which jams the bat's sonar and spoils the attack, cutting the bat's success about tenfold.

When did bats start echolocating? Onychonycteris finneyi, the earliest bat known from a good fossil, lived 52 million years ago and already had full wings, yet its cochlea, the coiled hearing organ, was small as in a fruit bat, not enlarged like an echolocator's. In 2008 Nancy Simmons and her colleagues argued that this shows bats flew first and evolved echolocation later. The debate is not closed: a 2010 look at the same skull suggested it may have echolocated after all.

infrasound-and-hearing-through-the-feet.context_blurb: Several large animals, including elephants, giraffes, and some whales, communicate using very low-frequency sounds that travel through air or ground. In elephants, the low frequencies even travel through the ground as vibration, and the animal picks them up through sensitive pads in its feet. Look closely at the specific low-frequency channels different animals use and the surprising distances that these signals can cover.

the-lateral-line-feeling-the-water-move.context_blurb: Fish and some amphibians have a specialized sense called the lateral line, running down each side of the body. It is tuned to pick up water movement, which lets a fish feel other animals, obstacles, and currents without seeing or hearing them. The interesting questions are how the lateral line works, why it is so useful for a schooling fish, and the ways it is being studied as a model for underwater sensing in robots.

endurance-aloft.context_blurb:
Some birds practically live in the sky. Albatrosses, swifts, frigatebirds, terns and godwits fly for days, months or even years with hardly a rest, and some of them sleep on the wing. Each of these long-haul fliers has found its own way to cross huge distances that would kill an ordinary bird.

A wandering albatross of the Southern Ocean has the broadest wingspan of all living birds, up to about 3.5 meters from tip to tip, wide enough to span a car. A common swift, a small dark bird of European skies, eats, drinks, mates and sleeps in the air, and once a youngster flies from its rooftop nest, it can stay aloft for about 10 months straight, never once touching down. The Arctic tern follows summer from one end of the Earth to the other: it raises its chicks in the Arctic, flies to Antarctica for the southern summer and back again, and covers about 70,900 kilometers a year, farther than any other animal.

An albatross can glide for hours or days without a flap because a tendon in each shoulder locks its outstretched wing in place, holding it open with no muscle effort. While fetching food for its chick, a parent can travel 10,000 to 15,000 kilometers in 10 to 20 days. Some albatrosses go so far that they fly right around the entire Southern Ocean, circling the bottom of the world. The tern's polar commute earns it another record: chasing summer from pole to pole, it spends about two-thirds of its life in continuous daylight and sees more sunlight in a year than any other animal. In October 2022 a five-month-old bar-tailed godwit, a long-billed shorebird, left Alaska wearing a satellite tag. It flew nonstop for eleven days and one hour, with no food, water or rest, all the way to Tasmania, about 13,560 kilometers away, the longest nonstop flight ever recorded for a bird.

What would ground an ordinary bird on such journeys is the energy it burns by flapping without a break, and each of these fliers dodges that cost with a wind-riding trick. Textbooks explain the albatross's trick, dynamic soaring, by the wind gradient: the wind moves slower close to the water and faster higher up, so the bird rises into the wind along a wave front, turns, and swoops downwind through the hollow between waves, gaining speed from the difference. Godwits prepare for their ocean crossing by rebuilding their bodies, shrinking the liver, kidneys and gut by up to a quarter to make room for fat and to enlarge the heart and flight muscles, because guts do not fly.

Great frigatebirds, black seabirds of the tropics with forked tails and seven-foot wings, cannot rest on the sea, because their feathers are not waterproof and would soak through. Henri Weimerskirch's team tracked them and found that they fly straight into towering cumulus clouds and ride the updrafts nearly 4,000 meters up, then glide long distances back down without flapping. They can stay aloft for up to two months. They even sleep on the wing, one half of the brain at a time. When a frigatebird circles on rising air, the waking half is the one linked to the eye facing into the turn, so it keeps watching where it is going. Niels Rattenborg's team fitted nesting frigatebirds with tiny brainwave recorders and found they slept in flight, mostly around sunset, but only about 42 minutes a day, a small fraction of what they sleep on land.

The textbook story of the albatross is now disputed. In 2013 Gottfried Sachs reconstructed real albatross flights from GPS and motion sensors and found that the wind gradient contributes almost nothing. In his data most of the free energy comes in the upper turn of each loop, at the moment the bird wheels from flying into the wind to flying with it. Each loop stayed within 15 meters of the sea and lasted about 10 seconds, and scientists still argue over where in the cycle the gain really happens.
