flight-evolved-four-separate-times.context_blurb:
True flight means flapping your way off the ground and staying aloft under your own power, and it is rare. Flying squirrels, colugos, gliding lizards and flying fish only glide, falling in style. In the whole history of life, unrelated animals invented powered flight from scratch only a handful of times, each building its wings in a different way.

Among mammals, only bats truly fly: a colugo of Southeast Asian rainforests can leap and coast a long way on a flap of skin, but it cannot climb through the air as a bat does. Insects built flight in a way nothing else has, because their wings are outgrowths of the body wall, sprouting straight out of the back rather than rebuilt from legs, which is why a dragonfly keeps all six legs and still flies.

Powered flight evolved four times, in insects, pterosaurs, birds and bats, and none of them inherited it from a flying ancestor. Insects came first: winged insects were already flying about 325 million years ago, long before any animal with a backbone took to the air. In the Late Triassic, more than 220 million years ago, the pterosaurs, long-jawed reptiles with leathery wings, became the first vertebrates ever to truly fly, beating the earliest birds by more than 60 million years.

Each flier built its wing differently. A bat's wing is a web of skin spread between its fingers, so its order name, Chiroptera, is Greek for "hand-wing." A pterosaur's skin wing hung from a single, enormously long fourth finger, longer than its whole forearm, reaching down to its legs. The biggest of them, Quetzalcoatlus, cruised over North America about 70 million years ago, as tall as a giraffe with wings 33 to 36 feet across, the biggest creature ever to fly. A bird spreads feathers over its whole arm, powered by huge chest muscles. Those muscles are anchored to the keel, a deep blade of bone jutting from the breastbone, so a strong flier like a pigeon has a big keel, while a flightless ostrich has almost none.

Oddly, both of a bird's big flight muscles sit low on its chest. The pectoralis pulls the wing down for the power stroke. The supracoracoideus raises it again for the recovery stroke: its tendon runs up through a tunnel of bone over the shoulder, like a rope over a pulley, so a chest muscle can pull the wing upward. These three groups are only distant relatives, yet all of them rebuilt the same starting part, the forelimb they all got from a common four-footed ancestor, and each stretched different bones of it. Pterosaurs stretched a single finger and birds the whole arm. A bat stretched four of its finger bones, and if you hold its wing up to the light you can see the four long bones spreading through the skin like umbrella ribs.

How did a giant pterosaur as tall as a giraffe get off the ground? Birds take off by leaping from their legs, but Michael Habib saw that in pterosaurs the upper arm bone is much tougher than the thigh bone, the opposite of the pattern in birds. In 2008 he proposed that the giant pole-vaulted off all four limbs, crouching and hurling itself upward on its folded, powerful arms before its wings snapped open. Others still argue that the very largest pterosaurs could barely fly. Insects faced their own limit. A housefly's wings flap roughly 200 times each second, too fast for a nerve to send one signal per stroke. Its secret is a pair of opposing muscle sheets in the thorax: when one contracts it stretches the other, which fires back after a tiny delay, so the thorax rings like a struck bell and a single nerve pulse keeps dozens of wingbeats going.

gliding-not-flying.context_blurb:
Many animals sail between trees without true flight. Flying squirrels, colugos, Draco lizards, flying frogs, flying snakes and flying fish all glide: they cannot climb through the air by flapping, but they turn a fall into a long, steered journey. Each of them evolved its gliding gear separately, out of a different part of the body.

A flying squirrel launches from a tree at night and opens the furry membrane that joins its front and back legs. With no wings to beat, it steers and brakes with its flattened, bushy tail, which works as a rudder, and it can also bank by lowering one arm. In Southeast Asian rainforests, a lizard about as long as a pencil, nicknamed the flying dragon, glides between tree trunks on bright, fan-like wings: it is the Draco, and it usually glides about 10 meters, sometimes as far as 60. The paradise tree snake has no limbs at all, yet it glides 10 meters or more by flaring its ribs to flatten its round body into a wide, slightly hollow ribbon.

The Draco's wings are spread by four to seven greatly elongated ribs, which fan outward like umbrella ribs and are worked by muscles that other lizards use only for breathing. In the forests of Borneo, a bright green frog named after the naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace escapes danger by leaping into the air and sailing more than 15 meters on the huge webbing between its fingers and toes, four orange-and-black parachutes at once. The champion glider among mammals is the colugo of Southeast Asia, whose gliding membrane is the most complete of any animal, stretching from the neck out to every fingertip and toe tip and back along the whole tail. One colugo covered about 150 meters in a single glide.

Jake Socha of Virginia Tech spent more than twenty years on flying snakes and created the first realistic computer model of a snake gliding, and his virtual experiments showed that its S-shaped wriggling in midair keeps it from tumbling and stretches its glide. Line the gliders up and a pattern appears: every one of them built its wing from a different part of the body, a skin flap in the squirrel and colugo, giant fins in the flying fish, ribs in the Draco, a flattened body in the snake and webbed feet in the frog, yet they all reach the same result. Gliding has evolved again and again, a case of convergent evolution. People nickname the colugo the flying lemur, but it neither flies nor is a lemur: DNA shows its closest living relatives are the primates, the group that includes monkeys and people, not the bats some scientists had guessed. A flying squirrel has its own refinement. A rod of cartilage at its wrist swings out to stretch its membrane beyond the reach of its arm bones, and the tips curl upward. Wind studies showed that those upturned tips cut the drag of air swirling off the wingtips, just like the winglets on an airliner.

Gliding is ancient. In 2017 scientists described Maiopatagium and Vilevolodon, small furred creatures from Jurassic forests near Beijing, when dinosaurs still ruled. They were not true mammals but early relatives on the line that led to mammals. Their fossils preserve gliding membranes, proof that mammal ancestors were gliding roughly 100 million years before the first modern gliding mammals.

hovering-in-place.context_blurb: A handful of animals, hummingbirds, hoverflies, dragonflies, and some hawks, can hold their position in the air without any forward motion. Hovering costs a lot more energy than regular flight and demands very specific wing kinematics. Look closely at the different hovering techniques animals use, from the figure-eight stroke of a hummingbird to the fast flutter of a hoverfly, and the physics that explains why not every flier can do it.

animals-that-generate-electricity.context_blurb:
A handful of fish carry living batteries inside their bodies. In the murky Amazon the electric eel can knock a horse off its feet, and in the sea the torpedo ray stuns its prey with a jolt of its own making. These animals make power from muscle, and they use it to hunt and to defend themselves.

Despite its name, the electric eel belongs to the knifefish family rather than the eels, and its closest familiar cousins are catfish and carp, far nearer kin than the moray. Its power comes from electrocytes, flat cells made from the kind of cell that in other animals merely twitches a muscle, and roughly 6,000 of them sit end to end in each stack like batteries wired in series, with about 35 stacks side by side down each flank.

For two centuries scientists recognized only a single electric eel, until a 2019 study of 107 specimens divided it into three species, and the new Volta's electric eel fired 860 volts, the most powerful jolt yet recorded from a living creature and well past the old record of 650. It also fights smart. The biologist Kenneth Catania filmed eels with high-speed cameras and saw that an eel curls its body around struggling prey, bringing its positive head and negative tail together, which at least doubles the shock in an "electric embrace" that drives the prey's muscles to exhaustion.

In 1800 the explorer Alexander von Humboldt described eels leaping from a pool to attack horses, a tale mocked for two centuries until Catania filmed it in 2016: out of the water, an eel presses its chin against the threat so the full jolt drives straight into the body instead of spreading out and weakening through the water. The torpedo ray, a flat fish of the sea, keeps its two kidney-shaped electric organs inside its broad pectoral fins, the wide "wings" of its body, and the great torpedo can deliver about 220 volts, enough to knock down a person. Strangely, the eel's current is small. Its blast is high voltage but low current, peaking near 1 ampere, about one tenth of what a household socket carries; the danger is that high voltage pushing current across a body in rapid volleys of up to 500 pulses a second, each lasting about two thousandths of a second.

Evolution invented this weapon more than once. Electric organs arose separately at least six times in fishes, from the eel to the torpedo ray to the elephantnose fish, and a 2014 genome study found that each unrelated lineage reached into the same genetic toolbox, switching on the same genes and developmental pathways to turn muscle cells into electrocytes.

electroreception-reading-the-body-electr.context_blurb:
Every living animal leaks a faint electric field: each heartbeat and muscle twitch sends a tiny current into the water around it. Sharks, rays, the platypus and certain fish can feel those fields, a sense called electroreception. It lets them find prey hidden from eyes, nose and ears, and some animals even make electric fields of their own.

A flounder buried in the sand is invisible and gives off no scent a shark can follow, but its beating heart and twitching muscles still leak faint electricity into the seawater, and the shark homes in on that and digs the fish out. Adrianus Kalmijn proved it by burying electrodes in sand: sharks dug up the wires and ignored a dead fish nearby.

Cameras fixed to great whites caught something that looks reckless: in the final instant before biting a thrashing seal, the shark shuts its eyes to protect them and completes the strike blind, steering by its electric sense alone. The platypus goes further: diving for food on a dark river bottom, it seals its eyes, ears and nostrils shut and hunts with about 40,000 electroreceptors scattered over its rubbery bill, which pick up the muscle signals of hidden prey.

The platypus bill also carries push-rod sensors that feel pressure. When a shrimp flicks its tail, the electric signal races through the water faster than the pressure wave and reaches the bill a split second earlier, and the platypus times the gap between the two to judge how far away the shrimp is. In muddy, pitch-dark rivers, the elephantnose fish and the knifefish cannot count on prey leaking much electricity. Instead each one makes its own weak electric field with an organ in its tail and feels how nearby objects bend that field, a kind of living radar. When two knifefish meet with fields at nearly the same frequency, the signals interfere, so within milliseconds each fish shifts its own frequency away from the other's, a reflex called the jamming avoidance response. Insects have the sense too: a 2013 study by Clarke's team showed that bumblebees detect the weak static charge carried by flowers through their body hairs, which bend in the charge's presence.

A shark's electric sense lives in the ampullae of Lorenzini, pores packed with a see-through jelly that conducts the signal inward. In 2016 Josberger and colleagues found that this jelly, about 97 percent water, conducts protons better than any other biological material ever tested, coming within about 40 times of Nafion, the best proton-conducting plastic engineers have made for fuel cells. Sharks and skates, which are flat relatives of rays shaped like kites, build their electric sense from the same kind of cell, and both start each signal through the same calcium channel. In 2018 Bellono, Leitch and Julius found that the difference lies in a second channel: sharks add one that makes the cell fire sharp, repeated spikes, ideal for catching a prey's twitch, while skates use one that produces soft, finely graded ripples, better for reading the weak signals of another skate seeking a mate.

navigating-by-earths-magnetic-field.context_blurb: A number of animals, from pigeons and migratory songbirds to sea turtles, salmon, and even some insects, navigate using Earth's magnetic field. The field varies in predictable ways over the surface of the planet, which gives migrating animals a built-in map. The interesting questions are how different animals detect magnetism, where researchers think the receptors sit, and why the physics behind the sense is still an active research mystery.

dunkleosteus.context_blurb:
Dunkleosteus was a giant armored fish the length of a bus that ruled the seas of the Late Devonian period, roughly 380 to 360 million years ago, a time called the Age of Fishes. It belonged to the placoderms, an extinct group of "plate-skinned" fish, and it was the top predator of its world.

Its head and shoulders were cased in thick, interlocking plates of bone, fitted together like tank armor. Every placoderm died out in the extinction that ended the Devonian, about 359 million years ago. For a fish that bit harder than a great white shark, it had a strange mouth. Dunkleosteus had no teeth at all; instead, the front edges of its jaw bones grew into self-sharpening bony blades.

A great white bites with about 4,000 newtons. When Anderson and Westneat built a model of Dunkleosteus jaws in 2007, they found it focused about 5,300 newtons right at the tip of the blade, enough to cut through armor and bone. It used that bite even on its own kind. In 2016 Hall and colleagues described punctures and scrapes on Dunkleosteus head plates that match the bladed jaws of another Dunkleosteus, evidence that it attacked and ate members of its own kind. Its fossils also turn up beside tight masses of fish bone and half-broken prey, some of them containing teeth of Orodus, a relative of sharks. Paleontologists read these clumps, called boluses, as material Dunkleosteus vomited back up because it could not digest bone and other hard parts. They give a rare look at the menu of an animal 360 million years dead.

For years artists showed it feeding by suction, its jaws snapping open in about 20 milliseconds to suck in prey. In 2025 Engelman and colleagues argued that the real skull was built with much more cartilage than the old model allowed, and that its cleaver-like blades look like those of predators that bite with a wide gape and tear their prey into pieces. How it really fed is still debated.

helicoprion.context_blurb:
Helicoprion was a shark-like predator of the Permian seas, roughly 290 to 270 million years ago, long before the first dinosaurs. For over a century it was known almost entirely from one strange fossil, a tightly coiled spiral, and nobody could agree where on the animal that spiral belonged.

The spiral is made of teeth, a whorl of them set like the blade of a saw and wound like a clock spring, which is why the name Helicoprion means "spiral saw" in Greek.

For a hundred years scientists argued over where it went. In 2013 Leif Tapanila's team CT-scanned a well-preserved fossil and found the whorl coiled inside the lower jaw, at the back of the mouth near the jaw joint. Why had no one found the rest of the animal? Like sharks, Helicoprion had a skeleton of cartilage, which rots away instead of fossilizing, so the hard tooth whorl was almost the only part that survived.

The whorl held every tooth the animal ever grew, because it never shed one. New teeth sprouted at the front, and the older, worn teeth rolled inward toward the center of the coil, so the tiny innermost teeth are the ones it grew as a baby. The scan of the skull brought another surprise: apart from its teeth, Helicoprion was built like the ratfishes and chimaeras, not like a shark. A 2015 study by Ramsay and colleagues showed that the jaw worked like a circular saw. As the lower jaw rotated shut, the foremost teeth of the whorl hooked prey and dragged it inward, the middle teeth pierced and cut, and the rear teeth pushed the food toward the throat. It probably sliced through soft prey such as squid.

megalodon.context_blurb: Megalodon was a huge shark that lived in oceans around the world from about 23 to 3.6 million years ago. It is almost certainly the largest shark that ever lived, with teeth more than seven inches long. Megalodon is known mostly from its teeth, which are abundant in Miocene and Pliocene sediments, and from a handful of vertebrae. The interesting questions are what paleontologists have figured out about its size, ecology, and why it went extinct, as well as what pop culture tends to get wrong about it.

ichthyosaur.context_blurb: The ichthyosaurs were a group of large marine reptiles that lived in the oceans for most of the Mesozoic, from about 250 to 90 million years ago. They were shaped like dolphins or tuna, with streamlined bodies and vertical tail flukes, but they were reptiles, not fish or mammals. Ichthyosaurs are a textbook case of convergent evolution, and the first scientifically described one was found by Mary Anning on the English coast in the early 1800s.

mosasaur.context_blurb: Mosasaurs were a group of huge marine reptiles that lived in the oceans from about 100 million to 66 million years ago, dying out at the same mass extinction that killed the non-bird dinosaurs. They were long, snake-headed, flipper-driven predators, with jaws built like a snake's for swallowing large prey. The interesting questions are where mosasaurs fit in the reptile family tree, how big they got, and what has been learned from well-preserved skeletons in Kansas, the Netherlands, and Morocco.

plesiosaur.context_blurb: The plesiosaurs were a group of large marine reptiles that lived in the oceans for most of the Mesozoic. They had two body shapes: a short-necked, big-headed form sometimes called the pliosaurs, and a long-necked, small-headed form that gave the whole group its popular image. The long-necked plesiosaur body is often the inspiration behind sea-monster illustrations, from the Loch Ness monster to many cartoons. The interesting question is how plesiosaurs actually lived and swam.

scent-trails-and-the-moth-that-smells-a-.context_blurb: Many animals, from ants to moths to mammals, communicate with chemical trails and plumes. A male silk moth can detect the scent of a female from several kilometers away using a tiny number of specialized receptors on his huge feathered antennae. Ants lay down pheromone trails to lead nestmates to food. Look closely at the chemistry of scent communication, the specific sensory organs animals use to pick up these cues, and the surprising distances a scent can carry a message across still air.

super-smellers.context_blurb: Some animals have senses of smell much more powerful than ours. Bloodhounds, bears, elephants, moths, and sharks are all famous for exceptional olfaction. The record-holder, by some measures, is the African elephant. The interesting questions are how a sense of smell is measured, which animals come out on top, and what an exceptional sense of smell actually buys an animal in the wild.

tasting-with-the-whole-body.context_blurb: Several animals have taste receptors on parts of their bodies that no vertebrate textbook would call obvious. Catfish taste with much of their outer surface; octopus arms taste with their suckers; butterflies taste with their feet. Look closely at the animals that have moved chemical sensing out of the mouth, what each one uses that distributed taste for, and the different ways the sensory tissue is wired.

feeling-in-the-dark-the-touch-specialist.context_blurb:
Where eyes are useless, in black soil or murky water, some animals read the world by touch. Moles, seals, manatees and naked mole-rats carry touch organs so sensitive that they work almost like eyes, and some of these animals can feel, decide and act faster than you can blink.

In the wet, dark soil of eastern North American wetlands digs a small mammal with the strangest face on Earth. It is the star-nosed mole: around its nostrils sits a ring of 22 pink, fleshy tentacles, and despite its looks the star is not for smelling at all but is the most sensitive touch organ known in any mammal.

Packed with more than 25,000 tiny touch sensors, the star lets the mole identify a worm and swallow it in about 120 milliseconds, roughly a quarter of a second, a world record for a feeding mammal. Harbor seals hunt in murky coastal water by feel. In Georg Dehnhardt's 2001 experiment, a blindfolded seal followed the invisible wake a fish had left, its swirling trail of disturbed water, sensing it with its whiskers alone. With its whiskers masked, the seal would not even begin to search. A manatee sorts water plants in cloudy water with about 600 stiff bristles on its face, which it works like fingers. Researchers judge that touch to be at least as fine as an elephant feeling with the tip of its trunk.

A naked mole-rat, a wrinkled, nearly hairless rodent of East African desert tunnels, has rows of stiff sensory hairs along its sides and tail that work as feelers. Thanks to them it can run backward through its tunnels as fast and as surely as it runs forward, useful where there is no room to turn around. When Kenneth Catania studied high-speed film of the mole at work, he saw that the star never glides smoothly across the soil. It dabs 10 to 15 spots every second, jumping from point to point the way our eyes flick across a scene in quick darts called saccades, so Catania called the star a "tactile eye."

seeing-heat-the-pit-vipers-infrared-eye.context_blurb: A handful of snakes, including pit vipers and some boas and pythons, can see the heat given off by warm-blooded prey. They do it with specialized pit organs on the sides of their faces, which work like infrared cameras. Look closely at the way these pit organs feed their signals into the snake's brain, how the two sides combine to give the snake something close to a thermal image of its surroundings, and the limits of this sense.

pterosaur-quetzalcoatlus.context_blurb: Quetzalcoatlus was a huge pterosaur that lived in what is now Texas at the end of the age of the dinosaurs, about 68 to 66 million years ago. Pterosaurs are an extinct group of winged animals that were close cousins of the dinosaurs rather than true dinosaurs themselves. Quetzalcoatlus was one of the largest animals that has ever taken to the air. Modern paleontology has had to carefully work out how such a huge animal could have taken off at all, and what it was doing on the ground when it was not aloft.
